JOHN BARLEYCORN'S DIARY. AN UNCOLOURED PICTURE. John Barleycorn walked oulr one morn While th' dew clung weet to th' ripenin corn; He sang reet cheerily, dud John, An' fooak o' wondered wod were on. One says to him, "Theaw'rt early eawt, Id's soon for thee to be aheawt." "The birds come eawt ere th' worms be gone, Aw'm gooin' 0' huntin' loos," says John. An' deawn bi' th' wood 'walked Harry Hood; Nooan liked ale moor then Harry dud; Bud neaw he'd settled deawn to wark, He sung as merry as a lark. He'd med a vow he'd drink no moor, Nor be the for) he'd bin befoor. "Just wait till we pass th' public yon; Aw think aw've fun a mate," says John. "Here, Harry, let's co' here an' sup, • A drop ov ale 'II set tho up." "Oh reet," says Harry, "as it's thee: To tell tho th' truth aw do feel dree." They supped a while, an' John says "Well, Thall never leove mo to rnisell." "Now," Harry says, "Awl! werk to-morn, Thou'rt a rare old friend, John Barleycorn." Hood sheawts " Hurray "—he feels so llaY ' At sich a lucky holiday; John Barleycorn a blow dealt eawt As med Hood's senses reel quite eawt. " Ged whoatn. the drunken loo," says he,. "There's nowt bud pies 'd step wi' thee. Thy hey'd 'll werch reet weel i'th morn, Thal' remember owd John Barleycorn." John went eawt, an' looked abeawt ; He spied a farmer hale an' steawt. He'd done a rare good trade thad day l' horses, cattle. ooats, an' hay. "Here," says the tempter;"Come me, We'll hey a day o' mirth an' glee; Moor then tha's hed sin' tha were born; Come, sit deawn wi' John Barleycorn!" Wl' no alarm at ony harm This victim took his tempter's arm. He went away so drunk thad day, Th' owd farmer couldn'd see his way. John Barleycorn laughed at his plight; He laughed so loud 'at th' hoes' took fright. Id master were fun killed i'th' morn; He were murdered bi' John Barleycorn. He'd bait to draw booth High an' Low,— He tackled th' better, end an' o'— VVi' costly wines he sterted th' game, Then robbed their money an' good name. Fro' palaces he took his slaves, Then landed 'em i' pauper's graves. That's one day's werk; one page aw've torn Fro' th' diary o' John Barleycorn.
RARLES LANCASTER.

HOCSEHOLO ARRANGEMENTS THREE CENTURIES AGO.— What would servants in the present day say to such a code of rules and regulations as was adopted 300 years ago in the household of Sir J. Harrington, who is well known as the translator of Ariosto ? A servant absent from prayers to be fined 2d.; for uttering an oath, Id.; and the same sum for leaving a door open; a fine of 2d.. from Lady Dar to Michaelmas, for all who are in bed after seven or out after nine; a fine of Id. for any beds unmade, fire unlit, or candle-box uncleaned after eight; a fine of 4d. for any man detected teaching the children obscene words; a fine of id. for any man waiting with- out a trencher, or who is absent at a meal; for any one breaking any of the butler's glass, 12d.; a fine of 2d. for any one who. has not laid the table for dinner by half- past ten, or the supper by six; a fine of 4d. for any one absent a day without leave: for any man striking another, a fine of id.; for any follower visiting the cook, Id.; a fine of id. for any man appearing in a foul skirt, broken hose, untied shoes, or torn doublet; a fine of Id. for any stranger's room left for four hours after he be dressed; a fine of Id. if the hall be not cleaned by eight in winter and seven in summer; the porter to be fined id. if the court-gate be not shut during meals; a fine of 3d. if the stairs be not cleaned every Friday after dinner. All these fines were deducted by the st ward at the quarterly payment of the men's wages. " Lixv, THE GREAT MOUNTAINS."—I never see a lofty mountain enveloped with dark mist without a feeling of 'profound awe. That mist seems a veil behind which, in the inmost sanctuary of nature, God is doing His won- derful work of mediation in nature. Behind that veil the clouds are forming the sources of rivers and streams, and the rocks are crumbling into soil that will enrich and fertilise the plains. Behind that veil the mountains are sustaining the violence of the storm, that other regions may be calm; are dreary and desolate and for- saken. that other regions may be bright and beautiful, and blessed with the most varied and joyful life. They are elevated above the rest of the earth, and endowed with with exceptional grandeur, not for their own sakes only, but that they may diffuse the blessings of Heaven over the parched places of the earth that need them, sacrific- ing themselves in so doing. And in all this lam re- minded of the awful darkness around Calvary, that- hill "of God" above all others. I think of the Incarnate Righteousness that sacrificed Himself there for a lost and perishing world. The Son of God within that veil, in the inmost and holiest sanctuary of the universe, is suf- fering and dying, in order that the lost innocence ot man may be regained, and the lost beauty of the world re- stored ; and I feel indeed that the righteousness of God is like the great mountains, not only in grandeur of nature, and stability of endurance and goodness of operation, but also in that quality which is the most transcendent of all—self-sacrifice: losing that we might gain: becoming poor, that we might become rich; be- coming sin for us, that we might become the righteous- ness of God in Him. On Calvary we can no longer abstract the righteousness of God from the living person who is the Saviour of the sinner, who loves him with such infinite tenderness that He laid down His life for him, and who is spending all His efforts to draw him to Himself. And there, while we fear that we cannot atone for the least transgression of God's law, we know that divine justice is satisfied with the sacrifice of infinite love.—Dr. Hugh Macmillan, i "The Quiver" for February. How DID MR. O'BRIEN GET His TROUSERS P—ls it how O'Brien got his breeches yer axin? Shure an' that same is aisly tould. Paddy O'Neill an' myself did that bit ov diversion, an' sorra a whist did the boys know about it. "Danny. can you fly?" sez he. "Yes—like a stone," sea I. " Och, be aisy—shure it's sober arnist I am," sea he. " Well, thin, begin foolin'," sea I," till I get yer manein'." " Arrah," sea he, "thim spalpeens have stole O'Brien's breeches." "May the black cat fly away with thim for that same," sea I. "Could yea not git to the tap ov the prison an' shove a pair down ?" sez he.: "Paddy," sea I, "lave that to me. Our ould gander could lift me that height as aisv as ye plaze. But what's the use at all, at all? Galrcen mudn't wear the dirty breeches that came down the chimney, an' maybe have the smell av the GOvernor's dinner stickiti' to the stitches. Fire them into the window wid an cold '9B blunderbuss," sez I. " Aisy, Danny," sez he' "we most surprise thim." "Tip thim the blarney," sea I. "Tell then you're his grandmouther, an' wantit to pay his riot." "Bother the lint," sez he. "Shore his heart is aall rint allridy ; it's breeches he needs." "Where is be 2" sea I. "In bed," sez he. "Thin Peggy Dillon's your man," sez L "Sure many's the bright bhoy she's brought into the warld naked—she'll manage thirn." "Now, it's jokin' yea are after, Danny," sez he. " Sorra a joke," sea I. So we axed Peggy what to do. "Aisy enough." says Peggy. "Roull the breeches up in an Irish grievance, and niver a spalpeen from Dublin Castle will look at it." "More power to Your elbow, Peggy," sez I. So we roulled the breeches up in a petition from evicted tenants, an' Peggy got dressed an Mercy an' myself as Justice, an' we marched to the prison, an sure the door opened as nately as if Saint Peter himsilf wanted in. The Governor and warders an' some ov the tip top quality were all standin' round, but they had all on beautiful golden eye-glasses from Dublin Castle, an' they niver gave a look at the Irish, grievances where O'Brien's breeches were, nor to Peggy nor mesiff, as we were dressed as Mercy an' Justice. "Be bould, Peggy," sez I, "be bould." So she slipt up to where O'Brien waz lyin'. "The top of the mornin', sur," sez she. " Here is a prisint from the fairies." Regorra. I wish ye saw how nate a fit they were, an' sure that's the way " O'Brien got his breeches."— People's Journal. BEDRIDDEN FOE Six Mourns.—The sudden restora- tion to health of Mr. Thomas Edwards, of Birmingham, who has been an invalid for many years, is now quite the talk of the city. It seems that for a number of years he has been a great sufferer from rheumatic gout, some- times being bedridden for six months at a time. During all the while he has tried various doctors, and used many so-called rheumatic remedies, in his effort to obtain re- lief, without avail. Finally, Mr. George Bellhouse, chief of the Birmingham Fire Brigade, gave him a bottle of St. Jacobs Oil; which he applied, and from the very first application he experienced very great relief from pain. Mr. Edwards is 62 years of age, and says that never dur- ing his life has he found anything to equal the Oil for re- Moving pain.
PAPERS FOR THE PEOPLE. BY MANI BiPTE. V.-THE LANDLORD.

"This house to let." This is a very significant notice to most people, and attracts little attention, but when a man has set his chimney on fire seven or eight times in one quarter, and is on the point of being evicted, theie notices become a matter of intense interest to him. Although you mightn't think it, every time one of those notices is posted up in a window, it contains in its block capitals a complete play, if it is only assisted with a little of your imagination. Some evening when you get home and find the door lacked, and you have left your latch-key in your other pocket, just hunt up one of these notices and stare at it till your wife returns, and if your experience is worth anything the characters of the play will march before you. The notice says there is a house to let; the house to let suggests an owner commonly called a landlord, and the landlord suggests that you pay up all arrears of rent unconditionally. Now. I have a suggestion to make to landlords as a body. It is, that those notices be printed, with a picture on them representing one man standing behind a door with an uplifted picking stick in his hand, and another man entering the door with a look of un- suspecting ignorance on his face. This suggestion is forced out by an uncontrollable desire for the public good, as it is about ten to one that the house-seeker would make inquiries as to what it meant, which might , possibly lead to his learning the character of the land- lord, and I consider that quite as essential as the character of a servant. I had intended arranging!' sort of rented comedy, but thinking that if I worked in the landlord as the villain,.some touchy landlords, might be offended, I abandoned the project. We will assume, then, that your landlord has a character. Most of the landlords that I have lived under have had characters, but we were only made acquainted With them after having transformed the house from mud cabin into a semi-palace at our own expense. Our landlord is, on the whole, much like other landlords, cool, exacting, and self-possessed. He never loses his temper only on one point, namely, arrears. The only way we can insult him is to tender the planer's rent before it is due. We pay a given sum to live, move, and have our being inside a given number of brick walls, and all items of plaster, paint, wall-paper, &c., are extra, for which we are under a deep and lifelong obli- gation. I never saw our landlord's eye blaze with indignation I but once, and that was when we waited upon him and informed him gently that we wouldn't pay any more rent till he turned off the extra stream of water that was , supplying the family from a downspout After arguing I the point keenly for Bowe time, he said that some land- lords would have put us on an extra water rate, but I that because he was too liberal we tried to impose on him, which we considered a very, thin argument. As it was about the time when the Irish rent question had reached its height, however, he didn't turn over any remarks about bailiffs, and he had that spout sepaired. We didn't have much time to consider that "ftl to us," for he evened matters up very quickly. If you have got the idea of getting square with your landlords take my advice and give it up at once. As I intend to do our landlord justice I think I had better mention that I had seen him ruffled; but ordi- narily he is rather of a jocular kurn. We say to him, "Mr. Rentbook, the latch is off the backyard door, the slates want looking to, and there is a draught coma under the back door strong enough to blow us up the chimney."

He assu- mes a look of studied stupidity as he inquires if we really experience any inconvenience by a draught coining under the back-yard door. After we get irritated he sees our point, and promises to "have it seen to at once."

We haven't wade notes of how many times he has used this phrase, but we venture to say that the number is going on rapidly for a thousand. We have no doubt whatever that the cares of a landlord are multitudinous, and in consequence his memory fails him; if this isn't so, he has got something to answer for. If the chimney smokes enough to convert us into smoked beef, and we can induce him to come down and look at it, he explains that his and all chimneys smoke when the wind is in a certain quarter, and the only way he can stop it is by being without fire. At a crisis like this it is gratifying for me to think that if he goes on at the same rate he will not always be without fire. His powers of argument are strong, and he gets every opportunity of developing them. When we were leaving. one house the landlord objected to our taking the plants that we had reared with our own hands, and by all the powers of logic he showed that the plants were his, and I almost believed that the seeds had come down by hereditary right through generations of his family. I stall not tell what we did with those plants, however, as it might tend to injure landlords in future. . .

One day, durindthe frost, our water-pipe burst. We promptly hammered it flat against the wall, stopping the leakage, and our water supply at the same time. We next waited upon our landlord, and communicated the fact to him. He argued that it was the duty of the Waterworks to mend that pipe, so we went to the Water Office; they asked us a lot of particulars, and then told us that it was the landlord's work; and after carrying messages between the two for nearly half-a-day, we were referred by the landlord to a certain pinmber. When we told Mr. Rentbook that we wished the pipe had burst under his office stove, he took it quite as a joke, and to keep us from doing something dreadful we hurried out. We said to our landlord last summer:—
4 Mr. Rentbook, if this house isn't beautified in three weeks, we move out."
The reply was what we expected, "All right; we'll see what can be done."

_ We waited upon him when the three weeks expired, and said, "Mr. Rentbook, what about the house being beautified?" Then he seemed puzzled, and asked us what number we lived at, and when we told him, he said : " Does it want doing badly ?" Then he proceeded to argue that it was done on such and such a date, and that with ordinary care any house should be kept decent for so long. We then repeated our threat of leaving if the house wasn't done by the next three weeks; and as the date fixed came and the painters didn't, and as we hadn't got another house, we exhibited a weak point, and stayed. This sort of thing has been going on for about four years, and as we once beautified at our own expense, and the landlord imme- diately clapped on a raise of 6d. per week in the rent, we don't care to try it again. With one landlord that wouldn't beautify we tried the experiment of moving out, and the consequence was that we had no sooner got out the last remnants of our personal estate than he had quite an army of decorators on the premises. This is one trait of the landlord's character that ha a puzzled us to understand more than any other. I think I shall write to The Paper Hanger's Gazette for advice as to what course to pursue in a case like this. If you want any repairs, and can possibly get the landlord to call and see what wants doing, the best time to select is washing-day. If your wife deals with him on that day, his bland style doesn't work worth two cents, 'and if he is in the least possible repairing mood that is the way to fetch him. I have known this method to work satisfactorily during a long and varied experience (that is as satisfactorily as any method could work with a landlord), and tender it gratis to suffering humanity in a spirit of overflowing benevolence. The greatest difficulty is in a house where the rent is paid weekly. The landlord generally sends a thick- skinned youth to collect the rent, and all enquiries from, and instructions to him, might as well be shouted down the slop-stone pipe, for he has a worse memory than his principal, and it is not likely he will cultivate it, when he can get his wages more easily without. We once went to an ironmonger's and ordered quite an extensive quantity of house fittings, such as door knobs, window fasteners, Sm., intending to fix them our- selves, and when they were all arranged on the counter, we said to the ironmonger, "You can put them down to the account of Mr. Rentbook."
His reply consisted of two words, "not Much," and we heaved a sigh and came out, thinking sadly that we had tried all that mortals could try.

- -- WARRINGTON v. HOCROZLE HORNETS (" A " Teams).—:- The Warrington "A" team journeyed to Rochdale on Saturday to play their return fixture with the Rochdale Hornets "A' team. It will be remembered that when the Hornets came ta Warrington the home team were victorious, and Saturday's match was anxiously looked forward to by the supporters of the Rochdale club, fully 3,000 spectators assembling to witness the contest. In order to ensure the match being played straw had been put on the field to protect it from the frost, but notwith- standing this the ground was very hard, although greasy on the surface, and practically unfit to play upon. After an,nspection had been made, however, it was ultimately decided to play the match, in Consideration of the lard gate. The home team were determined, if possible,' t reverse the verdict of the former meeting, and mustered up a strong team, whilst Warrington were, unfortunately, minus two of their usual three-quarter backs, viz., Ap- pleton and Evans, their places being filled by Sanson and Carson. . The game was principally a forward one, in which department the home team slightly excelled. Two 30's being agreed upon, Pilling kicked off for the home team at 3-30, Jolley returning, the ball going into touch in the Hornets' 25. From the line out Hawkesworth put in a kick, Jolley being held by Holman before he could return. From a scrimmage in centre the home forwards broke away with a dribble, but Jolley returned with a Inice punt to Hawkesworth, who kicked to Sanson, this player gaining a free kick, the ball being sent into touch in midfield. The Warrington forwards rushed the oval to ,tlie ,Hornets' quarter-dag„ but Nuttall got this pleil away with a good dribble to the Warrington half. trobus now passed to Daniels, this Omer being collated by Bamford. Nuttall thlew to Hawiresworth, but An- trobus intercepted the pass, anti dribbled to Thorpe, who was held by Thornley. Operations were now transferred to near the Warrington goal line, where, after a pro- tracted scrimmage, Binns succeeded in grounding the ball over the line. Holman's kick at goal failed. Jolley re- started from centre, Bamford returning to Sanson, who sent the ball into touch. Craghan, Donohue, Dillon, and Sanson put in a good dribble, but Bamford neutralized by kicking into touch. From the line out the Warring- ton forwards made a good rush to the Hornets' goal line, Jones collaring Barton with the ball in his possession. Half-time was called with the score--Flemets one try to Warrington nothing. On change of ends Whittle rt.- started, Bamford returning to Jolley, who was held by Wilson. The home forwards, led by Rhodes, Pilling, and Buckley, made a splendid dribble, Sanson savingby kick- ing dead. The visitors immediately afterwards had to save by touching down. Jolley dropped out, Bamford returning well; and after even play in midfield, Antrobus passed to Daniels, but Barton intercepted and dribbled to near the Warrington line, Daniels saving well. Nuttall now got hold, and after a strong run grounded the ball over the line, the kick at goal again failing. The home team, who now had the best of the packs, worked the ball to the visitors' 25, Daniels getting the ball away with a good kick, but the relief was only temporary, as Bamford secured and got away with a splendid run, be- ing tackled by Jolley about a yard from the line; but he succeeded in placing the tall over the line near the corner flag, no goal resulting. 'On call of time the score stood— Hornets, three tries, three minor points, to Warrington nil. Teams :—Warrington Full back, Jolley; three- quarter backs, Daniels. Carson, and Sanson; half backs, Whittle and Antrtbus (captain) ; forwards,"Dillon, Crag- han, Molyneaux, Thomley, Donohue, Isherwood, Jones, Eyes, and Bate. Rochdale Hornets: Full back, Thorpe; three-quarter backs, Bamford, Barton arid Hawkes- worth ; half backs, W. H.. Pilling and ; forwards, A. B. Pilling (captain), Binns, Wilson, Forster, Buckley, Sugden, McHugh, Rhodes, and Holman.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. ROCHDALE HORNITIN.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. ROCHDALE HORNITIN.

It has never been the good fortune of the Warring- tonians to lower the colours of, the Hornets of Rochdale renown, and, though strenuous efforts were made op Saturday at the Wilderspool enclosure, the " wirepullers4' were unable to reverse the previous verdict of this season, the game, as then, remaining drawn. The prospects of the match being brought to an issue looked rather gloomy on Friday, but the rapid thaw of Saturday morning set all doubts on one side, although the ground was not in a very favourable condition for a good display of football. On the teams emerging from the pavilion, lately erected on the ground, it was seen that Barnes, the Warrington skipper, was an absentee, not having recovered from the injury received at Halifax. It may be as well to stath here that it will be some time before he again figures in his usual position. The visitors arrived with a strong team, and at 3-35 Wild set the oval in motion, Jolley replying well to centre flag. From the first scrimmage formed, a smart pass to Evans, who was playing centre in place of Barnes, gave that player an opportunity to display his capabilities as a centre, but he stuck to the leather too long, Griffiths collaring him before he parted with it. The visitors gradually invaded the Warrington quarters,but the home forwards, headed by Povey and Frank Turner, took play back to neutral ground. Scholes showed up with a neat dribble, but the advantage gained was more than equalised by a dashing run on the part of Jolley, who fell when scoring seemed a certainty. Nolan tackled Warren when the latter . was endeavouring to get away. Shortly after a serious accident occurred, Brearley, one of the Rochdale Hornets' forwards, having to retire with his leg broken. It was at first thought that no serious injury had happened, but on inspection being made by a doctor op the field it was found to be of the nature des- cribed above. He was carried to the pavilion, where the injured limb was attended to. This sad accident cast quite a gloom over the whole proceedings, and sym- pathetic feelings were expressed with Brearley and his fellow club mates. On the game being resumed Fair Turner took the leather to the Hornets' 25, and the same player again made a desperate effort from a line-out, but the defence of the visitors was too good. W. Smith re- lieved, and Dillon responded with a neat dribble. Holt steered the visiting forwards well into Warrington quar- ters, but a rush by the home team's forwards was well saved by W. Smith. Scholes tackled Bandies here, and Nevins failing to respond to a phut by Pennington, the game was found to be at half-way. Not to be denied, Speakman passed to Evans, and the game, which was 'chiefly confined to the forwards, settled down at the " insects' " quarter-flag. Fair Turner and Povey each in turn tried hard to cross the line, but without avail, and Ashworth and Scholes brought about a timely relief, dribbling well into the Warrington territory. Massey pressed the visitors' back, and a pass from W. Smith to his brother at three-quarter was not taken advantage of. Evans now secured a neat pass from Fair Turner, but the greasy nature of the leather prevented him taking ad- vantage of it. Bandies saved a rush of the Rochdale men, and Povey responded with a dribble for Warrington. A smart dribble by the Hornets forced the first minor for Rochdale. Frank Turner dropped out, and no return being made, play rested at half-way.. A mistake by Nevins almost let in the visiting team, but Warrington, by the aid of Jolley, placed the home team on the aggres- sive. Timely relief was brought about by Nolan with a smart run, but Littlewood dribbled back in neat style, Griffiths saving. Warren passed smartly to Evans, and Massey put in some useful work, but the saving clause had to be adopted by Nevins shortly alter. The drop- out found Daviesand Littlewood spoiling the return, and I another minor followed, half time arrivingwith the score —Rochdale Hornets 3 minors to Warrington nil. :Franks Turner re-started the second half, and the kick-off scored" a minor. Bandies replied to Wild's drop-out, W. Smith making his mark from the latter's return. This helped I his side but little for the Warringtonians put on a spurt, and placed the Rochdale team on the defensive. Passing by Speakman, Evans, and Massey was now indulged in, the latter hem pushed pushed into touch close to the line. Massey and Jolley were each responsible for sterling work, and pretty passing by the home backs took the game on the Hornets' lines. Exchange kicking by Tat- tersall, Nolan, and Masey was now indulged in, but; after some give-and-take play, Dillon and Povey were'to the fore with a neat dribble, only to have their career checked by a good kick of Griffiths. Hayes and Warren were applauded for some grand play, passing and re-pas- sing to one another with precision. A rush of the home forwards was neutralized by a good run on the part of Pennington, a minor resulting from the running of the last-named. The game was now very fast, and from Frank Turner's drop-out both teams successively had the best of it. Jolley tackled Scholes smartly, but the minor had to be awarded the visitors. Little relief was brought from the drop-out, for Nolan put in a grand run, and when all opposition seemed to have disappeared Jolley appeared on the scene, and collared his man just on the point of scoring. Matters were improved by Speakman and Massey, and a rush by Ashton and Davies forced Nolan to save. From now to the call of time each side strove hard to obtain the mastery, and in the end the game remained drawn, Rochdale scoring six minors to Warrington three. The game calls for little comment, the slippery and greasy state of the leather interfering sadly with good football; and this, coupled with the sad accident above referred to, robbed the match of much interest that would otilierwise have been shown. On behalf of War- rington, Nevins has been seen to better advantage, and Evans made but a poor substitute for Barnes. and cer- tainly was too selfish. Jolley and Massey each had to make their own work, and both performed it in their well-known finished style Warren and Speakman both I played a strong game, and of the forwards, Dillon Povey, and Fair Turner deserve commendation. On behalf of Rochdale Hornets, Pennington, Scholes, Nolan, and Groves were the pick. The following were the teams : Warrington : Full back, W. Nevins; three-quarter backs, J. Jolley, J. W. Evans, J. T. Massey • half backs, W. Speakman (captain) and J. E. Warren; forwards, H. Ashton, Fair Turner,

The match on Saturda btitween Warrington and Rochdale Hornets, bn the ground of the former, was not a particularly satisfactory affair. In the first place the unfortunate accident through 'which one of the visitors received a broken leg almost at the commencement, necessarily threw somewhat of a gloom over the rest of the proceedings; and, in the Ilecond, plkce,the ground, soft and slippery above and frost-bound beneath, was not favouralhe to any high-class play. Brilliant back play was out of the question alike from the slipperiness of the ball and the ground, and the encounters often de- generated into mere loose scrimmages. At the same time it mud he admitted that, towards the close of the game especially, there was not a little excitement, as each team in its turn threatened to score a deciding point, which, however, was not done, as nothing more than minors Ma been notched when "no side" was declared. 1

Considering that the Hornets were minus a player, the form they displayed on Saturday proved clearly that they deserved the repntatiori thefhavetwonl and had the ground been in fair condition the match would un- 'doubtedly have been one of the best played this season on the Wilderspool ground. . . _ _

Warrington ." teani on Saturday sustained the most decisive defeat of the season at their meeting with Rochdale Hornets "A " team on the ground of the latter, the score being three tries and three minors to nil against them. Apart hum the fact that the Hornets "A" team is one of the most powerful "A" combina- tions in Lancashire, it is Only fair to take note of the fact that the Warringtonians were short of two or three of their most effective players, and that the state of the ground at Rochdale was even more unfavourable than at Warrington to combined play, which is the forte of the Warringtonians.

div.head: WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
RESIGNATION _ OF THE SECRETARY'.

_ The annual meeting of the members of the General Council of the Warrington Liberal Associa- tion was held last night week, in the committee- room of the Liberal Club, Bewsey-strest, for the pur- pose of electing a president and vice-presidents of the association, and transacting other business. The chair was taken by the president of the association, Mr. J. G. McMinnies, J:P., and amongst those also present were Mr. John CrOstield, J.P., Councillors F. A. Roberts and H. Fleming, Mr. A. Browne, Mr. John Walker, Mr. T. Birchall, Mr. Samuel Barlow, Mr. S. Kenyon, Mr. W. Stirrup, Mr. ' Clay, Mr. Bowers, Mr. R. Roberts, Mr. B. Roberts (sectary of the association), i&c: Letters apologising for non-attendance had been re- ceived from Dr. Gornall, Councillor W. Pierpoint, Mr. Kiernan, and Mr. W. I. Lawton: The attend- ance was large, and ' the proceedings were enthu- siastic.

The CHAIRMAN, who was received with cheers, said: This meeting may be taken to be the annual meeting of the Council, and as such it seems to be a 'fitting opportunity for reviewing what we have done during the past twelve months—to take stock, as it were, of our position and prospects; to see where we are and where we are going. (Cheers.) The last twelve months has been a very fatal one to us in the loss of many of our most influential friends. In Mr. Charles troadbent we lost a friend who was always ready to assist 118—never missing when he was wanted. Politics to him were not.a matter of pleasure, as they are to some of us, but they were a matter of duty, and he performed his duty whenever he was asked to assist the Liberal party. We shall miss hinkfor many a day. (Cheers.) We have also to lament the loss of our friend Mr. Peter Rylands, who for many years occupied a prominent position in the Liberal party, and who was the most ac- tive, and the most eloquent, man that we had amongst all our leaders. (Hear, hear.) I daresay that if his death had happened a couple of years sooner we might have felt his loss more keenly, but there are many men in this room who will never forget the services he ren- siered during a long life. (Cheers.) But the greatest loss that we have sustained during the twelve months was 'occasioned by the death of Mr. George Crosfield. (Hear, hear.) I never knew a time in my experience of the Liberal party when Mr. Crosfield was not a zealous and earnest member of it, and he continued his labours for ,the party as long as he was able to do so, and after- wards, by wise counsels and most munificent subscrip- tions, he did all that he could to maintain the position and prosperity of the party. (Cheers.) I think it not unlikely that in some respects we have in his brother a worthy successor of Mr. George Crosfield—(cheers)---a man as'earnest and as thorough, and perhaps as gene's. ous but still, taking Mr. George Crosfield for all in all, during the few years I have to live I think! shall never look upon his like again C,Cheers). We shall miss for many a day the gay wisdom of Mr. Pilcher—a man whose wise counsel was never missing when it was required, a warm and, I am sure, an affectionate friend, a man who, whenever the question of human progress was to the front, religious, or political, or material, svas never wanting in his support, (Cheers). Another political character has disappeared during the twelve months—an earnest and a warm and a powerful opponent of ours. I did not know the late Captain Reynolds as well as many gentlemen in this room, but there was a time in our lives when we met in connection with a legal business in which we were both interested, and when we met. frequently, and during the intimacy I learned to admire, and esteem, and respect him. jCheers). He was by far the ablest and the most formidable of our opponents. (Hear, hear). But this will not prevent me from saying now that I bear my testimony to his high qualities as a generous, genial, warm-hearted, and honourable gentleman. (Cheers). Well now, the lesson we have to learn from our bereavements during the last twelve months is that we must be more and more zealously devoted towards the Liberal cause. And this is the lesson which the younger men among us should especially learn. We have for many years been inviting our young friends to come to the front and show themselves with us. It has been a matter of considerable pleasure to me to see dur. ing the last twelve months two young men coming to the front, and promising to be a great assistance to us. I mean Mr. Gordon Rylands and Mr. Arthur Crosfield. (Hear, hear). I hope that their example will be followed, not only in the successors of our leaders, but in the rank mid file of the party, so that we may have grow- ing up a young army of young men who will bear up the banner of political progress wten it falls, perhaps, .from weary and fainting hands. (Cheers). Just a word or two about general politics. We have suffered, as all Liberal constituencies lhave suffered, from the melan- choly schism that has happened in the Liberal party. What the extent of that schism has been in Warrington I cannot tell. lam afraid from the poll in 1888 that it was greater than we had supposed. But it is a matter of congratulation to me, and ought to be so to you, that we have not either by word or deed done anything to widen the breach between ourselves and those who thought proper to go from us. (Cheers). And this has been the case throughout the kingdom. It has been a surprise to me that no greater feeling of exasperation .has been shown by the bulk of the Liberal party to the small secession that went from them than we have seen during the last eighteen months. This is as it should be. The question that divides us now will be, before long, re- moved out of the way. Home Rule will be granted to Ireland—(Cheers)—and he is a bold man who is'prepared to say that it will not be granted by the present Government. (Laughter). My own opinion is that before 1890 the present Government will bring in a Home Rule measure that will be satisfactory to the Irish nation and also satisfactory to the Liberal party in Great Britain. (Chevrs.) Well, now, supposing that this element of division is taken out of the way, you will be in every way in the position that you were eight years ago—the same in numbers if you are united, with the same good cause, with the same great leader in Mr. Gladstone— (cheers)—and you will be in theposition, if you have the same earnestness, and the same zeal, you will be in the position of doing in 1890 what you, did in 1880. (Cheers.) But, meanwhile, those of us who have kept together so far must keep together to the end. There must be no dissension amongst us. If any root of bitternesSspring up amongst us, it must be put out of the way. If people go about trying to sow dissension, do not regard them, have no communion with them ; they are enemies sowing tares. (Cheers.)

Mr. F. A. normal's, at the call of the chairman, ex- plained that he had been waited upon by a deputatiob which had strongly pressed him to occupy the position of Chairman of the Executive as heretofore. He felt, he said, that he could not give the time which he had been in the habit of giving to the work. He had a strong opinion as to the importance of the office, and the duties that were required of the person who held it. He was afraid that he would not be able to do all that he thought should be done, but he was impressed by the pressing request that he should retain he post, and would consent to do so under the circumstances. (Cheers.) •

The -----cl-- following letter had bee' n ad resse by Mr. H. Roberts, agent and secretary of the Association; to the president, resigning his appointment : A Dear Mr. McMinnies,—After eareful consideration, I have decided to resign my appointment as secretary and agent of the Warrington Liberal AsSociation. The rea- sons which have led me to this decision are entirely of a personal and private character, and refer only to my health and the requirements of my business. By the end of March next—at which date I should wish to be relieved, if possible—l shall have completed fifteen years of service in the Liberal cause in Warrington. , It is not an easy matter to retire from a position, which, while it has brought its discomforts and , anxieties, has con- ferred upon me a reSponsibility, a confidence, and a I trust which I have considered it an honour to retain so long. In looking back , upon my official career, I am: conscious of many shortcomings and imperfections, but the memory of them reminds me only the more forcibly of the kindly consideration I have so frequently received at the hands of the Liberals of my native town. I trustl I may for many years to come fill an honourable and useful position amongst the workers for the Liberal I cause in Warrington, and that before long we may; re-' I joice together in accomplishing.: the restoration of this , Borough to its rightful position as a Liberal constituency:l 1 cannot conclude without expressing to yourself the deep sense of gratitude which I feel for a confidence and support extended to me, without .stint, during the 1 whole of the period in which I have held my appoint- ment, and through you I would offer my heartfelt thanks to the Liberals of Warrington of all ranks, at whose hands I have ever received kindly consideration and approval —I remain, dear Mr. McMinnies, faithfully yours, HENRY ROBERTS. 17, Muteum-street, Warrington, Feb. 11, 1888. Referring to this letter the CHAIRMAN said that during' the last fifteen years Mr. Roberts had filled the office he had known him well and intimately, and he believed that to no man in the town were they moreo-indebted than they were to Mr. Roberts for the services he had rendered to the party. (Cheers.) Mr. Roberts was an i 1 exceptional man. His opinions n reference to voting land registration were held in the highest esteem by lead- ing politicians in the country, and he (the chairman) had seen letters from cabinet and ex-cabinet ministers asking the opinion of, Mr. Roberts in reference to those two subjects. (Hear, hear.) Mr. McMinnies then read a letter from Dr. Gornall, in which that gentleman said, in respect to Mr. Roberts that they would never look , upon his like again as a Liberal agent. (Cheers.) This, Dr. Gornall added, was even acknowledged by their op- ponents, who would be delighted that they had not to op- pose them in the Revision Court a layman who possessed as much legal knondedge in reference to electoral law as all the Tory lawyers in Warrington put together. (Laughter and cheers.) He (Mr, McMinnies ) proposed a resolution to the effect that the members of the council received with regret the letter of Mr. Roberts resigning his position as secretary and'agent ; that they desired to express their high appreciation of his services to the party, and to thank him for those services • and that they hoped that in the future he might be happy and prosperous.. (Cheers). Mr. JOHN CROSFIELD seconded the resolution. He I did not, he said, think that any member of the Liberal 'party knew Mr. Roberts more intimately than he did, and he could bear his testimony, along with Mr. McMin- nies, to his great ability in all departments connected with the work of an agent for the Liberal party, and especially to his knowledge in regard to registration. I He would also like to point out that the services of a 'man like Mr. Henry Roberts were much greater than they could estimate by pounds, shillings, and pence. He knew what a weight of responsibility Mr. Roberts had felt on many occasions. The fact was that Mr. Roberts had broken down in health through the responsibilities connected with the Liberal party, and his business, and, deeply as he regretted the loss of his services, he had told Mr. Roberts that his own health should be his first con- sideration, and that he was quite right in resigning. (Cheers). Mr. S. BARLOW warmly supported the resolution, which was carried with unanimity., Mr. ROBERTS, in reply, said that he had felt for some ' time past that his business had so increased that he could not injustice to his own health carry on the two things successfully much longer. He therefore thought it due to himself and them that he should resign the ap- Ointment of secretary of the association. He hoped, however' that when his health was restored, they would still find him something to do which would enable him to keep in the front rank of tho workers of the party —(cheers)—and which, if necessary, would send him again to represent them in the Revision Court. (Cheers:) The work in that court had been a great strain, but the combative and argumentative work there had been agreeable to him, and he felt that he was able to hold his own with reference to registration with any man in England. (Cheers.) He believed that the clearness of his head, so far as it had been clear, and his ability to carry things out straightforwardly, had been principally owing to the feet that he had never tasted intoxicating liquors. (Hear, hear.) He asked them to extend to his successor, whoever that might be, the same consideration and kindly feeling that they had always extended to him. (Cheers.) He hoped in the future to be as strong a Radical as in the past, and he hoped to see the day when Warrington should take the position that it should as a Liberal constituency. (Cheers.) Mr. WALIEHR mentioned the assistance that had been given to Mr. 'II. Roberts by his brother, Mr. Wm. Roberts, who had a great capacity for organisation and was deserving of a good word. It was decided that the question of the election of a new secretary should be referred to the Seb-managment Committee, and the meeting concluded by a cordial vote of thanks being passed to the chairman on the mo- tion of Mr. JOHN CROSFIBLD.

div.head: CHAPTER VI
div.p: CHAPTER VI
EYES INTO EYES.

Money affairs are at such a low ebb with the Stan- hopes—though the world knows it not—that it is im- possible for them to give a ball, as they had always promised themselves to do, when Irene came out. In fact, it is only by borrowing at a heavy interest that Mr. Stanhope is able to strugvle through the season without letting the house in Egon-square. He has made this effort for Irene's sake, because he does not think it right that her brothers should have all the advantages while she is deprived of that first plunge into life from which the brilliancy or dimness of most girls' fortunes date. One of the grandest fetes of the year is then chosen for Irene's debut, which is to be made at the Russian Ambassador's ball in the last week in May.

Her presentation at Court is put off till the following spring, since, owing to the hesitation about bringing her ont'at all, most of the Drawing-rooms have been allowed to pass; and,though not naturally mercenary people, it is devoutly hoped by both her parents that when she is presented it u ill be as a bride, .

Mr. Stanhope, now that he has begun to talk on business matters with his wife, impresses it on her very strongly that Irene must marry that season,sinee it will be quite impossible for him to give her another chance.

Sweet, innocent Irene, dressed in virginal white I She trips down the staircase to receives lovely bouquet Mr. Stanhope has ordered for her from Covent Garden expressly for this ball, and which he is holding there ready to give her. She looks up in his face with her soft eyes and kisses him. While pressing to his heart the victim he has decided to make her, she says: "Wish me lots of enjoyment and a happy evening, papa." "I do, my child, I do," he answers with a sort of wince, as if the edges of a presentiment are cutting him, and then he passes on into his study and closes the door.

Recent troubles had rendered Mr. Stanhope far too low-spirited to think of accompanying his wife and daughter to this ball. They arrived there when the festivity was at its height. Lady Fedora had no idea that the debut from which she expected so much should be made in half-empty rooms. Lf Irene was to produce any effect at all it should be on a crowd; nor was Lady Fedora disappointed. Innocence and beauty have never yet failed to make their mark, and many were the whispers of "Who is the debutante? How .lovely she is ' That reached Lady Fedora's ears, nor could Irene fail to notice the buzz of admira- tion that followed her steps; and instead of making her shy, as Lady Fedora had half feared it would, it seemed to raise her spirits and her self-esteem. Never did Lady Fedora remember to have seen her child look so sparklingly and bewilderingly beautiful as she did that night. She was a true Stanhope and rising at once to the exigency of the occasion, she arranged her dances and parried her partner's compliments as if she were accus- tomed to the whole programme. And among the bevy of men who flocked about Irene, solicitous for her hand in the dance, was there one, Lady Fedora wondered—while she looked from one t 3 the other of them—who was a sufficently good parte to claim that little hand for life?

There was the Honourable Julius Blain, with a prospective coronet; the Earl of Monkfield with a newly-acquired title; Mr. Budge Jeston' with enough broad acres to counterbalance .the absence of blue blood,and considered by most mothers the parti of the year.

Oh, they were -a goodly assemblage, and they basked in Irene's smiles and pretty taking ways, till the sight of her daughter's triumph made good loving Lady Fedora's heart flutter, and so engrossed was she in watching the scene that was being played out close to her that she failed to look beyond the compliments of those butterfly adorers, or to allow her eyes to wander even for one brief moment to the face of a tall, dark man, who, standing with his back against the wall, never removed his gaze from Irene. He had not asked to be presented to her; he made no sign of admiration, save that rivctted, silent gaze ; and the dark, deep-set eyes that watched her bore so mournful an expression that it seemed almost as if he regarded her as a memory rather than the embodiment of a sweet vision of to-day. He was not a very young man ; there was room in his life for memories. The once black hair about his temples was sprinkled with grey, and round about the deep-set eyes the hand of Time had set its stamp; yet, for all this not only in the past, but now, Prince Sergius. LenskOff was reckoned one of the handsomest men of his day,and to find favour in his eyes was a boon for which many a faqhionable beauty in more capitals than that of England craved. He had known Henry Stanhope well in years gone by, when the Englishman was an attachtc at the Rus- sian Court,and Prince Sergius,some ten years younger, was making his first plunge into the vortex, and was enjoying to the full the many pleasures St. Petersburg can offer. They had met but seldom since those joyous, careless days of their youth—their paths had been along such different roads that intimacy had been impossibie—once or twice only at a cheery ttte-h-tilte dinner in Paris, during which they talked over some of the escapades in which they had played the heroes. Now, for some years, they had not even thus met,nor did Henry Stanhope know that Prince Sergius was in London. In the eyes of the world, Prince Sergius was a widower, a widower with an enormous fortune,one of those fabulous fortunes whic'i only few nobles in Europe possess. Yet no mother would have regarded Prince Sergius as a parti, or imagined the chance of his marry- ing a fair young beauty as otherwise than most remote; and already had he been marked dangerous. With the facility the Russians have for languages he spoke English perfectlyknd French like a native ; his manners, when he cho•;e, were as courteous and urbane as Henry Stanhope's own, but there were times when no man better understood how ta play the churl. It seemed to those more or less acquainted with him that he was decidedly in a churlish mood at the Ambassador's ball, for he never left his place by the wall nor ad- dressed a word to anyone, and as he was not the sort of man from whom people courted a gratuitous snub' no one ventured to address him.

He had thus perfect opportunity to feast his eyes on Irene's beauty ;and watch her graceful form gliding through the figures of the mazy dance muttering to himself every now and again with bated breath.— Henry Etanhope's daughter, so she is Henry Stanhope's daughter." Once and once only he bestowed a glance on Lady Fedora, but speedily returned it to Irene. Henry Stanhope's wife had evidently not awakened the same interest in his heart as had his child. And yet, after a long, long while, passed in gazing and thinking, he sought the Ambassadress and begged her to present him to Lady Fedora Stanhope, the wife of his old friend. One less practised in savoir faire would have ignored the mother and have sought an introdaction to the girl, but Prince Sergins was a stickler for etiquette, and he knew, moreover, that people like the Stanhopes were unapproachable except with due form.

Lady Fedora was delighted to make Prince Sergius' acquaintance. She had heard much of Mtn from her 11u-band, who would be pleased to meet her old friend again. In fact, Lady Fedora's generally calm, repose- ful manner being taken into consideration, she became quite gushing in her reception of Prince Sergius, who was not altogether quite as sure as Lady Fedora was that Henry Stanhope would be so very glad to see him. When Irene returned from a visit she had been paying, with one of her partners, to the supper-room, this distinguished-looking foreigner was at once pre- sented to her. She looked at him a little curiously with those clear, candid eyes of hers, simply because he was her father's friend. She had not noticed him leaning against the wall—not she! She would never forget him,however, now that they had met face to face and looked into each othe'r's eyes. What she read in his made her speedily cast hers down to the ground, and become crimson to the very roots of her hair. It was as if a sudden revelation had filled her whole soul. What was it She knew something of love since she had of late been assisting in the somewhat clandestine love affairs of Geoffrey and Phyllis, but their love was not at all like this, and Irene turned away from Prince Sergius with a little rapid gesture, that seemed to imply, "I wish I had never seen you." , Lady Fedora thought her rude,and was about either to expostulate or excuse; but the Prince stopped her; he could read Irene's feelings as though they were written en an open book. He had read many a young, unclosed heart before. "Miss Stanhope will make allowances," he said; "I am only a fierce, ugly Russian—no longer young. But I am her father's old friend."
A smile came back to Irene's face at his words. "2" Fierce and ugly," she repeated, "you do not pa.T

yourself high compliments, Prince," He shrugged his shoulders. "I love the truth," he repeated, "and while the truth tells me how beautiful you are, it is equally' candid in making my own inferiority most apparent. Beauty and the Beast, eh? It is a fairy story that has been translated into every language." "You must not flatter Irene, she is too young; thie is only her first ball to-night," said Lady Fedora,protesto lag, though her heart meanwhile was overflowing with delight. "She has yet to learn how many of the compliments men offer are mere words." "She has yet to learn that I never say what I do not mean,"answered the Prince gravely, and a little stiffly. It did not exactly please his princeship that he should be classed as "men," and unless Lady Fedora wished to put him down a little, she was, perhaps just a trifle wanting in her usual tact. "I never dance," he said, offering his arm to Irene, "but if Mademoiselle will condescend to walk with 'le round these rooms which our Ambassadress has converted into a iperfect bower of beauty, she will, I tope, learn to understand me better.

r Irene could not refuse, but if she had been gay and at home all the earlier part of the evening she was shy enough now, as just touching the Prince's arm with the tips of her little gloved hand she set off to make the grand tour. Miss Stanhope and Prince Serc'ius Leb.slzoff were the observed of all observers. Even Geoffrey, who had ar- rived late at this ball,from some other party, paused to t tke breath when he passed his sister on the arm of this important looking Russian.' And wherefore? The set to which the Stanhopes btlonged to meet a foreign Prince was an incident of amost daily recurrence. It was the strange attributes, the celebrity that this particular Prince Sergius pos.. iessed, which made everyone surprised that he should have singled out Irene for his especial favour. Geoffrey scarcely liked that it should be so—he knew nothing personally of Prince S,?rgins, but he had overheard several remarks made by acquaintances who had not noticed that he was near them. He struggled through the crowd only bowing to several girls with whom he usually danced, each of whoni one day hoped to be th mistress of Warleigh Hall, and eventually he reached the place where Lady Fedora was sitting. "What is thi4, mother; why is Irene walking about with that man 2" he blurted out with more honesty than coartesy. Hush,my dear Geoff. I don't understand what you mean, He is Prince Sa•gias Lenskoif, one of your father's oldest friends." _

"My father'sifriend I There must:be some mistake. I never heard my father speak of him." "Before you were born—before he was married your father and Prince Sergius were much together in St. Petersburg." "Ah ! My father has settle I down into a family man since then, while Prince Sergins— "ls a widower and admires Irene," whispered his mother. "Don't, Geoffrey, don't be tiresome—do let things drift—but this is no place for conversation, go and dance, my dear boy, and leave me to take care of your sister. • Geoffrey did as she bade him, that is he went away, but there was a troubled look on his brow, and the idea that the names of Prince Sergius and that of his fair 7oung sister could be coupled even during the fleeting hours of a midsummer fete gave him deep displeasure._

. - Meanwhile Prince Sergius and Irene sat among the roses on a balcony converted into a bower,as it seemed, especially for them, since no one came to di3pute iti possession with them. And there they talked the gay moments away, or rather Prince Sergius talked, and Inn 3 listened or only answered in monosyllables. A new vista was bein; opened for her, and almost staggering with emotion, she felt as if she were standing on the confines of an undiscovered country. And after all what was he saying? Yothing that put down on paper would not sees worthless and puerile, but no man knew better thasi Prince Sergins how to accompany words of no seeming importance with such glances and such a manner al set his listener all aflame.

Irene did not then a3k herself whether the feeling Prince Sergius was arousing was love or hate; she only knew that a strange transformation was chang- ing her whole nature, and that never again in this world would she be the same Irene Stanhope who had started forth that evening to the dance clad in a sweet simplicity, as unspotted as the dress Of vir- ginal white that marked ner debut. . Wise-looking Lady Fedora never guessed what a neW light that half-hour's conversation with Prince Serguis would cast on the girl's life. How could she 7 She had never had the good or evil fortune to meet a man of the type of Prince Sergins Lenskoff. But when at last Irene returned to her motherly chaperonage; she saw at once that she was deeply impressed, ana it was with joy the good mother noticed it. If, as she hoped, Irene had won Prince Sorgins and his immense wealth what a relief it would be to her father's mind—how he would bless the decision that one more effort should be made to give Irene the chance of this season. The boys, too, what an ad- vantage to them to have Prince Sergius for a brother-in-law. All this being considered,Lady Fedora rose to depart. "Come, Irene, you must not stay too late; the rosee on your cheeks are already beginning to fade." Good, prudent mother; she had no intention of out- staying her triumph, so she fussed off to go down- stairs, feeling quite a flutter at her own heart when Prince Sergius offered her his arm. Irene followed in the wake alone, none of her now ex-admirers offering to escort her, it seemed as if by common consent they would not interfere with Prince Sergius. Could they have read the girl's future as it wee already mapped out, even while she followed her mother to the carriage they would have pitied her. Was not some portion of it perhaps revealed in her already saddened, grave face. The merry-hearted child had set forth joyously to the ball that night ; the woman with a thousand emotions throbbing and contending for place in her heart, drove silently home from it. (To be continued.)

Naw YORK, &crux/var.—According to a telsgram from Chicago published here, the police in that city, Who have been endeavouring to discover the assassins of Mr. Amos Snell, the millionaire, who was murdered by burglars at' his residence on the Bth lust.,' now state their conviction that the author of the crime is William B. Tascottia young man, aged 22, the son of most respectable and-wealthy 'Parents, but who is described, as incorrigible. He has not, however,. vet been arrested. ICR‘v YORK, Sownky:—,lioneral Sheridan, Commander- in•Chief of the.llnited States Army, has announced that under no circumstances wonld he accept nomination as a candidate for the Presidency. r21t,1, YORK, MONIMY MORNING. Intelligence has aerled this city of a terrible calamity which has 0e.r..- en the town of Monnt•Vernon, Illinois. A cyclone of Ssual violence laid a large portion of the town in and before its fury was spent, a fire burst out `nong the houses which still "stood, and raged with a ,erceness which can only be compared to that of Cyclone itself. Very few houses now remain, and People are in the greatest distress. The fatalities __aye been numerous. The :first report mentions thirty People as having been tilled, either, by the falling ruins or in the flames, whilst itii stated that 200 others have sustained severe injuries. Owing to the storm the tele- graph wires are down, and suevis arrives slowly; hence 1:10 intelligence beyond that from.-Mount_Vermst has c°rse to hand. But it is presumable that the vicinity ot that town must have suffered, considerably from the CY'-'one. ' Further particulars are published of the terrible dis- • tater which befel the lowa of Mount Vernon (Illinois) rlie town is about two miles long east and west, fir.d the ' Course of the tornado took in about two-thirds of the ('-ctuit end, the western portion escaping. The larger por- • non of the business pert, known as the Square, was ! totally destroyed. A fire 'broke out immediately among :the ti ruins, and raged with great 'fury, adding horror to situation. Cries and groans were heard in all tiiree "I°us• Two egurches lay amass of ruins. The public ntchool building and the hotel were also gone, and of a 1.1.4 mg row of business houses on one side of the •qUare not one was left standing. The town locked 'indeed as if it had been visited by .a violent earth- 'quake. The survivors had to)tave. the injured rand dying in order to fight the ftnios, which were only Subdued after a stubborn ontest of several hours. • 'Forty-nix persons are kn nto be killed, and &any •others injured. The sceise/it midnight was peculiarly • :distressing:. Through thd great :heaps of ruins men, 'Yearnen, and boys were ru,egling in their efforts to Teach those iMprisoned beneath the timbers and bricks. 'Cries came from every pile of (Faris. In some streets. where great clouds swept with resistless force, the dead 'lay in the warm rain,' which 'mingled with their blood. above the scene of desolatian the eliv was red from the, . 'conflagration, and the wind, which was blowing 'strongly, was laden with the blazing brands. ueh. a picture appalled the • stoutest heart. Many of the survivors taaught '.of nothing but themselves. With the names 'roaring behind Cud upon all sides of them they fled in uncentrollable "terror,over the bodies, dead and 'injured, and the mass of reins .which pinned them to the earth. For hours it, 'looked as though the victims would ,be burned where they lay. --- It is stated that the Local Government Bill will estab- lish county' councils, to be elected by ratepayers. The counties will be divided into wards, each of which will elect a councillor for three years, a third retiring annually. Many urban authorities, such as union as- sessment committees, will cease to exist, while some of the duties of others, like these of boards of guardians as rural sanitary authorities and school attendance com- mittees, will be transferred to the county authorities, LORD SPENCER AT ABlLTON.—Addressinda mass meet- ins of the Liberals of Ashton-thider-Lyne .3n Wednesday night, Earl Spencer reviewed the course of events since his visit to Manchester a fair weeks ago, and held that the policy adopted by the Liberal leaders in the Reuse of Commons had been amply justified. • Since the opening of the session, he said, it had become more clear than ow that the only alternative to Home Rule was coer•

Lord Randolph Churchill went down to Oxford on Wednesday and ad- drmsed the Union Society on the question of Home Rule. The proposal before the Society was that in order to sa.tisfy the "just aspirations Of the Irish people" it was necessFy that a statutory Parliament should be estab- lished in Dublin. Lord Randolph repelled the charge of having spoken contemptuously of the Irish people; and tben,entered upon a long historical exatifination of the Irish question. He contrasted the different methods pursued by Mr. Pitt and Mr. Gladstone for the pacifica- tion of Ireland, and denied that there was any real analogy between the " just aspirations of the Irish people and the successful efforts of the Greeks the Italians, and the Hungarians to attain national indepen- &ace. Such a statutory parliament, he contended, 'would not satisfy the Irish; and he said it was utter 'nonsense to think that a duality of parliaments would cproduce greater union than now existed. In a statutory Parliament were set up the crazy, cranky machinery of 'Government would be soon shattered by the armed resis- tance of Protestant Ulster; but he did not apprehend that Home Rule would be granted until England had ceased to rule as an Empire. • "Ni

SHUFFLING THE GOVERNMENT CARDS. Baron Henry de Worms ha a been appointed Under- Secretary of State for the Colonies, in place of the Earl of Onslow, Who ha s accepted the position of Parlia- mentary Secretary to the Board of Trade. Baron Henry de Worms will continue to be President of the Inter- national Conference upon' the Sugar Bounties. The arrangements in connection with the changes in Govern- ment offices are not yet complete, and for the present Lord Stanley of Preston will answer for the Board of Trade questions put in the House of Lords. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach, President of the Board of Trade, has ap- pointed `Sir Thpmas Blomefield, Bart., as his private secretary. Sir T. Blomefield acted in a similar capacity to the late President, Lord Stanley of Preston. Baron Henry de Worms, Under-Secretary for the Colonies, has appointed Mr. G. V. Piddes as his private secretary. Mr. Fiddes acted in the same capacity for the late Under- Secretary, the Earl of Onslow..Baron Henry de Worms has appointed Mr. W. T. Lawrance his unpaid private Beoreta73r. MR. 'BAIFOUR AND IRISH RESIDENT MAGISTRATES: . .

Mr. Balfour has sent the followinig reply to a War- rington correspondent, who drew his attention to observations with regard to the resident magistrates, madein the course of a speech delivered in that town by the Liberal candidate for the division "Irish Office, 18th February, 1888.—Dear sir,—l have received your letter of the 10th February, enclosing a newspaper cutting which purports to contain an ex- tract from a speech made at Warrington, on the Bth inst., 'by Mr. John Crosfield, a Liberal candidate for your division. Mr. Crosfield is reported to have spoken in very disparaging terms of the resident magis- trates who administer the summary jurisdiction under the Criminal Law and Procedure Act in Ireland, and to have supported hts statements by reference to a speech which he had heard Lord Spencer make, at Manchester, a few days previously. It is strange, if indeed it is true, that Lord Spencer should join in throwing any discredit upon either the character or the qualifications of the resident magistrates. Sir Geo. Trevelyan, when defending in Parliament the administration of the Crimes Act of 1882, testified to the care which he and Lord Spencer exer- cised to secure that only thoroughly suitable and effi- cient men were either appointed to, or retained in, that branch of the public service. The Government, he said, knowing that at a critical moment everything depends on the personal qualities and vigour of the men in re- sponsible positions, did not shrink from removing men Whose age and personal qualities did not render them fit for those positions, and replacing them by others. We have ,auried nut that work, and feel in ca.rrvinf it out we have teen wing wnat we wisnea, naving toe euurrtry served. Lord Spencer, after he had finally quitted Ire- land in 1885, bore public and generous testimony to the manner in which these gentlemen had discharged their duties during the period in which he occupied the post of Lord-Lieutenant, and enforced the provisions of the Crimes Act of 1882. 'I must; he said, 'speak of those who are independent of the Executive, and who have been too often in Parliament and the Press of Ireland Confused with the acts of the Executive Government—T mean the judges, magistrates, and juries, those who during the difficult times of almost unexampled danger, did their duty honestly, impar- tially, and fearlessly.' The great majority of the resident magistrates now serving in Ireland are amongst those of whom Lord Spencer thus spoke, and they are doing now, though under circumstances of aggravated diffi- culty, the same work, and in the same spirit of zeal and fidelity, RS before he changed his political opinions.—l am, yours faithfully, ARTHUR JAMES BALFOUR.
THE BY-ELECTIONS.

RE-ELECTION OF SIB. MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH. The nomination for VVest Bristol was fixed for Mon- day, and, as was generally expected, Sir Michael Hicks- Beach was re-elected without opposition. There were six nomination papers handed in on behalf of the right hon. gentleman, signed by Conservatives from all parts of the division. Sir Michael was not present, and the proceedings were of the most formal character.
A WARRINGTON TRESPASS CASE AT LIVERPOOL ASSIZES.. '

---- - In the Nisi Prins Court, at the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, before Mr. Justice Cave and a common jury, an action, brought by James Proctor Jones, cf Warrington, against William Leatherbarrow," of Widnes, to recover possession of certain land and premises and the return of certain goods and chat- tels, and also damages for detention and trespass, was heard. Mr. Mulholland appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Gully, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. Little fx the defendant. It was stated by the plaintiff that he had for a long time beenin business as an engineer and inventor at Warrington.. The defendant was a contractor at Widnes. In 1895 he took in one of the defendant's sons as an apprentice, and an intimacy sprang up between the parties. The defendant had premises at Farnworth. near Warrington, and he suggested that he (plaintiff) should take the premises and bring his plant there. About this time he took the defendant's second son as an apprentice. On De- cember 10,1886, he took possession of the premises , and proceeded to bring his plant there. It was a 'fact that in the following August he owed the de- fendant £l5O for money lent, and this was now counterclaimed for. He (plaintiff) had got his plant on the premises and was making money, for eight months the profits being £llO. but the de- fendant thought it was time to get some of his money back. On August 22nd last he met the defendant and his two sons who demanded the keys. He refused, and they said it did not matter, as they had taken pos- session of the premises. Since then he had been kept out of his business. In cross-examination, the plaintiff said he went into the premises in thetope and expectation that the defendent would join' him as partner, but he did not. The rent was to be £lO a year, but he had neither paid rent nor taxes, he- cause he had not been asked for any.—For the de- fence, Mr. Gully said the defendant had claimed the premises because they were his, and he claimed the goods because the plaintiff had given them as security for money lent. The defendant had means, and believed the plaintiff to be a clever workman, so he was willingto help him. He kept on lending him money,and the goods were given as security. The defendant never agreed to let the plaintiff the premises. and it was a curious thing that, though the plaintiff said he was a tenant, there was noth- ing beyond his own statement to prove it. He did not pay any rates, and there was no agreement as to what rent was to be paid. The plaintiff simply occupied the premises at will, and without any right to remain there.—The defendant was called, and in answer to Mr. Gully, said there was no truth in the suggested that he,turned out the plaintiff for the purpose of putting his own sons into the business. He had not since using the plant. His counter claim against the plaintiff was £153 9s.—The jury found for the plaintiff, with damages .£so.—His Lordship gave judgment for the plaintiff for The possession of the land and premises and delivery of the goods end chattels, and for the defendant on the counter claim for £lO3 ss, the sum claimed less the amount of damages.

div.head: DEPTFORD.
div.p: DEPTFORD.

Both parties are active-1i -€:n—g-a;,;d in preparing for the coming contest at Deptford, and considerable excitement is anticipated on the day of election. The Liberals ex- press themselves perfectly confident of the success of Mr. Willed Blunt, but say that, seeing the result of the recent trial in Dublin, he ought to he released to conduct his own candidature. The Conservatives also speak very hopefully of the prospects of Mr. Darling. Both parties have arranged for meetings this week.

div.head: DONCASTER.
div.p: DONCASTER.

On Saturday night, Mr. Henry Chaplain, M.P., ad- dressed a meeting in the Corn Exchange in support of the Liberal Unionist candidate, Mr. H. W. Fitzwilliam. He said that if they conceded Home Rule to the Nation- alist party they would place in the hands of that party the most powerfuLleveriin the world for the accomplish- ment of separation, if at any future time they thought fit to use it He utterly and entirely denied that the policy of the Government in Ireland had failed. The plan of campaign was nothing but public plinider. A Liberal demonstration was held in the Doncaster Corn Exchange on Monday. attended by about 4,000 persons. Mr.fitichanan, the newly-elected member for West Edinburgh, WaS publicly welcomed, and delivered an address in reply. He claimed that the elections in Dundee and West Edinburgh showed how public feeling was rising in the country, and were condemnatory of the •Government policy in Ireland. Sir W. Lawson, M.P., Mr. Herbert J. Gladstone, M.P., Mr. A. Illingworth. M.P., Mr. J. Rowntree, M.P., and Professor Thorold Rogers. M.P., were present and delivered addresses. A reedlution of confidence in the Liberal candidate was carried with a few dissentients. ANOTHER LIBERAL VICTORY.

The polling for the election of a representative tor the West Division of Edinburgh, in the room of Mr. T. R. Buchanan, who retired in consequence of a change in his views on the Irish question, commenced at eight o'clock' on Saturday. The candidates were Mr. Buchanan, who now represents.the Home- Rule Liberals, and Mr. Thomas Raleigh, alJninnist Liberal, who unsuccessfully contted South Edinburgh in 1885 as a Radical. During the first hour the polling wastrisk. A good deal of interest was shown in the proceedings, but no colours were used by either party, although the division was covered with large posters, setting forth the merits of therrespective candi- dates.
The Tesult was announced at 10 15 as follows : BUCHANAN (G) RALEIGH (U)

There were 24 spoiled papers. The constituency at pre- sent numbers 7,749, or 182 More than at the election of 1886. There were 1,207 abstentients. After the declara- tion of the poll, Mr. Buchanan addressed a large number of his supporters. He said they had won a splendid victory, and already he was sure the news of the victory had warmed the heart of the Grand Old Man. It had already brought comfort, and encouragement, and hope to every Irishman and to every friend of liberty, They had won -a battle the importance of which extended far beyond Edinburgh, and they had written " doom " upon the wall of the present Government. They had carried the cause of the real union of the Liberal party, the real union of the United Kingdom, and the real union of the British Empire to a groat and glorious victory. (Cheers.) Later on, from the door of his residence in Moray-place, Mr. Buchanan, nadressing a large crowd, alluded to the victory as a practical fram- ing to Mr. Balfour as to what the opinion of this country was regarding the course the Government were carry- ing on in Ireland, (Cheers.) The whole of Edinburgh had now declared in favour of the principles of freedom and liberty. Mr. Raleigh also addressed a meeting of his Commit- tee, and said they had been beaten but not disgraced. The legislative, unity of the country must be defended at all costa. What remained for the Unionists was to face their difficulties manfully.
