div.head: TEA PARTY AT PENKETH.
div.p: TEA PARTY AT PENKETH.

On Saturday evening, a tea party was given by the Penketh tanning Company, Limited, to its em- ploys and their wives. The tea was served in a new warehouse recently built, and may be regarded as both the annual tea party of the employ& and as a celebration of the completion of the new pre- mises. About 120 persons sat d)wn to an excellent tea, and afterwards a meeting was held, Mr. R. GARNETT occupied the chair, and remarked they were there that night as friends working together, and he did not hesitate to say that it gave him very great pleasure to see them. (Applause.) Some of them would perhaps remember the place where they were then assembled when it was faedifferent to what it was now. Mr. Garnett then related the circumstances of his buying the old Penketh brew"- ery, and of the formation of the Tanning Company in its stead, remarking that it was very pleasing to him to see the number of people who were directly and indirectly connected with the tannery. The number of persons employed at the brewery was about 20, whilst at the tannery they found employ- ment for something like 90. It was a source of gratifica- tion to him to know that the relations between those employed and the heads of departments were such that could be looked upon with great satisfaction. He believed Mr. Charles Parker had the esteem of every man and boy in connection with the place. (Applause.) Mr. Parker's desire was, he was sure' to do good to those with whom he came into contact. His one strong Wish had been to help those who were connected with the firm, and he (Mr. Garnett) was glad to know that the relations were such as commended themselv,es to his judgment. (Ap- plause.)—Mr. P. THOMPSON (one of the directors) said his knowledge of Penketh was chiefly connected with the tannery, but he must say that he had been greatly sur- prised at the wonderful development which had taken' place in that neighbourhood. Six years ago it was a very peculiar place to carry on the tanning business. They did not at first know what to do with the vats of the brewery, but in a very short time a transformation scene took place, and they found that the old buildings adapted themselves to the new business in a wonderful fashion. He very heartily endorsed the chairman's re- marks regretting the absence of the esteemed ,chairman of the company, Mr. W. Walker, of Whitehaven. He, felt somewhat sad as he missed the genial smile and hearty welcome of their late secretary, Mr. Parker. After his death he scarcely had the heart to.visit Penketh. i Mr. Parker met everyone n such a pleasant manner that it was always a pleasure to come and see him, and it i was with the most profound regret that they dwelt upon his memory. He (Mr. Thompson) was glad to see that another gentleman had been appointed secretary from whom they had the very highest expectations namely, Mr. William Wigfield. He hoped he would be able to win their esteem as well as the late secretary. (Ap- plause.)—The CHAIRMAN said he would take that oppor- tunity of referring to one question and that was thrift. There was a penny bank at Penketh, and at the present time there was something like £BOO belonging to the in- habitants of Penketh invested iq that club. He urged them to make such provision foi the time of their old age that they would not then be dependent upon the par- ish or the kindness of their friends.—Mr. E. Walker and Mr. W. E. Walker having addressed the meeting, Mr.l C. E. PARKER said he was pleased to see that, in the pre- ' vious addresses, prominence had been given to the part the workmen had taken in contributing to the success of the company. In the work of the past year, in the vari- ous improvements made in the erection of their new warehouse, there had been a great deal of good work and good thought, and he (the speaker) was glad and proud to recognise it. That new warehouse was not alone the work of the architect, the directors, or the manager, but it was the tangible embodiment of the best thought and labour of the many workers who had taken part in the rearing. He hoped no cause would ever arise to prevent the workers from continuing to share in the success of the company. (Applause.)—During the even- ing songs were rendered by Mr. John Budden Mr. R. H. Posnett, Mrs. C. E. Parker, Miss Fanny Garnett, and Mr. R. E. Parker. The proceedings were brought to a close with the singing of the National Anthem.

'SHOOTING IN urn Svnxwrs.—At the Leeds Assizes, on Wednesday, Ralph Williamson, a Sheffield confectioner, was sentenced to 15 months' imprisonment for shooting at a man named Bridges in one of the streets of Shef- field on the night of the 6th February. Bridges was about to chastise Williamson for misbehaviour towards his daughter when Williamson fired at him. • Mr. Justice Day, while not excusing the prosecutor's violence, said that if more fathers adopted the same course there would be fewer girls brought to the endless miseries witnessed in our courts of law.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The British steamers Roebuck and Edinburgh have been in collision 30 miles south-east of St. Vincent. The former vessel sank, and the crew were landed at Gib- raltar, where the latter put in with her fore compart- ment full of water and her bows damaged. A DANGEROUS Paecrics.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Friday, Bernard M'Cullen was charged with sleeping in a coke oven.—The prisoner said he had come from Whitehaven, and was on his way to the Ship Canal at Warrington.—Discharged on a promise to leave the town. _ . .

On Saturday night, the Glasgow Fire Brigade were summoned to an outbreak which had occurred at 20, Brown-street, in the dwelling of William WLeod. On the firemen entering the house they discovered the wife, of 11PLeod lying dead. Her clothes were in a blaze, and the body was frightfully burned.

FALL DE A GAMEKEEPER AND RTS SON OVER A Rocs. —On Saturday, while Mr. Alexander Clark, head game- keeper to Sir John Ramsden, Loch Ericht Dalwhinnie, was out on Loch Ericht ground, accompanied by his son, they lost their way, owing to the severe weatber and the depth of snow, and fell over a high rock. Mr. Clark died soon afterwards from his injuries, and his son lies it; a precarious state. DISASTROUS BOILER EXPLOSION.—EarIy on Saturday morning one of the boilers at the paper works of Mr. Turner at New Mills, near Stockport, burst. Great havoc wastcaused among the buildings, the damage to which will amount to several thousand pounds; but happily no person was injured. The night hands were leaving rind the day workmen had not arrived when the accident occurred. Over-pressure is supposed to have caused the mishap. Tits ACCIDENT AT A WELSH QI7ARRY.—Me. Griffith Jones Williams. the coroner for Merionethshire opened an inquest at Festiniog on Saturday upon the bodies of the five men who were killed on Thursday by the fall of a bridge at the Welsh slate quarries. Formal evidence of identity haying been given, the inquiry was adjourned for the attendance of an inspector from the Board of Trade. A subscription has been opened for the widows and families of the deceased.

THE IMPRISONED CROFTERS.—Mrs. Gordon Braille, On her way to Lewis to advocate her scheme of crofter emigration to Tasmania, stopped some time at Edinburgh, where by permission of the authorities she visited the female crofters who were sentenced to imprisonment for their share in the recent disturbances. Mrs. Baillie found them very much dejected, as they were entirely ignor- ant of the condition of their families, whom they had been compelled to leave in the direst distress. At the Bolton Police Court, on Monday, singular revela- tions were made during the hearing of a charge preferred against Nicholas Fish, landlord of the George and Dragon Hotel, for a breach of the Licensing Act The defendant had been in the habit of giving a weekly subscription to the labourers out of work, and two calling as usual, he allowed them to drink spirits from the taps. They drank themselves insensible, and one, named Wonky, died from the effects. The man drank rum, brandy,and whisky indiscriminately. THE PRIMATE ON RECREATION.—At the opening of the Oxford Hall, Bethnal Green, on Saturday, the Archbishop of Canterbury (Dr. Benson) referred to the importance of recreation grounds. He said he had himself given up a large field at Lambeth for the remotion of young men and children, and had refused to listen to appeals made to him to hand it over for use as an "open space" for grown-up people to walk up and down in—objecting as he did to having everything so spic-and-span that they would be afraid of children spoiling the grass.

Nxerrnia. HORSE FIRE: BRAVE RESCUE.OF EIGHT PERSONS —A very exciting scene occurred at a fire which broke out on ronday morning, at a house in Whitecross- street, London. tenanted by J. Balderson, a greengrocer, and his family. Before a fire-escape could arrive, several people were at the upper windows, surrounded by smoke and flames, and loudly screaming for help. They were implored to wait a few minutes, and when the fire-escape arrived, Fireman Mc.Kerell bravely ascended again and again, and brought down eight persons amid the blinding smoke and flames. The fire was subsequently extinguished,

THE ASSAULT ON LORD HOWARD DR WALPEN.—The charge aceaintt Major 'Kildare Burrowes of assault- ing Lord 'Howard zde Walden was proceeded with on Saturday at Westminster Police Court. In re-examina- tion Lord de Walden said he did not know Mrs. Burrowes when he found her in his house or he should.have treated her differently. He had forbidden his mother-in-law to come to the house,- She knew perfectly well she had no right to be there. During his wife's illness he went every night to the Carlton, and at ten o'clock generally left for the Grosvenor. Sometimes he could not do this, owing to the confusion in his household and delay in seeing the doctor. Police evidence of the assault followed. Medical evidence was given as to the injuries of the complainant. Mr. Partridge intimated that he should send the defen- dant for trial, and the case was adjourned. A DESPERATE ATTEMPT TO MURDER A WIFE.— Booth Shaw, an iron-turner, aged O, was brought up before Mr. Justice Day, at the West Riding Assizes at Leeds, on Saturday, to receive sentence for attempting to murder his wife, Lucy, at Bradford.—His Lordship said that had the poker, with which the prisoner beat the head of his wife, not broken by the force of the blow, and but for the intervention of a young man, the prisoner would undoubtedly have been tried for murder and convicted. This attack was the last of a long series of brutalities exercised towards his wife by the prisoner. She had often forgiven him, but once he had had to fly before the operation of the law. On this last occasion he threw lii r wife on the floor and, having kicked awl stamped upon her, he deliberately took up a poker and broke it over her head. It would be an injustice tc society to sentence such a brute to less than 20 years' penal servitude.

• THREE PERSON'S BURNED TO DEATH AT DI7DLEY.— On Sunday morning, a fire broke out on the premises of Mr. Joseph Russell, boot and shoe dealer, High-street. Dudley, and three persons were burnt to death At the time of the occurrence there were four person sleening in Um attics, Mr. Russell, Miss Ellen Russell, Miss Eliza Russell, who was on a visit, and a servant girl named Elizabeth Christman. .The fire broke out in the middle room of the building, and spread rapidly upwards, pre- venting the inmates from escaping.. They stood scream- ing for help, but when the fire escape was raised, and the attics entered, three of the inmates had perishen, their bodies being terribly burned. These were Mr. Russell, Miss Ellen Russell, and the servant girl. Miss Eliza Russell, who first discovered the fire, after vainly endeavouring to secure the retreat of the other three persons, rushed throtigh the attic window on to a tank, and from thence to an adjeiiiing building, where she was found by the firemen, half dead with fright and cold. SINOULAR DEATH OF A BOY BY HANOING.-A singular incident occurred at Bury, on Saturday, whereby a lad. 11 years of ag,'e, hanged himself in his bedroom. The lad's name was Edwin Platt, and he lived, along with his elder brother, John, ivro years older than himself, with his grandmother; in Brook-street, Freetown. Both lads went to school, and were kindly treated by their relative. The brothers slept together, and about -half-past seven o'clock they both awoke and had a pillow fight in bed. When John went downstairs deceased, who was in ,the habit of lying rathet late on Saturday mornings, told him to call him up at eleven o'clock. Deceased was left in bed, and nothing more was heard of him until half- past ten o'clock, when Mrs. Booth, an aunt, went up- stairs and found deceased hanging to a nail in the wall. He seems•to have tied a scarf and a leather strap toge- ther, to have tied the scarf round his neck and placed the buckle at the other end of the strap over the nail while standing on the foot of the bedstead. The boy was lively and high spirited, and not at all likely to have Committed suicide, and it is conjectured that be VMS in- dulging in a practical joke when he slipped off the foot of the bed and could not recover himself. He was quite dead when found.

, MURDER AND SUICIDE BY A MOTHER. A mur- der and suicide were committed at Sheffield, on Saturday morning. undervery distressing circumstances. There lived at \Weedon-street, Carbrook, a labourer, named Richard Henry Richards, with his wife and four children. The father worked at nights, and at nine o'clock on Friday evening Mrs. Richards took him his supper, and she then seemed more cheerful than usual. At six 'o3cloCk on Saturday morning she called the tw,i eldest boys to go to work. When one of them returned home to breakfast, not seeing his mother about, he went to her bedroom, and found her lying in bed with her throat cut. Her little daughter, two years of age, was by her side with her throat cut; and the youngest boy, aged five, was lying across the mother, and endeavouring to induce her to speak. The boy hastened for his father' who, on reaching the bedside, exclaimed. "Why, who has cut her throat?" She made answer, "I have done it, Dick." She died soon after, but the child, by breathing through the severed winlapipe, lived on for some hours. Richards arid his wife, who came to Sheffield About twelve years ago, are natives of Shrop- shire, and her mother and aunt were both subject to fits of extreme depression, and the aunt was once in an asylum. Mrs. Richards; it is supposed, when she Corn. was similarly attacked. mated the shocking deeds, - _

WIGAN COAL AND IRON COMPANY., LESIITED.—The report states that the coal trade of the district had continued in a depressed condition, prices had again been lower, but no change had been made in the wages paid to colliers. The iron furnaces in operation had continued to work well, but the iron trade had again been exceed- ingly depressed, though a slight rally took place towards the end of the half-year. In order to meet the altered conditions of the trade the directors had thought it desirable to place themselves in a position to supply steel to those customers who required it, and works having that object in view,had been commenced. The auditors state that the sum of £28,999 had been deducted for depreciation, whilst Mil additions to plant had amounted to £12,848. The debenture debt had been reduced by the sum of £ls,o,3olnlling-due and paid off within the half-year. After chartzing interest on deben- tures amounting to £2,130 ss. 4d., there was a profit of £7,114 on the whole operations of the company for the half-year, and this, added to the sum of £26 brought forward from last half-year, made a total Of £7,140 available for dividend. The directors propose to with- draw a sum of £2,000 from the reserve fund, and to recommend a dividend at (he rate of 1 per cent, per annum, free of income-tax, which will absorb £9,048, leaving £92 to be carried forward. This is the same as the dividend declared for the first half of last year.

Fair Traders who are fair-minded and open, therefore, to conviction, should turn to an article in the "Westminster Review" for February, on "Free Trade versus Fair Trade." They will find the points of their case, in so far is there is a case, well put, for "The Westminster "is philosophic in its Liberalism as well as advanced. But when the considerations are given for leaving well alone, the evidence is overwhelming. Those who advo- cate Fair Trade never lose sight of the fact tho agriculture is a great industry in this as in other countries; it is admitted that it is useless ts° talk of taxing imported manufactured goods, un- less some kind of protection is to be given to the farmer. Indeed, the fixed idea of the aversg3 Fair Trader is that some sacrifice must be made ill order to free us from agricultural depression; for, when that is accomplished, trade will be sure to improve. As a matter of fact, England is less agricultural than other countries; and we have need, above all things, to see to it that we pre- serve our supremacy in the neutral markets of the world, and as general carriers for the world. The census of 1880 shows that not more than 5.3 of the population of England and Wales were actively engaged in agricultural pursuits; while "no less than 24.5 per cent were engaged in manufactures." A great deal has been said from time to time as to the progress which our continental neighbours are making in their methods of manufacture, and we do not deny their progress, especially as to the manufacture of goods that require for their pro- duction artistic skill and technical knowledge. But as yet they are, in the main, a long way behind this country. Whilst, roundly speaking, 25 per cent of the population of England are employed in manufactures, in Prussia the per centage is only 13, in France 12, and in Austria 10. It is a perti- nent question to ask how it is that, with the supe- rior education given on the continent, England still takes the lead as a manufacturing country? If Free Trade is the huge blunder that somepeople would have us believe it to be, how is it that we still hold our place in the front rank? Our con- tention is that those who advocate Fair Trade know not what they do. England maintains her supremacy because her ports being open, and raw and partially manufactured goods coming to hand cheaply, she can manufacture cheaply, with the result, in the end, that she can sell, in most parts of the earth, at lower prices, than can be quoted by her handicapped competitors. Force Fair Trade upon us—raise prices all round—and it will inevitably follow that competition will be keener, and that we shall lose much of the foreign trade that we now keep al- most exclusively to ourselves. Take the case of what Free Trade has done for us in the shipping business. Between 1850 and 1860, when wooden walls were the order of the day, the United States, having an immense advantage in the way of

cheap timber, were active in ship-building, and se- cured "one-third of the total ocean-carrying trade of the world." The States were a Protec- tionist country then; but they have since then been "cut out" by England, a Free Trade coun- try. And why? Because, as seems patent to us, Free Trade, when the conditions of competition Were in other respects equal, turned the balance 11l our favour. Iron and steel took the place of timber in the making of ships; and then England and the United States stood, apart from the prin- ciple of Free Trade, on an equal footing. Amer- ica's resources as to ore, and coal, and labour, were at least as great as those of England, and the Battle of the Ships was a hard-fought one. But this country triumphed, and the triumph is com— plete. The tonnage of the United States is now "little more than 100,000 tons, or about one thirty-seventh part of the steam tonnage of the United Kingdom." Thirty years ago the United States built herself a million tons of new shipping every year; now their annual output has fallen to about 1.50,000; while the output of the United Kingdom has advanced from 220,000 to as much as a million tons in a single year." Facts such as these speak trumpet-tongued in favour of Free Trade. Let the Fair Traders tell us, if they can, brow matters would be mended by pntting the United States in a position to equal us in the carrying trade of the world, as would be the case : if we resorted, like the Americans, to Protection? We have won in the struggle, and we are reap- ing the fruits of the victory. Let us praise the bridge that has carried us safely over, and not like Inadnien undermine its bulwarks.

JUSTICE GRANTHAM followed in the train ef many other judges, on Tuesday, in referring to the drink traffic as a terrible source of crime ; but the terms in which he expressed himself were stronger and more emphatic than any we have Previously heard. It would seem as if he was de- termined to pierce the thick skins of the pachy- derms who are at the head of "the trade," and who, while growing rich as CRESUS out of the de- gradation of their fellow-creatures, profess, in their smug, respectable way, to be shocked at the *hocking things which so many poor wretches do Whilst under the influence of the liquor which they brew. The case before his lordship was one in which a seaman of the name of Goal:4:w was con- Irieted, on Monday, of attempting to murder his Wife by jumping on her and stabbing her a num- ber of times with a knife. It was elicited that the Prisoner, previous to the crime, had been supplied -with liquor after he was drunk, whereupon the Judge ordered the publican to be subpcened to ap- Pear in court next day. After referring on Tuesday to the disgraceful .state of things which the eyi- -4deooe disclosed, Mr. Justice GRANTHAM said is only regret was that he could not place the Offending publicans in the box to take the punish- Sent which would have to be inflicted upon the pri- acner for this crime. He intended to do all he •couid to punish keepers of houses who gave spirits, which acted as a poison on the men to whom they were given, in order that they might make unholy Profits out of this horrid traffic. It was a pity there Were men like the owners of the place mentioned who were content to live on ill-gotten gains, got Ut ef hard earned wages of poor men by putting tien into their houses to manage them. He sup- Posed they themselves were too respectable to man- age a large house of this kind, and they put in men to do their dirty work, not thinking that while they were all the time living on the fat ot the land they Were bringing to misery many poor wretched wo- • teen, and making children almost die of starvation because of the inducements offered to their fathers to drink away their money in the manner in which the prisoner had done. The great brewers, distillers, and public-house 'Owners, will, if this protest should reach their ears, he startled to find that it is possible for a judge to lil3Peeak of them in these terms. But they need to ,1 'tattled ; it requires to be brought home to them t7lat they do not get rid of their responsibility for °lag the devil's work by subscribing to a cathe- dral or building a church. How can these men '3'" Lead us not into temptation," when daily Itrld hourly they are baiting their traps in order that men may be led into temptation and fall therein? They may put miles of sweet meadow ,arid between their homes and their" hell-holes ;" but the taint is on them—they cannot escape from the consequences of their inequity. Society has heen altogether too easy with offenders of this tYPe ; they have been flattered and exalted be- cause they were rich. There are signs, however, of a better state of things, and it is not the least
4wilung these signs when one of Her Majesty's Judges speaks out from the seat of judgment, _ .

-- -and denounces the evil in words that blister and .hurn• But Mr. Justice GRANTHAM did more than condemn what was being done; he reminded the •tuthorities that they have a duty to perform. "It Was desirable," he said, "that the magistrates' at- tention should be called to this matter, in order that persons who served drink to drunken persons alight have a lesson given to them." It is to be hoped that magistrates, not only in Liverpool but elsewhere, will act upon the hint thus given them. There is a fine field of labour open to them. It is notorious that, compared with convictions for drunkenness, convictions of publicans for serving drink to drunken persons are ridiculously small. Where there is a sinner in the shape of a drunken

citizen, there is usually, somewhere, another sinner in the person of a publican who has supplied the cfrink. Of the two, the latter may indeed be the greater law breaker, in that he may have supplied drizk to several intoxicated men and women. We hear not a little about respect for law and order. Let the law be obeyed in this respect, and the community will be more orderly. Let publicans who break the law be brought before the magis- trates, and, at the proper time, let licenses be withdrawn from houses of evil repute. There Will then be less need for such scathing denun- ciation as that of Mr. Justice GRANTHAM at the Liverpool Assizes.

The Physical Recreation Society are doing use- ful work by exciting an interest in gymnastics in towns like Warrington which are not blessed with a gymnasium. The attendance, on Monday, at the assault-at-arms, given in the Drill Hall, by the Inembers of the Liverpool Gymnasium shows that there is no lack of interest, at any rate, in a tourna- /pent ; and it is not unreasonable tabforthat all that la needed in Warrington, for the establishment of gymnasium, is a well-directed effort. Mr. A. ALExANnEn displays the right spirit as Director ef the Liverpool institution; he is willing to lend what assistance he can in an honorary way, or he l'nll make a move in the town himself, if he is fairly BhPported by the leading inhabitants. Surely, After this, there should be no difficulty in getting together a Committee who will see a beginning hiade in one form or another. It would be a good thing if the venture could be made on such a scale a 8 to permit of school children being in some (legree drilled and exercised during school hours. Out-door sports are invaluable, and they are. the glory of English youths ; but it is well known that Particular games have a tendency to develop aPecial sets of muscles at the expense of other sets. I.lle best remedy for this is undoubtedly the well-

ordered and well-regulated exercise of the gym- nasium. Then there are many young men of se- dentary occupation who have little opportunity, especially in winter, of taking part in out-door sports. They have an especial need of exercise, and they are the last to obtain it. The conse- quence is that they begin to feel "out of sorts," and "off their feed." They turn to stimulants— get a "pick-me-up" which really proves a " knock- me-down " ; and their last state is worse than their first. It is easy to say that people can always take exercise, if they are determined about it. The mischief is that they are not determined. Man is a gregarious animal; he likes to eat, drink, and exercise himself along with his fellows. As things go, there is no lack of provision for eating and drinking in company; the defect consists in there being little or no provision for men taking exercise together. There is room, it should also be added, to stimulate a healthy spirit of emulation; and this is provided by the possibility of being called upon to display, in public, feats of strength and skill. Our singers and reciters take infinite pains to prepare themselves for gratifying large audi- ences, and why should not the youths of the gym- nasium do the same? On thd continent, and more especially in Germany, great attention is paid to physical training; and military drill is enforced to such an extent as to ensure that none of the young men shall be weak from lack of exercise. We are not advocates of compulsory military drill; exercise should be taken voluntarily and in a pleasanter way. There is every need of strength, bodily and mental, for the pace gets quicker every year; and, whilst there is no desire to ascertain whether the Englishman is a match for the Ger- man on the battlefield, there is every need to be ready to prove that he is not a whit behind him in the workshop, in the counting house, and on the mart. There is such a thing, of course, as over- training, and it is worse, individually, than under- training; but it will be soon enough to talk about that when, through the praise-worthy efforts .of Councillor WRIGHT, the projected Warrington Gymnasium is in full swing.

The proceedings at the meeting, on Monday, of the shareholders of the Ship Canal Co. show that the undertaking is in good heart. The momentary de- preciation of shares does not seriously disturb any- one, and the bulk of the shareholders will be dis- posed to take Sir Joseph Lee's advice and hold on. With regard to the new bill for the acquirement of additional land, it was intimated that it might not be necessary if landowners were found reasonable. It is due to landowners to say that, so far, they have, on the whole, met the Company in fair spirit. And so they ought to do; they will be the great- est gainers in the end.

A Liberal majority of 1194 for West Southwark is a very pretty figure as it stands, especially when it is remembered that the Liberal majority at the last election was 113 only. This is irritating to the Tories; but, odd as it may seem, they are more distressed at the majority of 46 for West Edin- burgh. Southwark is essentially a constituency of the Masses; but West Edinburgh is more typical of the Classes; and to actually lose a seat there— really, what could be worse ? If this is the case after six months of coercion, what will become of "the union of the Unionists " after twenty monthsl of it—to say nothing of twenty years?
LOCAL NEWS.

SALVATION ARMY, WIDNES.—Mrs. Rose Bentley, the converted music hall singer, has addressed well attended meetings at Widnes this week. EROWN'ED IN THE CANAL AT EUNCORN.-011 Tuesday afternoon Mr. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest at Runcorn on the body of Elizabeth Broom, six years of age, whose parents reside at 93, Percival's-lane.—On Fri- day evening the girl was sent to the Branch Post Office at Top Locks, and as she did not return a search was made for her. No clue as to her whereabouts could, however, be discovered, and the water of the canal was dragged, but it was not until Monday afternoon that the dead body was brought to the surface, a short distance from her home. A verdict of "Found drowned" was re- turned. DISTRIBUTION OF PRIZES AT WIDNES.—The prizes gained by the scholars attending St. Mary's and St. Paul's Sunday Schools, Widnes, for regular attendance and good behaviour, were presented by-Mrs. Wright-Williams on Thursday evening. The vicar, the Rev. J. Wright- Williams, presided, and speaking as to the question whether the giving of prizes was moral or immoral, lie said he thought it brought out many noble traits in a young mind, rivalries that in many instances were per- fectly fair, perfectly noble, and entirely Christian. The proceedings were interspeised with recitations and dialogues. The usual votes of thanks were accorded. THE WOUNDING CASE AT WIDNES.—At the Liverpool Assizes on Monday, before Mr. Justice Grantham, Mary Jane Keegan (39) was found guilty of having, on the 12th November, at Widnes, when in an intoxicated con- dition, unlawfully and maliciously wounded Ellen God- frey, an old woman over 60 years of age. His lordship, in passing sentence of twelvemonths' imprisonment, said this was another instance of the effects of that drunken- ness which prevailed among the prisoner's class. He was not sure whether—as he would like—he could not find some means of punishing those who supplied the drink. Publicans who supplied people with liquor when they were worse for drink, and allowed them to get drunk on their premises, ought to be placed in the dock side by side with the criminals themselves. ROSE OF SHARON LODGE, RUNCORN, G.U.o.o.—The proceedings at the meeting of the members of this lodge on Saturday evening possessed more than ordinary in- terest. Brother John Rogerson, who has ably fulfilled the duties of treasurer for eight years, is about to leave the town, and as a token of the esteem and regard in which his services are held, he was presented with a beautifully illuminated emblem, suitably framed and ap- propriately inscribed. Brother George Rutter made the tation on behalf of the lodge, and Brother Roger- son, in acknowledging the gift, mentioned the fact that he had been a member of the Order for 22 years, and had filled the various offices of the lodge from the lowest to the highest, and had also been G.M.for the district. (Applause.) He was happy in knowing that during his term of Office the lodge had been prosperous, and had now a membership of over 350, with a capital of about £2,500, outside the district funeral fund, whieh was £7OO. This success had been attained through the arduous labours of the various officers, and he returned thanks for the kindness extended to him. A DANGEROUS DOG AT LARGE AT RUNCORN.—At Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. James* Rey - nolds and Mr. A. Thomas, George Jepson Knight, ac- countant, High-street, was summoned to answer a charge of allowing his dog to be at large insecurely muzzled. Ile was also charged with having a dog which was danger- ous, and was not kept under proper control.—Mr. F. A. Lake defended.—John Ingham, a telegraph boy, said on the 13th inst. he was passing Mr. Ashton's office, when Mr. Knight's dog attacked him and bit him on thethigh. He at once went into Dr. McDougall's surgery, and he had the wound burned out. He had not spoken or done anything to the dog, which had a "bit of a strap" round its nose, but it was not securely muzzled.—Mr. Lake said he had advised his client to plead guilty. He explained that Mr. Knight was out of the town at the time, and this was the first intimation he had received that the dog was not securely muzzled. In. the second case there was no objection to the Bench making an order, as Mr. Knight had decided to destroy the dog as he did not desire to be summoned to the court. In the first case a fine of 5s was imposed, and in the second case an order that the dog should be securely fastened up or should be destroyed. The costs amounted to £1 17s. BIBLICAL EXAMINATION AT WIDNES.—OH Thursday afternoon, Mr. T. S. Timmis, chairman of the Widnes School Board, presented to each of the pupil teachers of the Board Schools who passed first class in the Scripture examination of 1886 a valuable prize, comisting either of Farrar's " Life of Christ," Thompson's " The Land and the Book," or Tennyson's works, all the gift of Mr. R. H. Davis. The presentation took place in Simms' Cross School, Mr. Davis and Mr. G. H. Danby also being present. Mr. Timmis, in presenting the prizes to the teachers, spoke of the necessity of a Biblical educa- tion, a subject on which Mr. Davis also spoke. The fol- lowing are the names of the winners :-4th year, Mary Burrill ; 3rd year, Sophia Smith, Eliza Leach, Jessie Benbone, and W. J. Davis ; 2nd year, Sarah Stringer, John Birkenhead, Elizabeth Glover, and William Jones; Ist year, M. E. Benbone, W. Kennan, and Mary F. Kirkham. The following were each accorded a prize for good conduct and industry whilst studying for the ex- amination :—Sarah Stringer, Jessie E. Itenbone, Mary F. Kirkham' and Kate W. Norris. It was stated by Mr. Danby that Mr. Davis intended presenting prizes to the successful students, and for good conduct and industry for the 1887 examination. The examiner for 1888 was the Vicar. FARM FIRES AT WIDNES .—About midnight on Sunday, a fire was discovered to have broken out on the farm pre- mises of Mr. John Kelsall, Lowerhouse-lane, Widnes. In- formation was at once conveyed to the fire engine sta- tion, and the brigade was quickly on the scene. The flames had got a good hold of an outbuilding containing hay and straw, and the fire was not extinguished until after nearly three hours persistent efforts. The building was completely gutted and besides the destruction of the hay Sze., a number of implements were much damaged. The loss is considerable, but fortunately it is covered by insurance in the Westminster Office. The property is owned by Madame de Falbe, of Hooton Hoo, Bedford- shire, About the same time a fire broke out in an out- building on the farm of Mr. Longton, Milton-road. Through the energetic efforts of a number of constables, under Inspector Keighley, and several other persons the flames were subdued without the intervention of the fire brigade. A large quantity of hay and straw was dam- aged. Four horses and a number of cattle were in an adjoining building, and would probably have been suf- focated but for the timely assistance of Mr. Martin Tay- lor, who liberated them. This property also belongs to Madame de Fs.lbe. Suspicions are entertained that the :es are the work of an incendiary. WIDNES FREI LIBRARY LECTURES.—The fourth of this series of free lectures was given in Lacey-street School- room on Monday evening. The lecturer was Dr. Hurter, and the subject he had undertaken to expound was "The philosopher's stone." The room was well filled with an appreciative audience, and Dr. O'Keeffe presi- ded. Dr. Hurter, at the outset, made a reference to the rise and progress of the chemical trade in Widnes, humourously describing the works as manufactories for producing pure gold from salt. The things which the people of Widnes strove to obtain, wealth and health, were held to be indispensable for human happiness all the world over, and at all times men had endeavoured to gather riches and to preserve health and long life to en- joy them. But not at all times were men satisfied to re- sort to such processes for obtaining gold as the people of this country were now using, processes known by the names of industry and thrift" These peoole looked out for a quicker and easier way of becoming rich, and they verily believed that there was such a way for obtaining gold and health and life everlasting by means of the philosopher's stone,which was credited with the power of changing the commoner metals into gold and silver. In an interesting manner, the lecturer related a number of the achievements and discoveries made by the philoso- phers in the search for this marvellous stone, and the immense wealth with which tradition credited them. The audience were much entertained by a number of ex- Messrs. There is a rumour that Mr. Chamberlain is to
—.- become "Sir Joseph" and a G.C.8.; but we refuse to believe it.. We cannot think he is so far gone as to give himself away in this fashion.

The result of the Doncaster election is dis- appointing; but it does not eclipse the glory of West Southwark and West Edinburgh. There must be a dark object in the picture, if only to show the strength of the light.

Sir Henry tiolland has been raised to the peerage, and has resolved to take the title of Baron Knutsford. Some people may think that one ford is as good as another in crossing a stream; but "Sir Henry" thinks otherwise; he is dead nuts on Knutsford.

The " Standard" says Mr. Coghill intends to move on the Procedure Rules—" That this House shall not sit later than the Ist day of August in each year." But what if the old Parliamentary hen has hatched nothing? Will she not, in that case, be allowed to sit a little longer?

It is to the credit of the Home Secretary that he gives no countenance to prize fighting. In this respect, he may be said to stare the Prince of Wales in the face. "Old Pam," when Prime Minister, and Sir G. Lewis, when Home Secretary, talked about a "set to" as if it were quite 'legal. So we are improving, however slowly. '

A Liverpool contemporary says:—" It is believed that next spring Lord Cross will resign the Secre- taryship for India, and that he will be succeeded by Lord Randolph Churchill." But what is to be done with Lord Cross? It will never do fcr the nation to lose his servioes. The thing is to find out the bent of his genius. How would it be to make him a Grand Groom of the Bedchamber, or a Gold Candlestick-in-waiting?
preseni

The sudden death of Provost Jellett, of Trinity College, Dublin, is found to be due to blood-poison- ing, "caused by the escape of sewer gas in his house,". although last year the sum of £250 was spent in " improving " the sanitary arrangements of the building. There has been negligence here which the law ought to regard as criminal. Builders who deliberately " scamp" their work should be treated as scamps.

• Little Josef Hofmann, the phenomenal pianist, is said to be severely overtaxed. His father has decided that he shall take a few years rest, and complete his education. There are people who in- sinuate that the father sees things in a new light, because of the thousands of dollars which are being subscribed to carry out the object. But what of that? We shouldn't ourselves mind rest- ing for a lifefime if the subscription was large enough.

At an inquest held at St. Helens, on Saturday, on the death of an old man named Daniel Kearns, it transpired that he was 80 years of age, and that he had died whilst tramping towards Warrington with his son in search of work. He had literally fallen by the way. There is something especially sad in the idea of this old man tramping on at eighty, and going till he could go no farther; and is there not something wrong in our social system when such a thing should be possible?

With regard to the jurors in the action of Blunt v. Byrne, it is stated that eleven jurors were in favour of the plaintiff on the issue that the meet- ing would not endanger the peace, and ten on other issues. The jurors were mainly of opinion that the Woodford meeting would have operated towards peace. This means that Mr. Blunt has been wrongfully imprisoned; he is where Mr. Bal- four might more properly be. But the gods are just; Mr. Ball our is getting his gruel outside.
WIS

Nothing succeeds like success, whether the campaign be military or agrarian. An item of news from Ireland informs us that the struggle between Mr. Burton, of Carrigholt Castle, and his West Clare tenants has at last been amicably set- tled. It is over fourteen months since the Plan of Campaign was adopted on Mr. Burton's estate. The tenants demanded a reduction of about l Os. and 6s. in the pound on judicial and leaseholders' rents respectively. This demand was at first re- fused, but this week it has been granted, the tenants paying a year's rent. This is regarded as a great victory for the Plan of Campaign.
fires

It will of course be said that the Campaigners are robbing the landlords; but it is not so. The reductions which are being demanded are found to be fair and reasonable. For instance, we learn that the standard rate of reduction adopted by the Clare Sub-Commissioners under the Land Act, in judgments given by them on Saturday, is between 40 and 50 per cent. This, as will be noted, is after the fashion of the Campaigners, whose object is not to rob the landlords, but to prevent the land- lords any longer robbing them. CfIAS

Another item of Irish news: "'When the of two newsvendors, charged with selling copies of 'United Ireland' and the Cork Herald' were called at Killarney Petty Sessions on Tuesday, it was announced that the police had withdrawn prosecution in each instance.' But why so ? The law is the law, and it must be enforced. What of twenty years of firm rule? Can it be that the Irish Secretary has got tired already of playing the part in the pantomime of the "bobby,' who runs in the little boys. "Why, it snits him to aT.

&MCGEE, WESTON, AND HALTON WATERWOBV.—The half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of this company will be held at the Company's Office on Monday after- noon. WIDNES LIBERAL CLUB.—The first general meeting of members was held on Saturday evening, when them was a very good attendance. The old committee was re- appointed, Messrs. Kiddie, Gordon, T. Singleton, H. Colquett, and J. Whitfield being added to their number. THE DOGS ORDER AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Thursday, Mr. T. S. Timmis, who presided, stated that the Dogs Order was still in force in Widnes and district in all its stringency until the end of March. The notices that had been published relaxing the rules did not apply to Widnes. WIDNES BAPTIST CHAPEL FORTHCOMING CONCERT.— On Monday evening next a grand concert in aid of the Widnes Baptist Chapel will be given in the Volunteer Hall. Mr. W. 11. Jude, of Liverpool, has been entrusted with the arrangements, and he has secured the services cd quite an array of talented vocalists. A MO-class entertainment may be anticipated, and the object is worthy of support. LECTURE ON PHOTOGRAPHY AT RIINCORN.—Under the

auspices of the Church Institute, a demonstration of photography was given in the National Schools on Tues- day evening by the Rev. W. Bryant, 8.A., and Mr. Charles Timmins. Mr. Bryant explained the optics and theory of photography, whilst Mr. Timmins gave a practical exposition of the art and science. By the aid of magnesium light Mr. 'Timmins photegraphed a bust in the presence of the audience, and stowed and des- cribed several processes of photography. Cordial votes of thanks were accorded to the gentlemen for the rich treat afforded. UNCLE AND NIPHEW AT VARIANCE AT WIDNES.—On Thursday. at Widnes Petty Sessions, Abraham Qlaff, a picture dealer, summoned his uncle, Samuel, Claff, fur- niture dealer, Widnes-road, for 2s 6d, the value of a pic- ture.—Mr. Knowles defended.—The complainant stated. that he sold four pictures to a Mr. Wright for 10s, pay- able by weekly instalments, on the 16th inst.. and re- ceived a shilling on account. On the following day the defendant went into Wright's house, and said they would have to be removed. The complainant was sent for to take the pictures away, and upon arriving at the house the defendant seized a picture and smashed it on his head. Wright then refused to settle the transaction.— . . . . . . . .

The Bench mformed the complainant that lie had his remedy against Wright in the County Court, and said they would grant him a summons against his uncle for assault. A WIDNES SOLICITOR'S DEFINITION OF Dnuxunsmcss.—At , Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, before Messrs. T. S. Timmis and H. Gaskell, junr., a soldier named Daniel Gilmore, who possesses the Victoria Cross for services tendered in defence of Rorkes Drift in the Zulu War, was summoned for being drunk and disorderly on Saturday night last. Constables Maitland and Cum- mings stated that the defendant was drunk on the night in question and was fighting with his knife in Barn. street, Widnes. Upon seeing the constables, Gilmour ran into the house—Mr. J. W. Knowles, solicitor, de- .. . .
fended and submitted that his client was not drunir or

he would not hay. had the sense to run into the house on observing the police. His idea of a drunken man was one of aloe fellows who embraced the lamppost, think- ing it was his wife or his sweetheart. Evidence was then called to prove that it was another man who was drunk and creating a disturbance, and not the defen- dant —The Bench considered there was a doubt in the case and dismissed the summons.

WIDNES POLICE COURT.—On Tuesday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage, Rose Kelly maffe her 81st appearance, and was fined 10s and costs for drunkenness; James Lancry, of Ditton, was fined 5s and costs for a similar offence.— On Wednesday, before Mr. G. Pilkington, James Shar- key and James Cousins, young men of no settled resi- dence, were sentenced to 14 days' hard labour for being on the premises of Messrs. Hutchinson and Co. chemical manufacturers, for an unlawful purpose.—On Thursday, before Mr. T. S. Timmis and Mr. H. PENICBTLI WES-LIWAN MUTUAL IMPILOVRISLILNT ASSOCIATION -.-On Wednesday evening, in the Wes- leyan Schoolroom, an interesting paper was- given by Mr. Sidney Garnett on his recent voyage•to,San. Francisco. The paper was well appreciated by a very good_ audience. Mr. Garnett described the various incidents of the voyage; and several views which he had, taken were handed round the room.

At the close the following members spoke in com- mendation of the paper, and various questions were asked :—Messrs. S. Watson. C. E. Parker. J. Peers, and D. Garnett. Tun SUDDEN IMATII IN THE STREET. Mr.. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Crriffin Hotel, Peasley Cross-lane, on Saturday, touch- ing the death of Daniel Kearns, 80 years of age, who died suddenly while passing along the street near the New Vaults, on the previous Thursday. Daniel Kearns, the deceased's son, stated that he and his father were travelling in search of work. Witness was a painter, but usually went about dur- ing the winter, while his trade was so bad, as a glazier. He and his father arrived at St. lielens from Liverpool about a fortnight ago, and lodged with Mrs Shepherd in John-street. On the previous Thursday morning they started for Warrington and had got near the New Vaults when his father was taken ill. He, however, rallied a little. but imme- dia,ely afterwards he fell down and expired. The jury returned a verdict of "Death from. natural causes."

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. T. S. Timmis presided, and there were present the Very Rev. Dean Finegan, the Rev. Father Clarke, Dr. O'Keeffe, Messrs. R. H. Davies, H. Wade Deacon, F. Heyes, J. W. Wareing, and G. H. Danby (clerk).

div.head: AN ALLEGED HARDSHIP.
div.p: AN ALLEGED HARDSHIP.

The District Education Committee reported that dur- ing the month of January (three weeks) there were 177 applications for the payment of fees, which were recom- mended to be paid in 172 cases. 180 persons appeared before the committee for contravention of the Education Act, and 47 were summoned and convicted by:the magis- trates. The committee recommended an alteration in the byelaws providing that "A child between ten and thirteen years of age shall not be required to attend school if such child has received a certificate from one of Her Majesty's Inspectors of Schools that it has reached the sixth standard prescribed by the code of 1876. A child between ten and thirteen years of age shown to the satisfaction of the School Board to be beneficially and necessarily employed shall not be required to attend school for more than five attendances in each week, during which the school is open, if such child has re- ceived a certificate from one of Her Majesty's Inspectors of Schools that it has reached the fifth standard."—Mr Deacon, in moving the adoption of the minutes, ex- plained that in the present byelaws a child between ten and thirteen could leave school when it had reached the fifth standard. The reason for the alteration was that there were a great many children running about the town that had passed the "required standard, and the committee thought they ought to do something to de- crease the number. There were at present in standards 5,6, and 7 in the whole of the schools in the district 960 children. Out of this number 193 were between 10 and 11 years, 354 between 11 and 12 years, and 219 between 12 and 13 years. At the end of next September all these children would be eligible to leave the school.— Dean Finegan thought the standard was a high one for some of the poor children in Widnes, and he contended that it would be a great hardship upon many parents.— The Chairman asked whether any School Boards had fixed the sixth standard.—The Clerk replied in the affir- mative, but said he did not know how these towns com- pared with Widnes.—Mr. Deacon said he had no objec- tion to referring the minutes back for a month in order to ascertain what was the custom of other Boards.—This was agreed to.
AN APPOINTMENT.

The School Managment Committee accepted the resigr- nation of William Thomas, caretaker a West Bank Schools, and:it was recommended that James Noone be appointed to his place a month on. trial, at a salary of
£1 5$ per week, with residence, taxes, water, coal, an gas free.—The minute was approved.
ADDITIONS AND ALTERATIONS.

The Sites and Building Committee recommended tha, the architects be empowered to take out the quantities for the builders for the enlargements at the Simin's Cross, Warrington-road, and West Bank Schools: and that the Committee be authorised to appoint a clerk of the works to superintend the alterations and additions at the various schools at a salary not exceeding two guineas. It was also recommended that the Board ac- cept subject to the approval of the Education Depart- ment, the tender ot Messrs. Jones and Sons, of Liver- pool, for the building of the school of cookery and addi- tions to the caretaker's house at Warrington-road Schools. It was decided to authorise the Local Board to complete the sewering of the streets adjoining Warring- ton-road Schooi.—The minutes were approved on the proposition of Mr. Davies; the Chairman observing that the alterations and additions would cost about £4,000.

div.head: FINANCE: OFFICE ASSISTANCE WANTED.
div.p: FINANCE: OFFICE ASSISTANCE WANTED.

The minutes of the Finance Committee stated that the receipts for January amounted to £ll2 13s, and assets amounting to £638 16s. It was recommended that the committee b. authorised to appoint a youth to assist in the office at a salary not exceeding ten shillings per week.—Dr. O'Keeffe moved the adoption of the minutes, and said an assistant was needed in the office, because the School Attendance Committee had given instructions to the school attendance officers not to do office work.— Mr. Deacon said it was the duty of the officers to get the children to school and not to act as clerks in the office.—Dean Finegan objected to the appointment of att adaitional clerk; and Father Clarke said the present staff in the office. was sufficient to do the work without the assistance of another clerk or of the attendance offi- cers.—Mr. Wareing, with the permission of Dr. O'Keeffe, moved that the minute be referred back to the commit- tee, who would devise sane less costly means of arrang- ing for the staff to do the work.—This was agreed to. There was no other business of public interest.

This concluded the business. MR. J. T. BRUNNER, M.P., AT STOCKPORT.

Mr. J. T. Brunner, 3f.P., opened a new Liberal Club at Stockport, on Saturday. Thera was a pro- cession through the town of several hundreds of Liberals, bearing banners, and. accompanied by brass bands. A carriage which brought up the rear con- tained Mr. Brunner, Mr. J. Dimon Barlow (the selected Liberal candidate for South Salford), and Colonel McClure, J.P: Before entering the club i premises, Mr. Brunner. addressed a large gathering in the open air. He said he never was more con- vinced that in supporting the " Grand Old Man —(cheers)—they were working by the side of one who, through his whole life, had followed the foot- steps not only of the Liberal leaders who had gone before him, but—he- said it with all reverence—in the footsteps of Christ—(hear, hear)—for he taught them to do unto others as they would be done by. They all knew perfectly well that the wrong they had done Ireland had been done in ignorance, but now, thank God, the veil had been lifted from their eyes, they knew the wants and aspirations of their countrymen in Ireland,. and they meant to give them the same liberties they possessed themselves. (Hear, hear.) Let them accept this as a fact, thab the tyrants in Ireland were not the National League, but the Government. (Loud cheers.) Their late' friend Mr. Chamberlain- (hisses and groans)—a departed statesman—(laug-hter)—parted from Mr. Gladstone and his old colleagues on the one point of allowing the Irish executive to be amenable to the Irish. Government : and he (the speaker) advised them, whenever it was put before them again that the Irish people were not fit to manage their own police, to shut their eyes and believe that just as they themselvea were fit to do that, so the Drish were fit. (Loud cheers.). In the evening Mr. Brunner addressed a large public meeting in the Albert Hall. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Eramott Barlow, J.P. Mr. BRUNNER, M.P., who was received with great cordiality, described the proceedings at Mit- thelstown, at which he was present. He had, he said, described that scene at least fifty times, and he had never yet failed to convince his hearers that a very black and dastardly deed was &nu in the name of the English people on that occasion. That meeting at Mitchelstown, he claimed, was a.legal meeting, and he claimed also that the police knew it was a legal meeting. The police attacked the crowd, and the men who resisted it had right on their side, yet one of those men had been picked out and had had 4 months' hard labour. Irbil% the police, who, illegally in attacking the crowd, did three. of them to death, were as free as he and those pre- sent. ("Shame.") There was no excuse whatever for the police to force themselves %Wendy through the crowd, and in doing so they acted in defianco of the instructions issued to them both by the Liberal and the Tory Government. There was ample room on either side to get close to the platform or brake, and the police reporter could have got within arm's length of every speaker. But what was the up- shot of all this The man who resisted that vio- lent attack was, as they knew, in prison, but those who had been guilty of murder were not to be pro- secuted. (A Voice: "That's Toryism," and " Hear, hear.") Having described a meeting at Bandon, Mr. Brunner said he had been also at a meeting at Lougbrea. in the very middle of the estates of the Most Noble the Earl of Clanricarde. (Laughter.) There it was evident, as at Bandon, that the Gov- ernment had not forgotten the words "Remember Mitchelstown," for the police did not interfere. They heard' a number of Englishmen in per-

1 feet quiet, and he believed that by that League meeting the cause of law and order was greatly advanced. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Brun- ner) .felt perfectly satisfied that that meeting would not be proclaimed; and why? Because the reputation of the Marquis of Clanricarde, not only in Ireland but in England, was so utterly, unsa- vory that no English gentleman who could avoid it would touch him with a long pole. (Laughter) and "Hear, hear.") Their Chairman had spoken. upon the question of Home Rule, and had told them that two years ago the Tories said Home Rule would be a disaster for England. Ile did not know whether in Stockport they had got over the idea. that Irishmen did them an injury when they came and worked side by side with them. He hoped they had.; but supposing that we could make Ireland as prosperous as England, there was no question that it would be to the benefit of Ireland. But would it not be for the benefit of Stockport also if there was as great a demand for labour in Ireland as there was in Stockport? Notwitstandin that, he was not going to appeal to them to support Home Rule for the benefit of their own Dockets: • he was going to appeal to their sense of fair play, and of what was right towards their neighbour. He believed that when the chance came they would grant to Ireland—no more and no less—the rights they claimed for themselves. He did not mean to say the rights they had, for they had not enough, but the rights they claimed to have. (Cheers.) In granting Home Rule to Ireland they would not be doing one tittle of harm to their own interests, for he claimed that justice to Ireland meant justice to all. (Cheers). The proceedings concluded with rotes of thanks to Mr. Brunner ;rid the chairman.

div.head: J-EWELLEMIC TRAVELLEIS AND HIS COMMISSION.
div.p: A J-EWELLEMIC TRAVELLEIS AND HIS COMMISSION.

At the Widnes County Court, yesterday, an action was heard in which Messrs. Harris and Sons, jewellers, Manchester, sued Philip Resew), of Wid- nes, for £3 12s. Bd.. balance due on sales effected on their behalf. There was a counter-claim for the same amount for commission on such sales. Mr. Swift was for the plaintiffs, and Mr. Bidet)] for the defendant. The defendant had been in the service of the plaintiffs as traveller for jewellery. In ad- dition to a salary he was to receive a commission of five per cent. on all sales over £520 a year from March, /835, to March, 1036. The defendant alleged that the sales had been £B3l, and he now claimed commission on sales amounting to £92. The pain- tiffs alleged that in the agreement with the defend- ant he was only to receive commission on sales ap- proved, and that the defendant had contrw;ted some bad business, in consequence of which there , was no. eommission due to. him. His Honour gave a verdict for the plaintiffS both on the claim anal counter claim, with costs.

div.head: I.IIIER.ALISX IN THE NORTHWICH DIVISION.
div.p: I.IIIER.ALISX IN THE NORTHWICH DIVISION.

At the meeting of the members of the General Council of the Northwich Division. Liberal Associa- tion to be held at Nortkwich to-clay (Saturday), Mr. W. Handley, the secretary, will present a reporeof the work of the Association for the past year: The report states that twelVe months ago the members met under peculiar and somewhat disappointing circumstances. The platform they had adopted, and) for which they had feught and contended, had apparently been condemned by the constituency; the general election•of 1886 follow- ing closely that a 1885, had deprived our views of all local representation in the Houseof Commons, and our respected representative was away on a tour of long dnration. They felt,, however, that such a position. of affairs was but of a temporary character, and did not reflect in anylargesense the opinion of the- majority of the constituency, but was solely duet° the suddenness with which the question of " IT,ome Rule for Ireland " had assumed the place of iirst importance.. The last annual meeting was held at Runcorn, and in. addition to the transaction of the usual ordinary business, the members unanimously decided: to affiliate with the National Liberal Federation, In the following month the Executive met, and: appointed registra- tion agents, and gave instructions forthe obtaining of the necessary books and forms for a vigorous ?rosecution of the registration, work. Mr. Brunner returned from his tour round the world in the fol- lowing June, and a demonstration welcoming his safe return was held in Winnington Park the same 'day, attended by large numlaers.from the different centres of the Division, showing that he still held an undivided place in the political affections of the constituency. Though the members had felt as— sured that locally the state of affairs was of a pass- ing nature they were startled and grieved at the cause of another appeal to the constituency, and sincerely and deeply sympathised with the sorrow— ing family in their sad: and sudden bereavement,. and respectfully bore their testimony to the many virtues of Mr. Robert Verdin. The election was fixed for August 13th, and the Unionist party selected' as their champion, Lord Henry Grosvenor - The association stuck to "the- Old Man and the cause ;" and Mr. Brunner, for the third time in twenty months, was their candidate. During the fortnight of the election campaign the amciataon held more than 100. public meetings, and this in addition to all the necessary hard work of can- vassi* and routine of preparing for the poll. Their minority of 458 waa swept away by the ad- vancing tide, and they reached' the high watermark of a Liberal majority of 1,1. The. association cheerfully ackno ivledged the valued assistance ren- dered in many ways by friends and sympathisers outside the Northwich constituency, which doubt- less contributed to the mag-afficent victory. Mr. Handley then refers to the registration work which immediately followed and quoted a table of figures showing a net Liberal gain of 110. The Executive Committee niet at Northwich on November 3rd, at which these results were. submitted, and considered satisfactory. The question of finances was espe- cially considered at this meeting, and a sub- committee was appointed with a view to exercising vigilance over income and expen- diture, the sum required annually for the work of the association being about .£3oot The Executive felt assured that, if the members of the Council not now subscribing would promise a small annual subscription, sufficitnt funds would be forthcoming to provide for and increase the effi- ciency of the Association. In conclusion Mr. Handley predicts that the Government was doomed, and urges the members of the Association to prepare for the inevitable struggle and assured victory.

ALLEGED CONCEALMENT OF BIRTH AT DUTTON.

An inquest was held on Thursday afternoon, at the Park Farm, Dutton, by Mr. J. E. Woraley. coro- ner, touching the death of an un-named infant, the daughter of Mary Jane Whitby, a domestic servant, a native of Runcorn, and employed at the farm. Fifteen gentlemen were sworn on the jury, and the following evidence was adduced : Mrs, Sarah Astbury said she lived at Dutton Park Farm. Mary Jane Whitby had been in her service I about two years and nine months, and was about 18 lyears of age. Witneee had accused Whitby of being encianre, but the latter denied it. Whitby *as rather a simple and not a forward girl. On Monday she- appeared to be very ill, and witness asked her what, was the matter with her., and she replied that she did not know, and at the girl's request some ginger and water were mixed, but this did not appear to do any good, and witness game hera little ruts-and tea, and Whitby afterwards informecrwitness that it had done her good. Witness sent for Whitby's mother, but before doing so told the girl that she thought she had either given birth, to a child or was about to do so. She replied that she had not. Whitby's mother arrived about three o'clock with her mother-in-law. Whitby's mother asked her. what she had done with the child, and Whitby re-- plied," It is in the shed in an old pan." The. elder woman went te the • place- indicated, and found the body of the child By the-Coroner: She did not appear to have made prepareliions for the birth of the child. brun7 Barker, wife of Joseph Barker,. bricklayer, of 32, Cooper-street, Runcorn, said Mary Jane Whitby was her daughter by a former husband. Herdaughter would be 17 years of age: Witness and her mother-in-law went to Dutton Park Farm on Monday afternoon, and found Whitby lying on a sofa. Witness asked here bow she was, and, whether she bad given birth to a child, She replied "yea," and on being asked where it was, she said in the shed, but denied that she had done anything wrong te•the child, or had any desire to destroy it. She, however. stated that after the child had been born it feil4. and on being asked whether the child had livekshe replied that it was • alive;, but that she did not know how long it had dived, as she was AO ill. She told witness that it was-not alive-when she took it downstairs.

Ann Barker,- wife of -Joseph Barker, of 42, Church- street, Runcorn, love corroborative evidence... Dr. J. W.- Smith, of Weaverhaany, gave evidence showing that he was sent for about four o'clock on Monday afternoon, and found Whitby lying on the sofa. Witness ascertained that a child had been. born. The body was found in a large covered pan in a shed, and the child was a female and fully developed. He ex.arained the child e but did-not. find any marks of' violence or bruises on the body. By direction of the Coroner, he had. made a peat- ' mortem examinatiou. In his opinion,. the child must have lived two or three mmutesufter birth;. but it might have lived longer. There was no doubt. that death was dueta want of care shortly after ite, birth. The girl wasin a very, weak state, and he could not imagine how she took the child down- stairs. In a conversation witness had with the girl, she informed.hina that she was confined about: five o'clock, and that the child was born alive, but that it fell on the floor. She said that she removed: the child from the room herself, and placed it in the wash-house without anyone knowing about it,. about half-past six in the morning. She also said she went to Mrs. Assbury's room in the night to tell. her that she was ill,. but could not awake her.—By Superintendent Hollingworth : There was no 'doubt that the child did not die from violence. ' Mrs. Astbury was re-called, and said that if • the OA had knocked at her bedroom door on Monday morning she would have heard her, although she 'admitted that she was-generally a sound sleeper. The Coroner explained the law on the onestion„ and said there were casea where it would be the shay of a jury to return * verdict of wilful murder against a mother where, with malice aforethought, thenhild was neglected so,as to cause its death, and the person implicated wouid be committed to the assizes to take her trial;, but if the jury were satis- fied, that the evidence- was such as to warrant them in bringing in a- verdict to the effect that the child died by misadventure, then they should return such a verdict. ..ts regarded the alleged congealment of birth, that would be another case altogether. -
Vie jury, after a short oonsultation, returned a verdict to the effect that the child died by raised- ._
venture.
SAD BURNING. FATALITY AT WARRINGTON.

.21. sad accident occurred. to a lady named Mrs.. Mary Bardsley, who lived with her sister in Wilson- Patten-street. on Saturday, afternoon. About four o'clock Miss Robinson left her sister knitting in a low. chair before the fire,.appare,ntly in her usual state of health. At half-past four a little girl came to the door and desired to see Mrs. Bardsley, and on going into the room the servant was astounded to find, her lying with her. head almost on, the tire, and with the upper part of her dress in flames.. Dr.. Sharratt and several, of the neighbours hay- ing been fetched, the unfcrtunate lady wasconveyed to the hospital, where it was found that although her body was little burned,. owing to the thickness of her garments, her head was.frightfully scorched,. and. she was totally unrecognisable. Her injuries werc immediately attended to,. though the doctors gave very little hope of her recogery. Mrs. Bards... ley. had no recollection of.how she came to fall into the- fire, but she had been for some time subject to fainting fits, and it is-surmised that she became unconscious and fell into the fire-. The noise of the opening door must haw roused her, for she rolled forward and tried to rub•her face_ She lingered in great pain until Thumlay morning, when she ex- pired at about twelve o'clock. The deceased was very well known and .re- spotted in the town, where she had lived all her life.. She. was 67 years of age. It is. expected that the interment will take place on Monday, in the burial ground attached to St. James's Church.
BREACH OF PROMISE AT W/RIIINGT(IN.

On Friday morning, in the Sheriff's Court, St. George's Hull, Liverpool, Mr. Lewis Williams sat as assessor; with a jury, to assess damages in an action for breach of promise of marriage, in which Miss Jenny Carr Howarth was the plaintiff and Mr. Thomas Langton the defen- dant. Mr. W. F. Taiylor was c.ournel for the plaintiff, and the defendant did not put in an appearance —lt was stated by Mr. Taylor, on behalf of the plaintiff, that there was no defence to the action,, and all the jury had to do was. to say what damages the plaintiff was entitle& to. There were no romantic elements in the case,, or amatory letters which were generally found in such actions. The plaintiff was thirty-four years of age, and was earning, when she met the defendant, herown living as a dressmaker in War- rington. The defendant, who was an agent of the Prue dential Insurance Company,,was betweea forty and fifty years of age, and plaintiff became acquainted with him in January, 1887, and in. March of the same. year the defendant proposed marriage to her. After various postponements it Was decided' that the marriage should take place in. September, and in August the usual notices were put up and signed, the wedding being arranged: for the 3rd September.. It was afterwards postponed to the 15th ot that mintiia and it was again put offin order to give the defendant an opportunity of consulting his mother. The date was finally fixed as the 25th September, and in the interval defendan` went with the plaintiff to Parr'S Bank and cashed a cheque to give her money to Fay things for the. house. He also bought furniture himself, took PA house, and even ordered coals. On Saturday, the 25th Septem- ber, thedefendant stayed at the house of a relative of the ple.sitiff until late in the evening, and at two o'clock next morning lie sent a friend to the plaintiff's house to say that the marriage would not take place at all, because his motler and dsters were dreadfully cut up about the proposed marriage, ane/that he could not marry her. He afterwards called on the plaintiff and told her the same thing, and said he was sorry about the matter. She replied that he had ffirted with her over and over again, and that he. must really make up his mind one way or the other. Redid not make up his mind as she asked him to do, and she then consulted a solicitor. Even after the issue of the writ, and so late as the 19th of the present month, he- wrote to her to meet him, signing himself' "Your loving Tom." The defendant, Mr. Tay- lor said, might be very loving, but lie did not come up to the scratch, and, therefore must pay for his conduct. Defendant had admitted to the plaintiff that he hadbetween £3OO and £4OO saveda and that his earnings averaged about £2 a week. Plain- tiff, in the course of her evidence, stated that the defen- dant took a house at Latchford, and kept it on for three months after declining to marry her. When she last saw him he cried, and said he was very sorry, but his sisters had persuaded him not to marry her, and had offered him £5O not to do so. Before giving up her business to marry the defendant her earnings were 255, a week.—. The jury awarded the plaintiff £5O.
