div.head: ROBBERY WITH VIOLENCE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: ROBBERY WITH VIOLENCE AT WARRINGTON.

At Liverpool Assizes. on, Wednesday, before Mr. Jades Grantham, Mabel Gandy (19), hawker; Bodelia Knockton (19), factory hand; John Hynes (29), bricklayer : and Daniel Hennessey (21), labourer, were indicted for having, at Warrington. on the Bth inst., robbed John flicking, with violenc,, stealing from him Sc in money and a muffler.—Mr. Collingwood Hope prosecuted, and Mr. A. G. Steel defended Hennessey. Mr. Collingwood Hope opened with a statement that on the Bth inst. hick- ing, who is an engine-driver, in the employ of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, had 'gone, in com- pany with a man named Evans, from Eastham to Warrington, at which place they arrived at about half-past three. In the evening, between nine and ten, they went to the Higher Angel public-house, in which the four prisoners were drinking. Gandy asked Evans, the prosecutor's companion, to stand them drinks all round, which he did. Subsequently Knockton asked prosecutor for sixpence. He be- lieved it would be made clear that the four prisoners were there as friends. Prosecutor and the men appeared to have stayed till eleven o'clock, and soon after prosecutor went out somewhat the worse for drink he was attacked by all tour prisoners. Gandy gave him a blow in the face, knocking him down, and Knockton caught hold of him by the throat. While the prosecutor was on the ground, With his mouth and nose bleeding, he was robbed of 8s and a muffler by one of the male prisoners, who rifled his pockets. Prosecutor was unable to see which of them it was. While on the ground he was severely kicked by the two men, and all the prisoners used violence to him.—Evidence was then taken, and it was shown that the prisoners, when placed along with a number of other persons at the police station, were identified by the prosecutor as the four by whom he had been assaulted. Among other items of proof against Gandy was the fact of her apron being found btaring blood spots and damp sludge, which, it was alleged, had been caused in the struggle. It also came out prematurely, owing to the persistency of Hynes in cross-examining a constable, that he had undergone a period of five years penal servitude, and that all were convicted thieves.—The Judge, in summing up. made refer- ence to the latter fact, observing that if ever there was an instance in which prisoners were unhappy in being their own counsel this was one; because had they been defended by counsel these unhappy re- cords would not have come out so early.—The jury found a verdict of guilty against all the prisoners, and the Judge, after making inquiry as to their characters individually, sentenced Gandy to fifteen calender months' imprisonment and Knockton to thirteen calender months. Hynes he sent to hard labour far eixteen Wen der months, and Hennessey to six calender months' imprisonment.

div.head: WARRINGTON LITERARY AND PHILOSOPHICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON LITERARY AND PHILO- SOPHICAL SOCIETY.

The monthly meeting of the members of this Society was held at the Museum on Tuesday even- ing, the president (Mr. R. Davies) presiding. There was a large attendance, the room being crowded. The following gentlemen were elected members, having been proposed at the previous meeting, viz.—The Rev. Priestley Prime, Dr. E. Geary, and Messrs. William Mullard, John Walker, Thomas Hall, Arthur Bennett, G. Barkas. and James Mac- Gregor.— It was announced by Mr. J. R. YOUNG, (one of the hon. secs.) that the paper at the March meeting would be read by Mr. Frank Shaw, of Manchestbr, on "Byron," and in April a paper on an art subject would be read by Mr. Barkas, master of the Warrington School of Art.—The paper of the evening was one on "Polarised Ligle.," by Mr.,Al- fred Fryer, of Manchester. The lecture which was illustrated by the oxy-hydrogen lantern proved to be very interesting, notwithstanding the somewhat ob- struse character of the subject, and the lecturer was frequently applauded.—At the conclusion of the paper, the president remarked that, according to geologists, the game of England as a manufacturing country would be Played out by about the close of the next century, for it was calculated by able men that at the rate they were using their coal and sendina it wholesale out of the country, they should have to do without that mineral in about 120 years. It behoved them, therefore to try what they could do in the meantime to supply the place of coal in anticipation of its going, and it was to re- 'searches in light and heat that they must look for what would to their descendants supply the place of the illu- minating material which they now used. (Applause.)— Alderman HOLMES moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Fryer. He did so, he said, with very great pleasure indeed. He knew that Mr. Fryer was very closely engaged in busi- ness pursuits, and had been for a considerable length of time, and therefore the following , of that study must be done at some sacrifice. He knew also that Mr. Fryer was always willing and anxious to do a good turn to his neighbours if it was in his power. (Applause.)—Mr. J. RYMER Younci, in seconding the vote of thanks, said that the polarikope had been of infi- nite importance in the world of analysis. On the simple fact given them by scientists that certain crystals had the power of splitting a ray of light falling upon them into two rays, which afterwards travelled in different directions, was based a system of examina- tion which analysts now used to determine the purity of many drugs and articles of food with the most absolute precision. In the days that were gone—not in the pre- sent—when quinine was exceedingly expensive, there were people who were so contemptible as to adulterate it. That was practically impossible at the present mo- ment, for in five or ten minutes by the aid of the polari- scope, they could now determine whether the quinine was good or not. (Applause.) How much further a study of the subject would be of assistance to them in analysis it would be wild to guess, but it was at present a fixed system which enabled the analyst to ascertain the purity of hundreds of articles. (Applause.)—The motion was then put to the meeting and heartily agreed to.—Mr. FRYER, in reply, said that no one with any pre- tensions to knowledge could fail to see that Warrington was rather a classic ground. The worthies of Warring- ton were indeed worthies, and many great and eminent men had lived in the town. He could not enter that building without thinking of two gentleman he loved and honoured, and whose names were familiar to many of them. One was the late John Jackson, whose library very fittingly adorned the Warrington library. was, indeed, a lovable, gentle, generous, unassuming, and learned man. (Applause.) There was another whose acquaintance be made in Canada, Philip Carpenter. (Applause.) He associated hire with the museum and with the town of Warrington. (Applause.)—A vote of thanks to the president brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
div.p: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL.
THE GERMAN STEAM NAVVY.

In a former issue we gave a view of what is known as the "American" type of steam navvy, several of which are at work on various parts of the Ship Canal. This week we give representations of the German steam navvy, type B, one of which has for some time been in operation on the canal near the village of Moore. We give three views of the German excavator; the larger one shows it in perspective; and the two smaller ones are designed to show two methods of operating; first, with the machine placed in the cutting itself, and second, from a position outside the banks of the excavation. These great excavators are made by the Lubeck Machine Construction Company, of Lubeck, Germany, and they are reckoned to be capable of displacing as much as 2,600 cubic yards of light soil, or about 1,960 yards of tenacious ground, in a working day of ten hours. They are, of course, worked by steam, are self pro- pelling, and are arranged to move on iron rails at a suitable guage. All the machines of this descrip- tion are conetructed to work either in cuttings or .excavations, but for each kind of work a special set of dredging buckets is required. The machine at Moore is fitted for excavating below the level of the rails. The form and fittings of the bucket are mo- dified in order to suit the scope of a cutting. It might be thought that damage would often result to the machinery by the contact of the buckets against boulders and other obstructions in the ground operated upon, but the mechanism con- tains the necessary safety appliances to meet such eventualities. The machine when as work is placed on rails, and inside these rails, and parallel with themeare laid the transport rails, on which the locomotives run that drag the trains of tip-wagons, as seen in the larger cut The buckets, are made to run on a powerful rack depending from the top of the machine, and as each bucket strikes the ground and is filled with soil the machinery forces it up another rack and the soil is then tipped into the wagons, which run through a kind of shed that forms the framework of the machine, the actual working portion of which is elevated. The appar- atus fills the tip-wagons automatically, the rails upon which the excavator works being so arranged that the delivery shute of the apparatus lies over the centre of the transport rails. When the machine is at work, an empty traln of ballast wagons is brought by the locomotive beneath the apparatus, and there remains stationary. The excavator, beginning at one end of the train, is ' made to slowly advance, -tearing up the soil as it does so, and, as the contents of the buckets are discharged by the delivery shute into the waggons, one after another of them becomes filled, until the whole train is fully loaded. The locomotive theu puffs off with the excavated materiel to wherever it has to be disposed of, and another locomotive brings up another train of empty waggons, which in their turn are filled. Thus the digging progresses with a rapidity that is scarcely conceivable without absolute ocular demonstration. The other day a visitor, who was watching the operations saw the navvy fill 16 waggons in 17 minutes; and, as each waggon would contain 6 tons, this means 96 tons in a little over a quarter of an hour. As no moving of the train is required during loading, the locomotive can, while that operation is going on, be' employed in removing another train. A train of thirty. wag- gons, of a capacity of three cubic yards each, can be filled in about thirty minutes, and if the dis- tance which the waggons have to be hauled is short, one locomotive will suffice for the removal of loaded waggons. The machine requires the ser- vices of three men. One is the foreman, who manages the reversing lever; the second is the i -stoker, whose business s to attend to the boiler and the steam engine; and the third is engaged at the loading shute. In addition to these three, from ten to fourteen labouring men are required for laying rails, procuring water, fuel, Sze., and doing other neeesaary jobs. For a full working day the coal consumed amounts to from 16 to 20 zwts., and the consumption of water ranges from 1,320 to 1,760 gallons per day of ten working hours. The machine is made of iron and steel, and is so constructed that all movements, except the turning of the filling shute, are effected by the steam engine. All the motions have similar gear, and are put in and out of work by frictional "clutches." The power necessary for keeping in 'motion the chain of buckets that dig up the soil is transferred by a hydraulic frictional • clutch," which acts with great precision, and the forward movement of the apparatus, as well as the lifting and lowering of the bucket frame, are effected by ordinary frictional clutches. The regulat- ing levers of all the movements are brought to one point, and managed by one man, the foreman usually taking that duty upon himself. The steam engine works with expansion and high steamPies- sure, and the boiler, a horizontal tubular one, is so placed that it forms an effective counterpiece to the working bucket chain. The wear and tear of the working parts is nearly exclusively confined to the pitch chain, its rollers, and the " polyons,' which come into direct contact with the excavated material, and these parts are, as far as possible, made of cast steel and case-hardened iron—materials capable of resisting tear and wear in the highest degree. Thus the cost of wear, and the expense of repairs, are comparatively small considering the vast amount of work performed. These parts are also arranged so that they can easily be renewed. The digging buckets are made of sheet steel, and are solidly riveted to the steel chain links.' Each bucket has a capacity of 0.3 cubic yards. The axles and wheel tires are of steel, and are mounted on springs. The bucket frame is elastically bedded and supported, in order to prevent breakage and de- rangement of the working parts The excavator itself is surrounded by a sheet-iron casing in order to protect the men.
No. G. THE DEVIATION OF THE WARRINGTON AND ALTRINCHAM RAILWAY, &c.

The phrase "limits of deviation" is of necessity frequently used in these articles; and, seeing that we have it on the authority of more than one dis- tinguished philosopher that lack of definition is an abundant source of misapprehension and contro- versy, it may, perhaps, be worth while pointing out in a few lines what this particular phrase means. It is hardly necessary to say that, from one end to the other of the intended route of the Ship Canal, the adjacent land has been carefully and minutely surveyed, and every field and house set forth on specially-prepared plans. Across these plans two parallel lines have been drawn, representing two. imaginary lines drawn across the country throngh the whole length of the canal, and all the land and other property enclosed, so to speak, within these lines may, under the all-sufficient authority of an Act of Parliament, be acquired by the Canal Com- pany, either by mutual bargain between them and the present owners, or, failing agreement, by com- pulsory purchase, through the medium of some

third partyor body acting as arbitrathr. These lines mark the " limits of deviation" of the canal works. They, of course, always include everything that lies in the way of the intended Ship Canal channel, but in order to meet the varying circum- stances and conditions of different localities, and to provide for eventualities-for in the making of canals, as in other things, the unexpected sometimes hap- pens—they also, in most parts, include much more than this. It should, however, be borne in mind that all that is within the "limits cf deviation" need not necessarily be acquired by the Canal Com- pany. For the most part it is optional with them whether they purchase or leave unpurchased pro- perty over which their legal powers extend; and it may without rashness be predicted that when the canal is an accomplished thing much that is now within the "limits of deviation" will still be in the bands of its present possessors untouched and un- altered. As it is with the canal, so it is with its principal auxiliary and subsidiary works, such as the making of new roads, the deviation of railways, and the diversion of rivers. Most of these have each their "limits of deviation," which include not only the land which it necessary for their due carry- ing out, but also a good deal of other property of various kinds which its present proprietors may or may not be required to sell.

div.head: NEW BRIDGES.
div.p: NEW BRIDGES.

It was mentioned last week that the railway at present running from Warrington in the direction of Lymm and Altrincham is to be deviated from its existing course for a distance of between two and three miles, the deviation commencing, on the Warrington side, at a point a short distance to the east of the level crossing over Wilderspool Causeway, and ending on the nearer side of Thel- wall Station, nnd not far from Thelwall Vicarage. The deviated railway, as we explained in the sketch of its intended route, Will rise or fall, according to the point of view of the spectator, at a'gradient of one in 135, and, as in its course it will cross not only the Runcorn and Latchford Canal, but also several mach-frequented roads, a description of the height of its embankments at various points, and the man- ner in which it is proposed to deal with the tho- roughfares it encroaches upon may not be without interest. In its course from the point of deviation the new railway will keep inclose proximity to the present railway through Wilderspool Meadows, but will, of course, gradually rise at the gradient men- tioned until it considerably overtops the old line of metals. It will be carried over the Runcorn and Latchford Canal at a height of 33 feet above the level of the waters of the canal, and the bridge will 'have 36 feet span and 25 feet headway. At the other eide of the canal the natural level of the ground rises to such an extent that the existing railway, which is carried over Wilderspool Mea- dows on embankments, passes over Wash-lane, the first roadway to be encountered, at a level crossing. The new line, however, in consequence of its ascen- ding gradient, will pass over Wash-lane at a height of 24 feet above the level of the road, and the thoroughfare, the level of which is, to remain un- altered, will here be spanned by a bridge of 25 feet span and 13 feet high. Again at the roadway (Grappenhall-lane), which leads past Latchford Station, the existing railway crosses at the level ; , but the new railway will be between 36 feet and 371 feet above the level of the road, and will be carried over by a bridge with-an arch of 35 feet span and a height of 16 feet. Knutsford-road is the next highway to be dealt with, and at this point the railway that is to be will be between 41 feet and , 42 feet above the level of the road, instead of at the level as the present railway is. The railway bridge at Knutsford-road will have a span of 35 feet and a height of 16 feet. It should be mentioned that both here and ay Latchford Station the present , levels of the roads will remain unaltered. The next road which is to be touched upon is Cross-lane, which is a connecting way between Knutsford-road and Thelwall road, but, as this road- way is to be closed, of course no provision is made in the way of a bridge. A little to the farther side of Cross-lane the new railway will reach its high- est point as it there crosses the Ship Cana/ by means of a viaduct 51 feet above the level of the'ground ; but, as the waters of the canal will here be con- siderably beneath the level of the ground, the via- duct will be no less than 78 feet 6 inches above the surface of the water. From this viaduct the new railway will begin to descend towards Thelwall in order to reach, as before stated, the present line of , metals on the near side of Thelwall station. In the ' course of its descent it will have to cross two roads , one of which branches off from Knutsford-road two or three hundred yards on the Warrington side of the Dog and Dart public-house, at Grappenhall, and runs down to Thelwall-road, into which if de- bauches a little to the Warrington side of Morris- Brook farm; and the Other turns sharply off from Knutsford-road just at the farther side to the Dog and Dart, and leads past Thelwall station to Lymm. At the first-named road the new railway will have so far descended that it will be only 38 feet above the roadway, the level of which will be unaltered, and over which it will be carried by a bridge with a -span of 25 feet, and a height ot 15 feet. The other road—that which turns off to the left at the Dog and Dart,—is of greater importance and much more frequented, and we do not need to inform those who are acquainted with it, that at present it is carried over the railway by a bridge, which is not sur- mounted without considerable effort by laden ve- hicles. In the time to come, however' this will be all changed. Instead of the roadway being carried over the railway, the railway will then be carried over the roadway. The roadway, at the point where it now crosses the railway, will be lowered 21 feet 5 inches, and the new railway will pass over the lowered road at a height cd 21 feet 5 inches, that is to say, at about the same heigh as the present roadway, and the bridge here will have a 35 feet span and be 16 feet high. This, it is needless to say, will make the road much more easy to travel, but the railway bridge here will, perhaps have another claim to notice. It will be an testhetic bridge, for we find it laid down in the Act of Par- liament that it is to be constructed according to an ornamental design which is to be submitted to, and subject to the "reasonable approval" of Mr. James Nicholson, of Thelwall Hall, lord of the manor of Thelwall. All the embankments, fences, and slopes in connection with this bridge are to be finished in a neat and ornamental manner to the reasonable satisfaction of Mr. Nichol- son. When we consider the style—evidently the embodiment of ideas of pure utility and rigid economy—of many of the railway and canal bridges in this neighbourhood we may well believe that in the future people with even the slightest prefer- ence for what is pleasing to the eye over that which is uncomely:and out of harmony with its surroundings, will feel somewhat grateful to Mr. Nicholson for having, as far as possible, preserved a very agree- able piece of rural scenery.

div.head: _LEVEL _CROSSINGS, &c.
div.p: THE _LEVEL _CROSSINGS, &c.

It will have been gathered from what has been stated above, that one of the results of the making of thisdeviation railway will be the doing away with of several level crossings, and this, considering the dangers and inconveniences of which crossings of this sort are the source, cannot but be an advan- tage. In all, four level crossings will,be removed, namely, One at Wash-lane, another at Latchford" station, a third at linutsford-road, and the fourth on the road we have referred to as connecting

Knutsford-roacl with Thelwall-road. Against this advantage, however, will have to be placed the raising through the residential parts of Latchford of a high embankment, which will hardly be re- garded by those living in the vicinity as even a "blessing in disguise.'

A VISIT TO WARBURTON. ' BY A Looxim-ON. In a month or two to come, when nature is dressed in her brightest garb, when the trees are budding, and the hedge-rows are green, when the birds are singing overhead, and everything looks gay and cheerful, a run out in the country "on the track" of the Ship Canal will be an enjoyable and altogether delightful affair. But in February—and in Such a cold, gruesome February as we have been having—it is altogether different; and nothing but a keen interest in the undertaking that is so fraught with momentous consequences to this part of the country would induce anyone not having some per- sonal duty to fulfil to pay a visit to any of the several sections where the work is being pushed so rapidly forward. Possessing that keen interest, however, your correspondent and a companion de- termined on Tuesday to devote a spare afternoon to going to Warburton to be spectators ot the havoc that is there being made of the contour of the landscape. Undeterred by a cloudy atmosphere, and a threatened storm of snow, with the eipecta- tion in addition of, a tramp through muddy country lanes, we made a start from Bank Quay low level station, on the London and North-Western Railway, soon after the hour of noon, and as what we saw was interesting to us, it may be interesting to your readers to.have a glance with us at this portion of the Manchester Ship Canal works. The most ex 7 peditious way to reach the scene of operations at Warburton is to book from Bank Quay or Arpley stations to the little village of Ileatley, a mile or so beyohd picturesque, Lymm, which brings you within a brisk quarter of an hour's walk of the , bridge at Warburton, where a toll is demanded .of the wayfarer before the substantial structure span- ning the Mersey can be crossed. But before progressing even so far as Heatley station, the very air begins, as the saying goes, "to smack" of the Ship Canal. As soon as you are comfortably seated in the train, almost, before it is in motion, and some time before you have charged your pipe with your favourite weed, conversation turns on the scheme that is to revolutionise both Lancashire and Cheshire, and before the iron " gee-gee " has puffed into the station at Latch- ford, a foretaste of what is to follow is gained by a transient glimpse of the wharf on the edge of the canal, of the material spread over the field running down to the canal, and of the lino of railway that has here been laid from the siding at Latchford, to facilitate the convey- ance of goods This line runs from the siding to the edge of the water, and by means of it all kinds of material, from the humble.barrow to the massive loco- motive or steam navvy, can be taken direct from the main line of railway and shipped on to barges and tug boats which early it forward to the ultimate destination. Scattered about on the land that , slopes down to the canal are various stacks of timber, little colonies of bar- rows, and of wheels of iron, and a number of neat-look- ing little waggons, one and all bearing the sign manual "T. A. W." in lettering of black. A couple more stoppages and the train steams into Heatley station. Thence •to Warburton is a pleasant enough walk, no doubt, in summer; but the country is flat and uninteresting, and in winter, with the roads dirty and the air bleak and piercing, there is nothing very attractive about it. On the road there are one or two quaint-looking buildings to be seen, and an old- fashioned village-house of call rejoicing in the name of the "Dog," while not tar away the handsome church of Warburton relieves the Somewhat monotonous character of the scenery. At Warburton Bridge each foot passen-. ger, before passing through a little turnstile at its entrance, is mulcted in the sum of a halfpenny by the good lady who is placed in charge, and it is worth notic- ing that the said good lady's husband, taking oppor- tunity by the hand, has erected on one side of the bridge a little building of wood where, before many days have passed, he expects to be doing a paying trade in articles likely to be purchased by the men engaged on the works, as well as by travellers passing that 'way. Already the tolls collected at the Bridge have sensibly increased with the additional traffic, and there is every prospect of the little speculation proving a remunerative one. As the bridge will, along with many other well-known land- marks of the neighbourhood, be presently improved off the face of the earth, the bridge-keeper is wise in thus taking time by the forelock and endeavouring to lay in provision for the future.

With the crossing of the river comes a complete change i of scene. Directly beyond, within a run, everything s life and bustle. On the right hand and on the left men are dotted about in every direction. These are the toilers of the earth—the hewers of wood and the drawers of water. They are reckoned of little importance in the social scale, but what should wedo without them? Some are wheeling barrows 'full of soil over planks, some are digging the surface earth, and others are leading about horses that are attached to the neat waggons that form ' such a feature of the undertaking. Everything seems , confusion to the unacquainted, yet everything As in the most perfect order. A master hand has control, and work is in reality going on by leaps and bounds. On the right hand store-rooms, offices, and engine sheds have been erected in such profusion as to cover a con- siderable space of ground, and the erection of workmen's dwellings is being rapidly proceeded with, although this portion of the enterprise has been somewhat interfered with by the recent short, but sharp, frosts. In one corner of the held quite an army of barrows lay ready for use as the work progtesses and they are required, and the beams of wood that are here stacked give the place the appearance of a large timber yard. The effect is heightened by the sound of the joiners' hammers and the buzzing of a steam saw mill, which is almost constantly at work. A ballast line has been laid from the edge of the river on this side of the works, an embankment is being thrown up, and a bridge has been built over the road that divides the measlows. On the other side of the meadows, on the left as you walk down to the works from the bridge, still greater activity prevails, for it is here that the actual work of i cutting s being pushed forward. Rather more than three hundred men are engaged on this section, and it is at this particular point that most of them are at present employed. Operations commenced hereabouts some two months ago, and the change effected in that time is something to be wondered at. Two cuttings are here being made simultaneously, leaving a ridge of earth to be subsequently removed from the centre of the course of the canal, and the locomotives find ample work in taking away the soil torn up by the "devils "in nearly a thousand specially constructed tip waggons, which, like those at Latchford,' all bear the initials of the con- ' tractor. Mr. T. A. Walker. Lines of rails branch about in all directiens, and one extends as far away in the dis- tance as the eye can travel. Several locomotive ballast engines are incessantly and noisily puffing about these lines with trains of waggons, and there are visilike and umnistakeable signs on every hand that the worka are proceeding very rapidly along. A panoramic glance at the whole, taken from the top of an embankment, teems with interest, and strikingly exemplifies the skill and courage of those who have plan- ned such a vast undertaking, and the ingenuity of those who have made it possible that such an undertaking can be carried out. The scene is also interesting by reason I of its great variety. The massive steam navvies tearing I up the soil, the cranes lifting heavy weights, the loco- motives running hither and thither, and the men busy with picks, and shovel's, and barrows, make up a tab- leau that cannot be properly appreciated without it is seen. Them is much to interest, too, in looking at the work in detail. Take, Ifor instance, one of the cuttings, where a steam navvy from the works at Lincoln of Messrs. Dunbar and Ruston is vigorously accomplishing its object under the guidance of the two or three work- men in charge. In less time than it takes to describe it, the teeth of the scuttle-shaped scoop tear up the earth, the scoop is filled, the soil is depesited in the waggon waiting to receive it, and the same operation is repeated over and over again with marvellous speed. The scoop three times filled drops into a waggon sufficient earth to load it, and it is quickly dragged away and another waggon brought up. In the cutting itself a number of men are engaged straightening• the sides with their sho- vels, while others look after the removal of the excavated soil, which is carried away in the waggons on the various lines of railway that intersect each other in all direc- tions. In the other cutting the machine is not at pre- sent at work, but it is getting up steam, and in the meantime a lad with a ',wooden leg is making some at- tempt at ctbaning it, and a number of navvies are en- gaged in various occupations. So far the ground dealt with by these two machines has been of a yielding na- ture, but when the bed rock beneath the softer surface matter is reached, blasting will have to be resorted to. Up to now, however, the hands engaged on this part of the undertaking find plenty of employment in rounding off the work of the steam diggers., It may be mentioned that at the point referred to the course of the canal will deviate very considerably from the track of the winding Mersey. Indeed, from Hollin- fare downwards, a complete new waterway will have to be formed, in obedience to the law that straight cuts are the shortest., Having seen all that is to be seen, we made the return journey, and, notwithstanding the discomfort experien- ced in tramping about in the soft soil, felt amply repaid for the trouble of the Visit. f •
On Thursday afternoon, a considerable portion of the Low Wood Hotel, between Windermere and Ambleside, was destroyed by fire. •The loss is estimated at £3,000 to £7,000.

THE MANCHESTER SHIP OA/CAL COMP,A.NY. MEETING OF SHAREHOLDERS. On Monday, the fifth ordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, was held at the St. James's Hall, Manchester. Lord Egerton of Tatton, the chairman of the company, pre- sided, and there was a large attendance of shareholders. The SECRETARY read the report of the directors, which was as fellows :—At the last general meeting of the com- pany the directors reported that they had succeeded in raising sufficient capital to enable the company to com- mence active operations for the purchase of land and the construction of the works. Two months later the directors gave possession of the first portion of the land required to the contractor, and• on the 11th of November the first sod was cut by the chairman in the presence of the directors, at Eastham, where the canal will join the estuary of the Mersey. In order to secure efficient supervision, the work of the board has been divided into four departments, each under the management of a committee, subject to the control of the board. 'FINANCE. The accounts for the half-year 2 s. d. s. l. ending 31st December, (887, show that the following shares have been allotted up to that date, viz. Preference 4,000,000 0 0 Ordinary 1,383,020 0 0 7,383,020 0 0 This leaves a balance of £616,980 unallotted, of which the company have the right to pay A 500,000 in fully,paid- up ordinary shares to the contractor if they should desire so to do. The amount paid up against calls was— Preference Shares 21,190,788 0 Ordinary Shares ---2,160,842 16 10 The calls in arrear were— Preference Shares 9,212 0 0 Ordinary Shares 54,063 3 2 The amount uncalled was— Preference Shares 2,800,000 0 0 Ordinary Shares 2,363,114 0 0 0 0 Leaving a balance of ordinary shares unissued of
Total capital £0,000,000 o o The Rital receipts from the formation of the I . company to the date of the account amount : to ' 2,834,01 7 0 And the total expenditure to ' • 2,409,363 16 3
Leaving a balance to the credit of capital ac- count of £425,607 10 9 •

The following are the principal items of expenditure for the half-year :—Balance of purchase money of Bndge- water and Mersey and Irwell undertakings, including stamp duty, £1,698,094 103 id; land purchase and com- pensation, £124,076 2s lid; construction of works, £255,000; engineering and surveying, £4,798 12s Id; office and general expenses, £11,126 14s lid; brokerage, £68,594 7s sd; interest on payments in advance of calls. £9,432 2s; interest on called-up capital; £27,749 17s 11d. The directors' estimate of further expenditure on capital account during the half-year ending 30th of June, 1888, is as follows, viz. Purchase of land and cempensation £600,000 Construction of works • Payment of interest and general expenses BO,OOO

Total £1,230,000 The net profit on the working of the Bridgewater Canals undertakings, from the sth of August to the 31st of December amounted to £30,205 1.45. The cash at bankers on current account amounted to £372815 is 3d, and on deposit £140,000 ; cash in ha4id, £214 lOs ; the accounts due to the company were £87,598 7s 6d, and the accounts owing by the company £130,169 38 Bd. The directors have to report that the response to the rails have been very satisfactory, having regard to the vast number of shareholders, which is now 39,710. The directors do not anticipate that it will be necessary to make a further, call before midsummer, when £1 per share, in addition to the £5 already paid, will probably be required; and the company will then be in a position to exercise the borrowing powers conferred upon them by their Act of 1885. The first payment of interest out of capital, authorised by the Company's Act of 1886, was made at the rate of 4 per cent, per annum on the Ist of January to all shareholders who were entitled to re- ceive the same. The next payment will be made on the Ist of July. The directors regret that they have not been able to issue the whole of the certificates for ordin- ary shares, but they have done so in all cases where they have been demanded. The work is one of c onsiderable magnitude, and would entail great expense if it were done under pressure. The directors, therefore, claim the indulgence of those shareholders who have not yet re- ceived their certificates, and it is hoped that during the present half year certificates for all the shares will be issued. The directors have acquired possession of a large portion of the land required for the canal, docks, and other works, and have handed it over to the contractor. In cases where agreement has been found impracticable, in consequence of the differences in the valuations of the company's surveyors and those of the landowners, the settlement will be by arbitration, or by a jury, as provi- ded for in the Acta Of Parliament which govern the com- pany. The land purchased has been acquired on terms satisfactory to the directors, and possession of the land has generally been given by the landowners on payment of a sum on account pending a settlement, which has Igreatly facilitated the progress of the works. , In conse- quence of the alteration of the line of the canal made by the House of Commons in 1885, the ecompany has been compelled to apply to Parliament for powers to purchase additional lands on the Cheshire shore of the estuary, for the deposit of spoil, and the sanction of the shareholders to the promotion of the bill for this purpose will be sought at a „epecial meeting of the company. The directors have to report that the negotiations for pur- chase without compulsory powers are approaching a satisfactory termination, and it may not be found neces- sary to proceed with the bill. Since the commencement of the work the contractor has shown great vigour in his operations. A large quantity of valuable plant has been brought upon the site of the works, and a start has been made on almost every section. The directors are so far satisfied with the progress made, and trust that the contractor will in a short time be at work on the entire

length. The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report, said he was very glad to be able to inform the share- holders that during the last six months satisfactory pro- press had been made with the canal. He was not able to bring forward such a sensational record of progress as at the last meeting, but they had been steadily building on the foundation they had laid. Everyone who had seen the work would admit that the contract Air had displayed much vigour, and had shown an amount of organisation which justified the confidence of the directors. Since the commencement of the year the contractor had got to work on nearly all the sections. There were eight sec- tions of the canal and two of railway, and with the view of giving the shareholders an idea of the magnitude of the work, he stated that there were now engaged upon the works 40 locomotives, 18 steam navvies, 7 steam excavators, 27 steam cranes, 14 portable engines, 4 pumping engines, 9 steam saw benches. 3 steam tugs, 14 flats and barges, 1,780 waggons, 2,500 barrows, 5,000,000 tons of rails, cevering about 10 miles, 70,000 sleepers, and 3,000 men were employed. At the present time 20 miles of lan& had been handed over to tha con- tractor, and the directors trusted that before long they , would be able to hand over, the whole of the land. Allud- ing next to the• arrears in the payment of calls, he said he thought the amount was very small, and on the other side he mentioned an item which had been, by a clerical error, omitted from the report. though it appeared in the statement of accounts, and that was that large sums were being paid in advance on the calls, and that at the present time so large a sum as -£674,128 stood to the credit of the company. (Cheers.) This showed the con- fidence of the shareholders in the directors. (Hear, hear,) He next stated that some negotiations were going on in respect to the payMent of income tax, and if the negotiations terminated in favour of the company the extra amount would be paid to the shareholdeit. (Hear. hear.) He thought it was unnecessary to' say much about the pollution of the rivers. He had no, reason to fear that anything would be done to prejudice the canal, and he felt bound to say that in this respect Salford had shown an excellent example. So far that Corporation had taken the lead, but he did not believe that Manches- ter would be left behind. (Cheers.) In conclusion, he referred to the loss the directors had sustained by the loss of Mr. Charles Moseley, who was a man of energy and ability—(hear, hear—and said that in Mr. Jenkin- son, who had been elected to succeed him on the Board, they had secured a sentleman of Indian experience. He moved the adoption of the report. (Cheers.) Sir JOSEPH LEE seconded the resolution, and said he had been asked why the shares of the company were now selling at a discount. (Laughter.) That was a very in question to answer, but he had no hesita- tion n advising them to hold their shares. He ventured to prophecy that if they did so they would in four years from last January, *hen the canal would be opened, find their shares at a premium. (Cheers.) The report was unanimously adopted. The retiring directors and the retiring auditors hav- ing been re-appointed, votes of thanks were Passed to Mr. James Reilly for the use of. the hall, and to the chairman.

The meeting then became special' in order to enable the shareholders to 4pprove the presentation to Parlia- ment of a bill to enable the company to acquire addi- tional lands. • The CHAIRMAN briefly explained the measure which would be placed before Parliament, and said that one of the requirements made by Mr. Forster and the Com- mittee of the House of Commons was that the canal should be made farther inland than was originally in- tended. This alteration increased the amount of cut- ting, and necessitated a larger surface of land for the deposit of soil. It had, therefbre, been fmind .neceSsary to apply to Pailiament far compulsory powers to pur- chase land near asthatri and near Prodsham. At present the directors had found no difficulty with the, owners of the land, and. though it might be necessary to keep the bill alive he did' not think that it would be reqnired, and that it Mighebe.drbPped. :(Hear, hear.) Sir J. C. LEE seconded the motion, which was carried, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c.
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c.

"Little Maroit, and other stories" by Mr. A Hoyer, is a handsome volume . published by Messrs. Griffith, Farren, and Co., (price 55.) Little Margit is a good and pretty little girl, who pays a visit W fairy land, and the story gives an account of all the wonderful things she saw there, of her call on the Man in the Moon, and how she got back again. The second story, "Podgie and Todgie "gives a descrip- tion of the good things in Cakeland, and of the great doings at the fairies' ball. Then there is the tale of • The Princess's Earring," "The Magic needle," and last but not lease in interest ani beauty the enchantment of "The Old Chateau. All the tales are charmingly told they will thor- oughly interest young folk; and at the same time teach them some,good lesson. The illustrations are by Mrs. IL M. Paget; they are all full of character? and some of them are very quaint. Toe book is Ns.el' printed, type large and clear, and the cover is quit a work. of art.

In the Camelot series for the current month, published by Mr. Walter Scott, we have " Volsunga Saga; t story of the Volsungs and Niblungs, with certain mat from the elder Edda." The volume is edited with an brit troduction and notes by Mr. H. Halliday Sparling. Mete: stories and folk lore of the Nortlunen of Europe are especially interesting to Englishmen who have so much of the blood of these Northrnen in their veins; we are not surprised that the legends are attracting attention of modern poets. The songs represent earliest form of verse, . but they are like the singei hardy and full of vitality. The same may be said of - prose narrative. "If you out these words they will bleed," as Emerson once said. Reaching the publiein this cheap form, the story of the Volsungs should have r large sale. The life of Sir Walter Scott is issued amongst Great Writers, and Scott was a great writer both as quantity and quality. He is atone as having stood in the front rank bah as novelist and poet. Byron, when he came on the scene, outshone him in i,erse ; but, as a writer of romance, he was in his day unrivalled. The life is written by Mr. C. D. Yonge, who has had, course, to draw largely 'on Lockhart's life of Scott. Bi the new story of the career a the great Scotchman told interestingly; and the critical estimate of Scott genius is searching and sound. " Atistralian Ballads" is the title of the issue in the Canterbury Poets Series for February. The poems are correctly described as inspired by life and scenery in Australia and New Zealand;' and they have been selec- ted and edited by Mr. D. B. W. Sladen, 8.A., to whoni the work has been a labour of love. The introduction makes us acquainted with the country and its singers in such a Way as to stimulate an interest in the balladS• These for the most part smell of the soil; but that is not to say they are themselves soiled. On the contrary, they carry the reader back to tho beauty, freshness and innocence of country life. Australia is regarded by these singers as the country of the future; but, as Mr. Slade]] has it, they are disposed to say:— We all are English, born in one great union Of blood and language, history, and song. All _English, and to cherish, our communion • We will present a common Irina to wrong. "The Mystery of a Hansom Cab" is the story of a murder and its consequences, which has been e.xtraor- dinarly successful. It is from the pen of a Mr. Fergue W. Hume, a young Australian writer not yet twent three years of age. It gives a vivid picture of I in Melbourne; and introduces several characters of a novel but 'certainly of a realistic type. Mother Gutter- snipe is a creation; but it may be questioned whether it would not have lie,en better if she had been left =- created. But the chief interest in the story lies in un- ravelling the mystery of the murder in the hansorn cab. Mr. Hume leads the reader cleverly on from one supposition to another ; and it is due to him to say that he is a masterhand in building up circumstantial evi- dence.' This story, like "Called Back," may be read once with breathless interest ; but it is not one to be read a second time.

"Elocution, Voice, and Gesture" is the title of a shil- ling hand-book by Mr. Rupert Garry, teacher of elocu- tion and dramatic art. It is published by Messra- Bemrose and Sons, London. The instruction-is conveyed in a concise and effective manner; there is no attempt at making a mystery of the art; and sound rules are given for the management of the voice. ReciterSf' speakers, and preachers would do well to possess them- selves of this hand-book; it contains something useful for all these claSses.

"The Manchester Quarterly," published for the Man- chester Literary Club by Mr. John Heywood, preserveS its good repute for good things. Mr. J. G. Phythin leads off with an interesting paper on "County Galway, which he has himself illustrated. There is freshness and vigour in his description of his experience of Irish life and character ; and his illustrations are striking. Mr. John Mortimer has a readable article on Alfred Domett, the" Waring" of Mr. limbert Browning. In "A Christ- mas Symposmin " we have a record of the proceeding, at the Christmas supper of the Manchester Liters'''. Club. Mr. J. Oscar Parker contributes a ballad onitbe Legend of Dolbadarn, which is accompanied by a Ape view of Llyn Pens, from a drawing by Mr. Ward Hey,- Other papers are "Reminiscences of London in 1839," by Charles Harwick, and "My Kingdom," by Mr. W. I. Wild.

Messrs. Smith, Elder, and Co., London, have just issued a popular edition of "Poems by Elizabeth Bar- rett Browning." It is printed from the edition of Mrs. Browning's works published in 1856, and it Contain; miner...4ns additions and alterations made for that edi- tion,,which are copyright. It is rendered, too, all the more valuable and interesting by a prefatory note writ- ten by Mr. Robert Browning, which corrects errors in a recent ".Memoir of Elizabeth Barrett Browning," frora the pen of Mr. J. H. Ingram. It will be a great 'boon tO many readers to have this authorised edition. in . this cheap, handy volume. Mrs. Browning ranks as the greatest of our female poets, and, as such, could draw a portrait with a few bold strokes; such, for instance, ail the three lines in her" Vision of Poets " : And poor proud 13yron, sad as grave, And.aalt as life ; forlornly brave, And quivering with the dart lie drave. The "English Illustrated Magazine" is strong, this month, in description and illustration of the animal kingdom, there being one article on "The weasel and his family," another on "Fowls." "Coaching DayS and Coaching Boys " loses none of its interest, either as to text or illustration; the fiction is strong; and Mr. H. D. Trail's "Et Cetera" is as effective as it is plea- sant.
SAD DEATLI OF A. WARRINGTON GENTLEMAN.

On Monday morning, Mr. James Morris, a gentle- man who had until some time ago carried on the business of a pawnbroker in Church-street, died oS the railway between Warrington and Glazebrook• The deceased, who has for some time been subject to heart disease, left home about eight o'clock on Monday morning in order to go to Manchester bY the train due at Warrington at 8-7. He had to hurry ansiderahly to catch the train, and arrived at the Central Station, Warrington, in an exhausted condition. He got in the same compartment with Mr. A. J. Jones, a relative of his. The latter soon after the train starred discovered that Mr. Morris was ill, and, knowing that he had been for some time subject to heart disease, he began to rub his hands, but in vain, for when the train arrived at Glazebrook Mr. Morris was dead. The body was removed from the train and placed in the waiting room and the friends of the deceased were communicated with. An inquiry, as to the death was held in the Parade Room, at the Police Station, Warrington, on TueSday afternoon by Mr. S. Brighouse, the coroner for the district. Inspector Simpson appeared on behalf of the Cheshire Lines Committee.—The Rev. Thomas Bithel McLean, vicar of Skehnersdale, near Ormskirk, said he knew that the deceased, who lived at Oak House, Church-street, had been troubled for at least 19 years with irregular action of the heart. He (deceased) wait in the habit of running to catch trains, and whenever he did so suffered pain for some minutes afterwards.—Mr. Arthur J. Jones deposed that ho left Warrington for Manchester by the 8-7 train in company with the de- ceased. There was no one in the compartment besides deceased and witness. When the train was near Pad- gate witness noticed that his companion leaned his head back and gasped. Witness asked him what was the matter, but got no reply. He saw deceased's lips grow white, and this made him suspect that he was dead. When the train, anived at Gla.zebrook medical aid was sought, and Dr. Jago arriVed, though he (witness) was not there when he arrived. Deceased always appeared Ito witness to be in good health. The train did not stop at Padgate. Deceased had hurried all the way from his residence to the station.—P.C. Sims, stationed at Hollins. I Green, stated that he saw the body of the deceased about 'ten minutes past ten on Monday morning. Dr. Jago had been there and he afterwards went and saw him, and he said that death as due to heart disease.—The jury re- turned a verdict of "Death from natural causes—most probably heart disease." The remains of the deceased gentleman were interred at the cemetery on Thursday afternoon. The hearse was drawn by four horses, and five broughams followed_ The funeral procession was witnessed by a large number of people, the deceased having been very well known. The coffin, which was of brown oak, was brass mounted,. and had on it an engraved brass plate bearing the in- scription—" James Morris, died February 19,1888, aged 70 years." A numberof wreaths were sent by sorrow- ing friends. Mr. J. Mounfield, as undertaker, had charge of the funeral arrangements.

A SHIP CANAL NUISANCE. Sir,—The Ship Canal is a grand excuse for half the vagrants taken before the magistrates. The magistrates must be getting rather weary of scamps of all kinds when arrested for begging or drunkenness, having come into the town "to get work on the Ship Canal." If all the vagabonds who tell this story were to gain eniploy- ment there (which most of them are wise enough not to attempt to do), the first good use to which the canal might be put on its completion would be ship some of these employes out of the district.--Yours truly, X. Y. Z.

THE LATEST PHASE OF GREENALLISM. Sir,—Please accept my thanks for the publicity you have recently given to the manner in which the respected clerk of the Borough Magistrates has been kept out of appointments which in common fairness should have fallen to his lot. Such rank jobbery deserves to be ex- posed, for it is anything but creditable to the parties concerned. Mr. H. Greenall is fortunate in having such influential fri•ends, but it is a pity that they should be allowed, in this way, to pitchfork their young relative into salaried appointments over the head of a gentleman who is older, who has in a great degree had the business connected with those appointments for some time under his charge, and who would naturally be expected to take the appointments when they became vacant. I am glad to see, by your last issue, that Mr. H. B. White sent a cheque for £2 2s as a donation to the funds of the Blue Coat Brotherly Society. It speaks well for him that after the treatment he has received in connec- tion with the clerkship to the trustees he is able to act with such magnanimity.—Yours, Sze., H. J.
hear that Mr. Buckton (Mr. H. Greenall's partner) has been appointed clerk to the Newton Magis- trates over Mr. White's head. Is this another job?
"POOR TIM !"

Sir,—The other day: ;.-y--(;ung -gentleman passing me in Bridge-street, exclaimed in tones of deep commisera- tion "Poor Tim," and casting my eyes along the street they rested upon a miserable object fumbling at a street corner with what had once been a shoe. " Ah, thought I, how are the mighty fallen." Time was when no Tory meeting could be held without a few remarks from "Mr. Timothy Ashcroft," who loomed large upon the plat- form in a neat suit set off bya massive gold guard suspen- ded across the waistcoat. But now, alas! no one unfamiliar with the quondam Latchford luminary, would recog- nise the former Tory orator in the attenuated figure that now haunts the streets, hiding his nakedness under a badly tattered overcoat, held together by pieces of string, a wretched pair of unmentionables, and a pair of shoe tops that seem to have long ago quarrelled with the soles. It is grieving to see "poor Tim" hobbling along in this melancholy plight, and it occurred to me that a brief description of his condition in your columns might result in an improvement of his state. Surely among the many wealthy people with whom he once stood shoulder to shoulder in support of Toryism in this town, there are some who can spare a cast-off garment or two to enable the poor, neglected politician to present a more decent and becoming appearance; and the local Tories generally might do many a worse thingthan raise a fund for his support. Though not a politician myself, I would gladly contribute mymite towards removing„ what appears to me, a town's disgrace.—Yours, &c. A SYMPATIIISER.
February 22nd, 1888. PROTESTANTISM AND METHODISM.

- -- Sir,—From letters which have appeared occasionally in "The Examiner" from writers who have not been over partial towards the Christian religion, it does, after all, appear that some of their statementshave acolouring of truth. Especially is this so if we ask ourselves is the Church doing its duty, and look at the attendance in the churches and chapels in Warrington and neighbourhood. I will not open this wide field of debate, but would you kindly allow me to mention once more that amongst the Wesleyan body last year (and previous years as well, I believe) there was a large decrease in membership. At a public meeting held on Tuesday evening in the Bold- street School, the Rev. William Brookes, in referring to this matter, had occasion to remark that "a large num- ber of members were lost annually through removals," which is quite correct, and said he—" I am sure those members must not have presented their membership ticket and removal note in the places to which they have removed." Of course, the ihference of this is very clear, but as to these ex-members having put upon them the entire responsibility, the wisdom of that is a matter of opinion. lam glad, however, to see that this matter, viz., the falling off in attendance and communicants at the public worship is receiving the attention of minis- ters, not only in the Wesleyan Church, but all churches. Whatever is done by them in the way of laying them- selves out for the church's welfare,will receive the hearty co-operation of all church and chapel lovers, and espe- cially if that undeveloped method, pastoral visitation, re- ceives the consideration and attention which I for one think it deserves.—Yours, &c., Warrington, February 16, 1888.
RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CHOIR.

div.head: INESLEYIN.
div.p: INESLEYIN.

Sir,—ln your report of the Concert last week, your eulogistic reference to my work in connection with the above society may be understood to confirm an erroneous' idea existing in some quarters that the society has been established entirely for my benefit, and that any pro- fits, (?) were for my remuneration. May I, therefore, be allowed to say, that neither myself nor any other member of the choir receive either directly, or in- directly any remuneration for services rendered. The ardent desire of every member is to see the society established on a sound financial basis, and receiving the public support and , appreciation, which, as you say, they deserve. To my mind it is a serious reflection on our towns- people that such undertakings as the " Madrigal Society," and the "Orchestral Society" had to be discontinued for want of public support, and yet for at least a week every year, the Public Hall is crowded night after night to listen to the soul reviving strains of "Johnny Schmo- ker " and the " Burlesque Band," or to receive the com- forting assurance that "John Brown's donkey's got a wooden leg." I maintain, sir, that half an hour devoted to the in- telligent study of the works of the great masters, would be productive of more real and lasting pleasure, than an extended acquaintance with sech trivialities could ever give. We have the satisfaction of knowing that our efforts have been well received and highly appreciated by those who have attended our concerts so far, and we hope to receive as we are determined to deserve the continued and increased support of all intelligent persons who sympathise with us in our endeavours to raise the stan- daxd of musical taste in our town—Yours faithfully, J. HOLFORD, Conductor, Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa Choir. Greenway Road, February 22nd, 1888.

div.head: MR. JUSTICE GRANTHAM ON DRINK AND CRIME.
div.p: MR. JUSTICE GRANTHAM ON DRINK AND CRIME.

Sir,—On Saturday la,st I had the pleasure of hearing Mr. Justice Grantham read his charge to the grand jury, and, as he spoke of the close connection between crime and drunkenness, I wondered what Sir A. R. Walker. who was on the grand jury, would think about it. The judge's subsequent remarks about supplying drink to people till they become intoxicated will meet with the warmest sympathy of a very large section of the general public. I was pleased to notice a short time ago that you drew attention to the large number of convictions for drunkenness, and the incredibly small number of convictions of publicans for supplying drink to people until they became intoxicated. It is high time thab this matter was brought home to our magistrates and to the police. It is said to be very difficult to bring of- fences of this kind home to the publicans, but might not the judge's example be followed, and every time a person is brought before the map;istrates for being drunk to find out.where they got the drink, and bring the pub- lican before the bench and endorse his license, or other- wise deal with him. I venture to think that, if this course was vigorously adopted, we should soon see a very sensible diminution of this curse of drunkenness in our midst. We are gaining a.most unenviable notoriety for female drunkenness, and it is nothing less than a gross scandal that this thing should go on unchecked year after year. Why are our magistrates and police so supine in the matter? Will they never move? The way to do so has been made abundantly plain by Mr. Justice Grantham, and, unless they are lost to every sense of shame, they will strenuously endeavour to put a stop to such a crying evil. Will the great brewers, who own so many houses in lA'arrington, see to it that their houses are conducted on better lines? I have not a word to say about the legitimate uses of these houses, but it is an undeniable fact that drinking is carried on to excess in. many of them, some of them being the resort of prosti- tutes and bad characters, whilst these said brewers " fat- ten on the unholy gains of this horrid traffic." How long! how long ! shall the cry of wretched women and starving children go unheeded? PRO BONO PUBLIC°. Warrington, Feb. 24.1885.

div.head: GTO;
div.p: GTO;
WARRIN(
N CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.

- - _ Sir was greatly amused when I read the letter aigne:i by "A Member." I wonder how it would look either hung up in a frame or under a glass case "He is intoxicated with the exuberance of his ownverbositv." The language used on one occasion by the late Lord Beaconsfield I think would apply to him. It is nothing new for me to hear that the society num- bers 2,000; but it certainly is to hear that their takings instead of being from twelve to thirteen hundred pounds, as I had been informed, are but ten hundred according to "A Member," who probably has had a peep behind the scenes. I think I need not notice what he says about the house and garden, as it is simply nonsense. He must know that very few, comparatively, speaking, have this privilege. If it should fall to their lot after years of honest toil, ' sobriety, and carefulness, has he not as much right as a manager or "A Member" to enjoy them P As to competition—frors what I know of business men they have nothing to feat! and do not object to it when straightforivard. It is imposition which they cannot compete against—professing to give with one hand and

taking away with the other ; throwing dust in the eyes Of the public that they may not see. As to the working-man buying from other tradespeople in order to help them to gain an independency, that is simply clap-trap. I say fearlessly the working-man does not see it to his advan- tage to join the Stores unless he is, like "A Member," blind and will not see, and will not compare being blinded by narrow prejudice. It has often been said, "There are none so blind as those who will not see." It was new to me to hear that the business, or rather the middle man, as he was termed, did not know what it was to toil or spin. I dare make this assertion, that he, as a rule, works harder and makes longer hours than "A Member." The mutual assistance he talks about sounds very "nice," but save me from it. "Man help thyself," but how is the working-man to help himself by paying fabulous prices for what he re- quires in order to get a small bonus in return? Not at any rate by paying 2s 6d per dozen for pastry flour when he can get it at is 10d and 2s, and paying 2s 2d for McDougall's self-raising flour when he can get it at is 10d, paying Is 5d for best seconds flour when he can get it at is 3d or ls, 4d, paying for syrup treacle 2id per lb. (I can get it anywhere at 2d and at some places for VA), common soda Id per lb. instead of paying 21t. for lid. Perhaps this will be sufficient to prove my case. I could name, if space would allow, such articles as cheese, pepper, &c., &c. I am reminded of persons I have known who, after having taken a lot of trouble with pigs, have sold them at a loss of a id per lb., com- forting themselves with the assurance that the money came all in a lump. If the tradesman could get ready money for all he sold, instead of giving such long credit, he would be able to sell cheaper still. I should like to know how it is if a purchaser spent 'lid he only gets a check for 7d? In conclusion, I am glad "A Member" quoted the grand old proverb, "Honesty is the best policy." I thoroughly believe in it, and it is because I do so that I say let us have it in reality and not in name.--I remain, yours,
A LOOKER ON.
