OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON. THURSDAY NIGHT.

I write this before the news of the result of the Doncaster election has reached the town. All that is known at present is that it will be a close fight, and that the Conservatives are full of hope that the local Fitzwilliam influence, backed by extraordinary efforts, will succeed in blotting out the perilously small majority by which the seat was won in 1886 for the Liberals. Most urgent commands and en- treaties have been sent from the Carlton pointing out the absolute necessity of the Government securing a majority. Mr. Caine went down on Wednesday, as representing the Dissen- tient Liberal interest, whilst the Tories have been , sedulously beaten up. However the election may go, the results achieved at the poll within the last' week have given a tremendous fillip to advancing Liberalism. Southwark followed upon Dundee, and West Edinburgh upon Southwark with increas- ing force. The importance of the West Edinburgh election was graphically put by Colonel Saunder- son, the emissary of a terrified Ministry, who pub- licly declared that at that particular juncture the Conservatives had better lose six seats than see West Edinburgh captured. West Edinburgh was not only won, but won by the transference of 900 votes to the side of Home Rule. There is a well-known tabular statement, which Lord Salisbury must often look at with apprehension, as Mr. Gladstone regards it with satisfaction. It shows that by a movement, less than half as strong throughout the con- stituencies, Mr. Gladstone will, at a General Elec- tion, be placed in power by an overwhelming majority. The memorable scene in the House of Commons on Friday night, when the news of the victory at Southwark burst in upon the crowded House and thundered along the benches, has been so often de- scribed that I will not attempt a ropetition. But it is important to note that the effect immediately produced on Mr. Goschen remains in accentuated form throughout the Conservative ranks. Mr. Ge- . chen began his speech in jubilant tone and aggres- sive manner. The Conservative gentlemen had just come 'back from dinner, full of good wine and large content. They boisterously cheered Mr. Goschen's attacks upon his old friends on the bench opposite. Mr. Gladstone was not in his place when Mr. Gos- chen commenced. He came in midway through ' the speech, and Mr. Goschen had just been refer- ring to the Mitchelstown telegram, the very men- tion of which sends good Conservatives howling with rage. He had vented this venemous passage 'in Mr. Gladstone's absence. Now that he had come back he could not resist the pleasure of going over it again, and was just, amid stormy cheers from the Conservatives, truculently asking where was the fruit from Mitchelstown ? when Mr. Arnold Mor- ley brought in the telegram announcing the South- wark victory. When the repeated bursts of cheer- ing had subsided, and Mr. Goschen fo,ind an oppor- tunity of continuing the speech, he was in a battered, damaged condition that ludicrously con- trasted with his earlier manner. No one better than he knew what Southwark meant, and his shout of triumph was suddenly turned into singing exceedingly small. .

When ale House met on Monday. it was already stale news that Edinburgh had followed South- wark, and that another long nail had been driven in the coffin of the Conservative Ministry. It was curious to note even on Monday night what a sub- tle silent change in some personal respects had been effected in the House. Mr. Gladstone's ap- pearance at the table, on whatever business, was made the occasion for a triumphant shout of wel- come from the Liberal benches. The Conservatives, formerly scorntul and insolent, now tacitly acknow- ledged him as master of the situation. It was curious and instructive to note, on Wednesday afternoon, how meekly Ministers and the Conser- vative majority sat at his feet whilst with authori- tative patriarchal air he discoursed on foreign politics. He was magnanimous enough to speak some words of approval on the foreign policy of Lord Salisbury, and Mr. W. H. Smith, in gratefully acknowledging this condescension, almost chortled in his joy. ' I still believe that, except for some extraordinary and unforeseen occurrence, such to the death of the Queen for example, the Conservatives will remain in office for the full length of their Parliamentary tether. The process of digging them out by suc- cesses at bye elections is so lengthy that it will last out the full four years yet at their command. But it is clear already that a few such expressions of public opinion as have recently found vent will have a most desirable effect in modifying their tendency, if not in shattering their power, to do evil.

To-morrow the House of Commons enters upon the discussion of the New Rules of Procedure. It is a noteworthy thing that throughout the discour- sive debate on the Address not a single speech has been devoted to the question of Procedure. As far as I remember, not a single reference has been made to the subject. This is a very unusual course, and is exceedingly promising from a business point of view. It was very different in 1882, when the Con- servatives, being in Opposition and in alliance with the Parnellites. every approach to the reform of Procedure was obstinately barricaded. Now the irony of circumstances has brought the Conserva- tives into a position where they officially advocate the Closure and are the custodians of a measure designed to expedite public business. The Liberals, though in opposition, will welcome .their appear- ance in a new character, and we may expect to see the House of Commons at its very beet in discus- sion of the New Rules. The absence of partisan activity upon their introduction has served to veil the importance of the proposed changes. They are nevertheless fundamental, and if carried, will work a radical change in the hours of Parliamentary sittings. The news about the Crown Prince varies from day to day, but it ever comes back to the one sad hope- less note. The doctors now, as was their habit be- fore tracheotomy was tried, make the very best of

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 25, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 25, 1888.

the case, and light up a b3acon fire when there is a I passing flash of hope. But they tilk more unre- servedly in communication with their professional brethren in London. and, having some personal ac- quaintance in that quarter, I gather there is little hope of ultimate recovery. This is pitiful in its personal aspect, and will be calamitous in its public , consequences. As Mr. Gladstone said in the touch- ing reference he made to the Crown Prince in the House of Commons, on Wednesday. his life is of in- estimable value to Europe. Of all the sovereigns, in esse or in pose, Europe cculd better spare any one than him. It is not only that he is so admirably fitted to fill the great throne which is his heritage, but that, should he die, the Crown will pass into hands which are not likely to work good either for Germany or for Europe. For the Crown Princess it will be a terrible blow beyond the loss of her hus- band. From the near prospect of being Empress of Germany, she will pass into the position of a shelved dowager, with a considerable family of younger children not too well provided for. Ten years ago the announcement of the death of Sir William Edmonstone would have created a mel- ancholy sensation in Parliamentary circles. Now a few lines in the newspapers report the event, and it is only the members of the already antique Dis- raelian Parliament that recognise, in the full title. the old gentleman who, in the Parliament of 1874, was never known by any other title than "The Admiral." Ile was one of the special features of that assembly, and was, in some respects, a type of its majority. He was singularly ignorant, obstin- ate, and prejudiced, his sole idea of political life being to vote for Mr. Disraeli, and grunt when Mr. Gladstone rose to address the House And yet he was so simple-hearted, of such unblemished honesty according to his lights, that lie was a prime favourite on both sides of the House. For more than six years, night after night, and, if necessary, all night through, he sat on the bench immediately be- hind the leader of the House, a place less worthily occupied to-day by Colonel Hughes-Hallett. It is said that the "Admiral" delivered only one speech. I do not remember even that articulate effort. But there was no speech delivered from either side of the House in which he did not take the part of chorus, He had two speeches learned off by heart, and recited verbatim as occasion arose. One was " Hear, hear !" which came forth with rattling per- sistency whenever a Conservative was speaking. The other was "No, no !" which he flung broadcast through speeches delivered from the Liberal side, rising to the highest flight of eloquence when Mr. Gladstone was on his legs. He was also master of an eloquent cough, which expressed all kinds of sen- timents, according to its varying tone and vehe- mence. Finally, the" Admiral ' had invented quite a new fashion of commentary. By use of his copy of the orders, he used to fan himself with more or less fury as circumstances demanded. It seemed to the Disraelian Parliament that existence would be impossible without its " Admiral ;" and now he quietly dies in obscurity, and in a newer House of Commons there is hardly one to recall his identity. Mr. Goschen would be more than human if he had not felt some special interest in the announce- ment of the death of Sir Robert Carden. The ex- chequerhas, since Mr. Goschen became its steward, had various windfalls in the way of death duty. The Senior Alderman of the City of London was re- puted to be one of its wealthiest members. Death duty upon at least a million sterling personality seemed a moderate computation, and Mr. Goschen, with Budget Day close at hand. may possibly have counted his chickens. The city has been shocked, wounded in its tenderest feelings, to find that one of its chief pillars has been removed, and at its foundation tkere has been found only a paltry £lOO,OOO. But this appearance of what is really aldermanic poverty is only illusory. Before he died Sir Robert Carden made over the bulk of his vast property to his son and heir Sir Frederick, thus de- livering the estate from the burden of death.duty. Through his long life, Sir Robert was an active and prominent supporter of the constitution. In his death he has struck the average, and the baffled State loses his expected contribution to its ex- chequer. The proceeding is not a new one. King Lear adopted it, though not with any eye upon es- caping taxation. But it is hoped that it will not spread among the Constitutional party, who as a rule have the fullest opportunity of swelling the death duties.

meadows and marshes to the river Weaver at Weston Point. At Ince Hall Wharf several barge loads of timber and other materials are being discharged, and a quantity of plant has been got on the ground from Ince statidn, about a mile away. A fine locomotive called "The Grange" is being removed from the station. On the land in the occupation of Mr. Astle, one of the English steam navvies is being put up. A 12-horse power saw mill is at work cutting up timber for various purposes, and men are busy felling timber and fences. Steam cranes and steam crabs are also at work, and more men have been put on than can be accommodated with lodgings, but a number of buildings are to be erected for their accommodation. IRLAM AND BARTON.

The ballast line at Irlam has been completed from the Cheshire Lines Railway Station to the banks of the Dwell. Satisfactory arrangements, it is said, have been made by. the Ship Canal Company for the acquirement of the land for the works at Barton, and in confirmation of this workmen have already begun to fell trees in Trafford Park, south-east of Barton Corn Mills, which are oppo- site Barton Locks. _ THE SALFORD SECTION. _ _

At the Salford end of the projected Ship Canal works ground has been broken in the extensive meadow which lies to the east of Trafford-road. Crossing the Trafford bridge from the Stretford-road side one comes to a long newly-built hoarding, shutting off the scene of operations from the gaze of the curious sightseer; and at the same time preventing the uninvited ingress of the throngs of. unemployed workmen who hourly present themselves, alas ! in the vain endeavour to obtain a day's labour. Passing the entrance gate and descending a steep bank the visitor finAls himself in the centre of a snow-clad ex- panse of loamy land, already encircled and intersected by at least a dozen lines of temporary railway. To his left is the Irwell, at present flowing uninterruptedly along its ancient filthy bed, and beyond it appear the trees of Sir Humphrey de Trafford's pleasaunce, and further yet the dome of the late Manchester Exhibition. To his right is the Manchester Racecourse, bordered by the colossal theatre in which Buffalo Bill is making his last appearance in England. The ground on which we are standing is that devoted to Dock No. 1, the largest of the series on the well-known plan, and already the steam navvy, or "devil," is hard at work, trenching out the loamy soil from the site of the coming basin and its ap- proaches, and feeding the busy trains of trucks which, drawn by a dozen or so of leconsotives, are con- stantly presenting themselves for fresh loads of earth and gravel. The navvy is scooping out earth to the depth of about 20 feet with as much facility as one scrapes out the inside of a Stilton cheese with a spoon. It is a superb piece of machinery, which seems quite capable of cutting a canal all by itself. The work al- ready done is highly suggestiie of the speed with which• the cutting operations can be carried on, and the large aggregation of men and machinery under the capable command of Mr. Knott have even now a good deal to show for their brief term of labour. Loop lines from the cutting point enable the busy locomotives to carry the dibris removed to the racecourse side of the meadow, where it is being piled up to form the ground-work of one of the most important quays of the Manchester series. A light railway is also in full work along the river bank on this side, by means of which the apparatus of cranes, wrenches, supplementary steam navidoes, and a vast quantity of rolling stock are being unshipped. On the opposite or southern side of the stream the ground is at present untouched, but the .widening process will take in a narrow slip of Sir Humphrey's bank, and a little lower down a curve in the river will have to be ob- literated. Work has not yet been commenced above Trafford Bridge, but ground will be broken at Throstle Nest with the opening of the coming season. The dock basin now being cut will be surrounded by enormous quays and jetties, and at its eastern end two magnificent locks will give admission to ocean-going vessels from the main canal.
OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
[FROM OUR OWN cortasseostmorr.l 23, Old Broad-street, B.C.

_ The uncertainty of the future, even for twenty-four hours is so great, that business on the Stock Exchange has become almost paralysed. Commencing badly,. on Monday, the markets have become worse from day to day, until at the time of writingthere is scarcely a single feature worthy of record. Ono rumour after, another, from the illness of the Crown Prince to the survival of the Paris bear operator Kalten Back, has tended to keep the prices down. _

Home nails have been specially affected by the bad traffic, and the speculative deferred stocks of the southern lines have been largely sold. Brighton A's and South Eastern Deferred are very depressed, and in view of the fortnightly settlement, which commences next Monday, there is little chance of improvement this side the account.

Americans, especially, are featureless, and it seems al- most hopeless to expect a rise in these stocks. Cana- dian lines are also depressed, and there is nothing to indicate any hcipe of improvement in that quarter. Hud- son Bay shares show improvement, and we shall not be surprised to see these go firmer again. We called atten- tion to this stock some time since and had the satisfac- tion of seeing our predictions verified, and we hazard an opinion again in favour of a rise. _ _

There have been some very heavy speculative dealings in copper shares during the past few days, and up to the time of writing the bears have had the best of it. It is reported that Kahen Back has once more returned to the scene of the exploits on the same line as before, and is becoming a heavy seller of Tintos. We can only caution investors against touching copper shares at all. In other mining securities there has been little activity. The prices show less decline in this market than in any other. All that is wanted to cause a rise is the public, but they will not come in during the present uncertain state of the market.

The feature of the week has been the success of the • Naval Construction and Armaments Company, Limited, which was issued by Messrs. Rothschild on Tuesday morning. The list opened at 10 o'clock and closed be- fore 12, by which time the capital had been subscribed four times over. By the following morning applications I were for twenty times the amount of the issue, and there can be no doubt that the very powerful board was sufficient to insure the success of this corn- I pany apart from the merits of the undertaking. On the other hand, one of the most ludicrous schemes recently offered the public is that of the Half-penny Letter Post Company, Limited, which undertakes to supply writing material and a penny stamp for a half- penny, and yet has the hardihood to assure the invest- ing public of a profit. Handicapped as the company is with a preliminary loss of 250 per cent., it requires a I very imaginative mind to anticipate such a scheme be- ing capable of earning the dividend. The promoters rely upon their profits from the advertisers, but evidently they have had no experience in this class of business or I they would not be so confident in such a scheme on the I chance of obtaining advertisements. I For the coming week investors would do well to be content with watching the course of markets, and with the exception of the company specified, and a careful 'selection of mining companies, there is little that presents any opportunity Loran early profit.

div.head: MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.) RUNCORN.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. (Continued from page 6.) RUNCORN.

Great progress is beiiiii-nte upon this section. In the magnitude and extent of the operations so far carried on, it is only rivalled by the more extensive works at East- ham. The depot at Norton is now a busy hive of indus- try, the offices, store-room, engine sheds, blacksmiths' shops, and other buildings being occupied by their res- pective tenants, who are kept in constant employ- ment. At the Big Field there are now three American navvies working merrily away, and five locomotives are required to remove the waggons as they are filled with soil. A cutting about twenty feet deep, and about a quarter of a mile in length, has now been made. The railway metals have also been extended to a point near the works of Wigg Bros. and Steele, at the Old Quay, and at this spot a number of labourers are engaged In excavating. An American Navvy will be fixed there in a few days. The soil which is now being thrown up is taken along the railway to the Big Field, and then across the bridge erected there by Messrs. Kirkham. The clay and soil is now being used to form one bank of the canal at Norton. At present there are about 700 men at work on this section.

div.head: GERMAN NAVVY.
div.p: THE GERMAN NAVVY.

The German navvy was introduced upon the Man- chester Ship Canal workings at Moore about a month ago, and was viewed with wonder by thousands of visi- tors to the neighbourhood. As is now well known, the principle of river dredging is applied to the excavation of land, and much curiosity exists as to whether the ponderous and uncazny-looking machine will fulfill the predictions of those interested in its success. When at work there is no doubt the navvy excavates with great expedition immense quantities of soil, but since the ma- chine was fixed at Moore it has not been in operation more than a few days. It has, unfortunately, broken down more than once, the last occasion being a week last Tuesday, and up to Thursday the make had not resumed its work of tearing up the ground. Mr. Walker made an inspection of the machine on Monday last, and perhaps he will be able to make suggestions that will lead to better results. That the navvy 39 admirably Suited to a soft, sandy soil there can be no question, but in a heavier or stiffer material its action is not so perfect. The machinery is of a very complicated character, and i when any impediment s met with, or the .mate- rial acted upon is not so yielding as usual, the strain upon the various parts is said to be very great. We understand that the navvy has been taken on approval, and the fact that it has not been rejected would seem to Show that it possesses merits which com- mend it to those most qualified to judge. The people of the locality may yet see it in constant operation. THELWALL AND LATCHFORD. The work in the direction of Thelwall is being carried on with undiminished vigour. During the week lines of metals have been laid down and already two handy- looking locomotives have been placed upon them. One of the locomotives is appropriately styled "Warrington," and the other bears the less familiar designation of " Caerwen." By the side of the road between Morris Brook farm and the ancient village of Thelwall the piles of timber and other material are being constantly aug- mented by fresh stock, and some wooden structures have been put up, including a small steam saw-mill. Away to the left, the hedges which formerly partitioned some of the fields have been completely removed, and in many cases their very roots eradicated from the ground. Several trees have likewise been cut down, and after having been operated upon at the saw mill, lie ready to be put to utilitarian purposes. The long ridge of spoil by the side of the intended channel of the canal daily as- sumes larger proportions. Across the river from Thel- wall the work: of excavating goes gaily on, and the embankment of soil is increasing so rapidly as almost to indicat4 that in a short time it will hide from view Wildegrave farm house, which stands near to the cutting. Communication is still kept up between the two badks of the river by means of a neatly-constructed raft, which is worked by ropes attached to pulleys on both banks of the river. It is stated that owing to some dissatisfaction, a number of men employed in removing the top soil have ceased to work, but it is expected that a settlement will soon be arrived at.

At Latchford Station there have been received during the week large consignments of machinery and other material, including another locomotive, which carries the title of " Moine." In consequence, those engaged on the special siding and at the wharf on the Runcorn and Latchford Canal, have been kept extremely busy in despatching the various consignments to their several destinations.

INCE, &c. During the past week a commencement has been made on the Ince section. About 200 men are working near Ince and Stanlow Point, land having been secured, and the centre line cut. On Stanlow Point, a narrow str:p of land which projects into the present bed of the Mersey for half a mile, and on which Stanlow House stands, a number of men are at work clearing away fences and trees, and preparing for the erection of various sheds and other buildings. From Stanlow Point to Ince, the Ship Canal will touch the foreshore of the Mersey, and strong embankments will be required. The river going close by is a deep stream, some 80 yards across. The canal is to cross this, and then through a portion of Ince Hall grounds, and:near the hall itself, which is owned by Captain Yates. The canal again skirts the shore, and comes right through the small light- house at Ince, where it again strikes inland through the

div.head: DAMAGE TO ROADS.
div.p: DAMAGE TO ROADS.

At the Birkenhead County Magistrates' Court, on Thursday, before Mr. Russell Lee and other magistrates, a summons was heard at the instance of the Wirral High- way Board against Mr. Walket, contractor for the Ship Canal, for payment of £BBB for damage aUeged to have been caused to roads in the Board's district by extraor- dinary traffic and excessive weight in connection with removing plant for the canal works from Hooton station to Eastbam.—For the prosecution it was argued that the roads were in good order and equal to the ordinary traffic of the district, which was agricultural and resi- dential, before the 28th October last, the date at which the extraordinary traffic commenced. Since that .date the amount claimed had been spent in keeping the roads in repair over the amount estimated at the beginning of the year to be spent on the roads.—Mr. Durandu, for the defendant, admitted liability to' a certain extent, but pleaded that the amount claimed was excessive, and that the roads had been inefficiently kept and ex- travagantly repaired. He called Mr. Donaldson, an engineer employed at the Ship Canal works, who had surveyed the road, and calculated that the work could have been done for £l9L—After a lengthened hearing the Bench gave judgment for the amount claimed, with costs.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT HOLLINS GREEN.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT HOLLINS GREEN.

A maw named Joseph-Willia—n7sT;rin—bel—o4; to Cadis- head, was working at the erection of a steam navvy at Hollins Green, on TUesday, when he accidently sustained an injury to his Mot. He was at once taken home in a conveyance and attended to. Fortunately the injury to the foot was not serious, and Williams will probably have recovered from the effects of the accident in the course of a few days. After having been sow months out of employment he had only a few days before ob- tained work in connection with the canal undertaking.
. BRUNNER, 3I9ND, AND CO., IJMTTED.

The half-yearly meeting of the shareholders of Messrs. Brunner, Mond, and Co., Limited, alkali manufacturers, Winnington, Northwich, was held at the Law Association R,oems, Liverpool. on Mon- day. Mr. John Crosfield presided, and amongst others present were—Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., Dr. Hewitt, Messrs. R Milner, C. S. Galloway, H. Cog- hill, J. P. Brunner. H. Brunner, C. M. Holland, James Handley, T. H. Forgan (secretary), &c, The Secretary read the notice convening the meeting, and the report of the directors was taken as read. It was at follows :—The balance sheet and profit and loss account, certified by the auditor, and now presented, show a balance to the credit of profit and loss account on the working of the half-year ended on the 31st December, 1887, of £89,111 19s 10d' which; with the amount of £35,544 Ds 9d, brought forward from the previous half- year, makes a total of £124,656 us 7d. The directors ' propose to deal, with the above balance as follows ;- 1 Dividend on the preference capital, at 7 per cent. per I annum, £11,043 4s 7d; dividend on the ordinary capital, 'at 25 per cent, per annum, £70,5; amount to be written off patent's account, £7,500; balance to be carried forward, £35,488 7s; total, £124,858 us 7d. The directors who retire by rotation are Mr. Charles J. Gal- loway and Dr. David Basil Hewitt, both of whom are eligible for re-election. The auditor retires, but is eligible for re-election.—Jomi CROSFIELD, chairman. The Chairman said the directors had much pleasure in presenting the balance sheet for the last half year, which they considered to be satisfactory, and he thought the sharehOlders would think the same. They had every i confidence that the success of the company n the future would be equal to what it had been in the past. (Ap- plause.) He moved the adoption of the report and statement of accounts, and that a dividend be paid to holders of preference shares at the rate of 7 per cent. per annum, and that a dividend at the rate of 25 per cent, per annum be paid to the holders of ordinary shares free of income tax.

Mr. H. Coghill seconded the resolution, which was unanimously carried. On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. H. Brunner, Mr. C. J. Galloway, of Thomey Holme, Knuts- ford, was re-elected a director of the company. The Chairman moved, and Mr. Holland seconded, that Dr. D. B. Hevkitt, of Winnington, be re-elected a director of the company.—Carried. Mr. Isherwood moved that Mr. T. W. Read, chartered accountant, Liverpool, be re-appointed auditor for the ensuing half year. Mr. Chalmers seconded the resolution, which was adopted. With a vote of thanks to Mr. Crosfield for presiding, the meeting ended.

At Newmarket, county Cork, on Thursday, the Rev. Father Kennedy, of Mediu, and eight others, were sen- tenced to two months' imprisonment for taking part in a proclaimed meeting. Hard labour was ordered in the case of all the defendants except Mr. Kennedy. An ap- peal is to be taken.

A Mao MunnEnan.—At Stratford, on Tuesday, a single woman named E. E. Ashton was remanded on the charge of having murdered her two children, aged respectively one and two years. The woman was in want, and she appears to have killed the children whilst in a state of temporary insanity. SKATING FATALITIES.—Two boys have been drowned at Allbrighton, near Wolverhampton, through the break- ing of the ice on a pool where they were sliding. Two young men, brothers, have lost their lives at Wellington, through venturing !3n a thinly-frozen pond. The less of three lives under similar circumstances, is reported from the neighbourhood of West Bromwich. CANADA AND THY FISHBRIES TRKATY.—The NOVO Scotia fishermen amt the people generally express satisfaction at the Fisheries Treaty as being an honourable settle- ment, ?whereby Canadian rights are all preserved. The. fishermen approve the provision granting American fisher- men free licenses for the purchase of bait in return for a free market for Canadian fish products in the United States.

THE Norrs SCANDAL.—The remarkable family affair at Bingham, which attracted some attention recently, came before the Grand Jury at the Notts Assizes on Thursday, when Miss Rayson was indicted for murder. Mr. Baron Pollock pointed out the weakness of tilt ease against the prisoner, who was too ill to have committed the violence to which the child found in her mother's garden had been subjected, and the Grand Jury threw out the bill, at the same time recommending that further investiga- tion should be made—a recommendation in which the learned Judge expressed his concurrence.
A pupil teacher named Dunlop dropped dead at Yeovil on Wednesday. He had been worrying about his exami- nation.

------- SHOT DAD.—At Thornham, near Rochdale, on Tues- day afternoon, Frederick Fitton, about five years old, was shot dead by a youth named Meanock. While at play in a stable, Meanock took up a gun which lay on a shelf, and pointing it at the child discharged it with fatal effect.

Munn=lN WALES.—A remarkable case is being tried at the Carmarthen Assizes. On a Saturday in November last, Thomas Davies, messenger at a tinplate works at Dafen, was murdered in a field on his way from a bank at Llanelly. Out of about £590 in gold and silver, which he had with him, he was robbed of £3OO, and his bag containing the rest was afterwards found in the field. The evidence against the prisoner David Rees, a tinplate worker, is for the most part of a circumstantial charac- ter. Two lads speak to seeing the prisoner looking through a hedge into the field at a time before the crime was committed and to his sending them away, and a boy of 11 testifies to actually seeing the prisoner and another man attack the deceased with an iron imple- ment, and after robbing him run away. Rees is said to have been hard up, and to have offered on the Wednes- day, before the murder to give a sovereign for the loan of £.5 till the Saturday. The case was adjourned.

GYMNASTIC TOURNAMENT AT WARRINGTON.

A gymnastic tournament by the members of the Liverpool Gymnasium, assisted by members of the Naval Brigade, was held on Monday evening in the Drill Hall, Warrington. The tournament was under the auspices of the National Physical Recreation Society, and was under the direction of Mr. A. Alexander, F.R.G.S., director of the Liverpool Gym- nasium, and its object was to promote the estab- lishment of a gymnasium in Warrington. There was a large attendance of spectators, amongst those present being the Dlayor (Alderman T. Sut- ton). The programme was introduced with "musical dumb-bell" exercise by members of the Liverpool Gymnasium, who acquitted themselves in a manner which evidenced a first-rate training. A performance.:on parallel ba.rs was the next item, and the feats of the gymnasts were much ap- plauded. The bayonet exercise of a number of the members of the Royal Naval Reserve, from the training ship Eagle, excited a good deal of interest among the spectators, as did also the subsequent cutlass drill. Among the other performances of the Liverpool Gymnasium members were high jumping, bar-bell exercises, horizontal bar, boxing, vaulting horse exercise, Indian club exercises, and running maze. Some sword feats by Mr. Alexander were much admired, and included the splitting of apples on a man's hand and neck, the cutting of a bar of lead, and the severing of a wooden roller poised on glasses filled with water without spilling any of the fluid, &c. There, was also a single-stick • and other contests between members of the Naval Reserve. Altogether, it was evident from the fre- quent applause that the tournament, so far as the entertaining of the spectators was concerned, had been a success. Towards the close, The liayon said that many of them would know why that tournament had been held there that night. From what, he could gather the intention was to ascertain to what .extent the promoters might rely upon the interest and support of the people of Warrington in the event of the establishment of a permanent gymnasium. His own opinion was that physical and manly exercises were fast taking a very important part in the education of this country, and .he thought it was being ascertained by those who are most competent to judge that in order to have a sound mind in a sound body it is necessary that mental education should be combined with a due propor- tion of physical exercise. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He hoped, therefore, that that idea might be fully car- ried out, and that they might induce Mr. Alexander to establish a gymnasium in Warrington, which would be a permament one and an advantage to the public. (Ap- plause.) In conclusion, the Mayor proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Alexander and to the young gentlemen who had come there voluntarily to give their service. (Applause.) Mr.F. MONKS, in secending the vote of thanks, said he hoped the performance they had seen that night might lead to the establishment of a gymnasium in Warring- ton. (Applause.) If he was to judge by the interest that was taken in football and other athletic sports in War- rington, he did not think they would lack any support, and, as far as he was personally concerned, he had al- ways taken a great interest in athletics, and should be glad to assist in the formation of a gymnasium in War- rington. (Applause.) Mr. Ausicasnica, who was received with applause, said he was there that night as the representative of the National Physical Recreation Society, which had for its object the promotion of gymnasia in those towns where nothing of the sort existed, and generally the pro- moting of athletic and healthful exercises. Hehad learned that there was no gymnasium in Warrington, and know- ing that the people there were an athletic loving people, he thought it his duty to come down there, and if they thought fit to establish a gymnasium he should be very glad to help them in an honorary way. (Applause.) If from any causes they were unable to take up the matter themselves, if he received sufficient promises of support from the leading men of Warrington, and especially from the young men, he should endeavour to establish a gym- nasium for them himself. (Applause.)

RAILWAY OFFICIALS IN TROUBLE.—The inquest was concluded on Wednesday in the case of the fatal colli- sion which occurred about a fortnight ago on the Hoy- lake Railway. It was shown that the staff system—this being a single line—had been departed from, and the jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against several of the officials, at the same time censuring the manage- ment of the railway generally. A CROWN CASE QI7ASHED.—In the Irish Court of Ex- chequer, on Wednesday, Chief Baron Palles and Mr. Jus- tice Andrews quashed an order of a, Crimes Act Court sentencing Mr. Walsh, proprietor of the "Wexford People," to two months' imprisonment for publishing reports of meetings of suppressed branches of the Na- tional League. Their Lordships held that the notice suppressing the branches in question had not been duly promulgated, and they gave costs against the Crown.

PRESCOT UNION.—The Guardians of this Union invite TENDERS for the erection of additional Day Rooms and Dormitories at the Union Workhouse, Whiston. Plans and specifications can be seen, and bills of quantities obtained, at the office of Mr. James Gandy, architect, Hall-street, St. Helens, on payment of one guinea. Sealed tenders, endorsed "Workhouse Extensions," to be sent to me not later than ten a.m. on Thursday, the 15th March next. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender. " S. H. HARTLEY, Union Clerk. Union Offices, Whiston, Prescet, 23rd February, 1888.

Sir William Harcourt is ill, but was a little better last evening. After the drawing room yesterday, the Queen went for ian hour's drive nan open carriage, despite the bitterly cold weather. FATAL BOATING ACCIDENT.—At the Cambridge Univer- sity Lent Races, on Friday afternoon, Mr. E. J. Camp- bell, of Clare' was killed on the spot by another boat running into him. The other races were stopped by the president. Mrranza ix IRELAND.—At Listowel, on Friday, two men named Moriarty and Hayes were charged with the murder of James Fitzmaurice at Lisnan on the 31st January. Miss Fitzmaurice positively identified the pri- soners, and both were committed for trial. • l• DONCASTER ELECTION.—TORY VICTORY. When the poll closed in the Doncaster division on Thursday night the ballot boxes were conveyed to Don- caster and deposited in the Guildhall, where the counting was commenced at ten o'clock on Friday morning. Only twelve clerks were employed in the Counting, and it was after noon before the result was known and announced, as follows : , Hon. H. W. Fitzwilliam (U) 5,634 Mr. I. S. Balfour (L) 5,423 Unionist majority 2ll At the last election the figures were—Mr. W. S. Shirley (L) 5,060; the Hon. H. W. Fitzwilliam (who was then described as a Conservative), 4,792; Liberal majority 268. In 1885 the poll was--Shirley (L), 5,680; Gathorne Hardy (C), 4,700; Liberal majority, 980. THE CROWN PRINCE. BERLIN, FRlDAY.—Professor Gerhardt has been sum- moned to San Remo. DEATH OF TWO ENGLISHMEN AT STANLEY FALLS. BRUSSELS, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—A Congo mail just to hand brings news that Captain Vaudeville and Lieu- tenant Warlsmont, who were sent out to co-operate with Tipo Tip in restoring order at Stanley Falls, both died on the way. LAST' NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock. The Earl of Chichester took the oath and his seat in succession to his father. The Pharmacy Acts Amend- ment Bill was read a second time, and a Select Com- mittee appointed to consider the provisions of the Truro Cathedral Bill. The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. QUESTIONS, BRADLAUGH gave notice that that day month he should bring forward his motion with respect to perpetual pensions.—The SOLICITOR-GENERAL for I axirrin, replying to Mr. Healy, said the General Prisons Board sanctioned Mr. Blunt wearing his private clothes, while attending the court at the late trial, but he declined the offer. When the member for South Gal- way (Mr. Sheehy) was brought up as a witness at Mr. Blunt's trial, at Portumna, the governor of the prison had not received authority to enable him to allow Mr. Sheehy the same privilege.— Replying to questions, Mr. W. Smug said the exigencies of Supply would prevent Monday being devoted to the ' motion Of Sir C. Russell on the subject of right of public meeting. Tim RULES OF PRocßounig.—Mr. W. H. Surrit moved that preference be given to the consideration of the Rules of Procedure whenever those rules were set down in the orders of the day.—Mr. GLADS'FONE, while promising support in shortening the discussion on Procedure Rules, thought it was unsatisfactory that the consideration of those rules should have preference over other important business. He expressed the hope that the consideration of Procedure Rules would not be carried on on party lines.—Mr. BRADLAUGH moved the insertion of words in the motion to prevent its having operation on Wednes- day. If the motion of the Government were carried, his hope of bringing on the second reading of the Oaths Bill would be lost.—After discussion, Mr. W. H. SMITH de- nied that there was any desire to take away the rights of private members.—Mr. Bradlaugh's proposal was re- jected by 249 to 150. Mr. Smith's motion was agreed to.—Mr. &arra then moved the first new rule, which re- lated to the sittings of the House, and provided that the House should meet at three, except on Wednesday, sit till eight, adjourn for an hour, resume at nine, and sit until one.—Mr. CHILDERS and other members thought that adjourning for an hour from eight eo nine a bad arrangement. The Government would not press that part of the rule. [LEFT SITTING.]
